"Would the gods might give

on Jurisprudence, which honored position he held for years, he- was
In the midst of his great usefulness.
On Friday evening, April 24, 1903, EDWARD MYERS PRESTON, Past
Graml Master of Masons Jn this Grand Jurisdiction, yielded to the
grim destroyer, Death. For some time he had combatted with a
brave hoo.rt against fate; but, yielding peacefully and calmly, he
sank to rest. Thie shock to us was like unto that of the falling on a
calm day of a mighty tree in the forest.
It- is the saddest duty, that one has to discharge, to pay tribute to
the memory of a dead brother, especially a true friend; but it is a
<luty which the living owe and which they have ever esteemed it a
privilege to perform, not according it as a right, for the dead demand
notbiing, bul bestowing it as simple reverence and devotion, the loo.sit
t.i1at one can do.
In the immediate shadow of death speech halts in sight of the
trembling hand, the weeping eye and the full hea.11t; but when thP.
clouds which alway!! return after the rain, are swept away, there
creeps into our ima.glnations-"Into the eye and prospect of our soul"an idea of the absent one; and to give expression to that idea, is th9
de~ire of every heaJrt.
Brolher Pres,t on was our twenty-ninth Grand Master, serving in
1895, and was tlu; eighteenth to pass the gates of Deatih.
The Grand Lodge was called in Special Communication, on April
26, 1903, in Nevada City, for fU!lleral services; and there, on that
peaceful Sunday afternoon, by the side of his wife, whom he so much
loved in lire, was laid to rest all that was mortal of our deceased
brother.
One o! Nature's noblemen, gentle, loving, kind and honest; an upl'ight ma.n. an able Masonic jurist-and a Mason tried and true.
What nobler epitaph could be written of any man? He loved his
God, his family, his country, and his brethren of the Mystic Tie. He
loved Masonry with a deathless devotion, and in his daily walks of
life and conversaition, illustrated the tenets we love; a living examplP.of the splendid v!rt.ues inculcated by Freemasonry.
Simple and unassUJID.ing, gentle and, most courteous to all, to have
known him, was to gather that inspiration that makes us all, -nobler
and better men. brothers.
·
He loved the right for rlght's sake; he believed in the fellowship
ol man, and found sweet rest in the brotherhood of man, under the
banners or Masonry. His life was more beautiful t h1a n cathedral or
t~mple, and WiU be in g<>od works more· lasting than iron or granite.

on rejected petitions. These latter have been ordered granted only

We m&de 1t our rule o! guidance to insist on the aBking for dispensation, immediately, if asked at all. The diSllensation should be

We want the non-affiliate to come in-not to keep him out. We

belong to some Lodge. We would therefore recommend legislaition
on this subject at this communication.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 13,

The Grand Secretary presented 'his Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows : .

.

'

To tlte M. •. W. '. Grand Lodge ofOaiifornia:In accordance with one of the provisions of the Constitution, the undersigned, for the thirteenth time, presents his report of those transactions of the
Grand Secretary's Office, during the year since the last Annual Communica~ion, which. may require action on the part of the Grand Lodge, or may be of
mterest to its officers or members.
On the 28t~ of December, 1902, two thousand two hundred and fifty copies
of the proceedmgs were printed and distributed, or reserved for future binding, in the customary manner, viz.: one copy to each of the present Grand
Officers ; one copy to each of the elective Past Grand Officers ; three copies to
each of the Grand Bodies, American and Foreign, with which we are in
correspondence ; one copy to each Inspector, and fonr copies to each of the
Lodges of our jurisdiction.
In accordance with a standing direction of the Grand Lodge, three hundred copies each of the proceedings of 1901 and 1902 have been bound together i~ the uniform style adopted from the commencement; the two years'
transactions form the twenty-fifth volume of the series which constitutes the
history of the Grand Lodge of California.
In obedience to an order of the Grand Lodge, at its last Annual Communication, the publication known as Anderson's Masonic Manual was purchased,
and, after a most careful revisal, a new edition was published and four copies
forwarded to each Lodge in the jurisdiction free of charge.
. A ~ew edition of the Constitution, embodying all amendments up to and
mcludmg the Annual Communication of 1902, has also been issued from this
o~ce~ copies of ~h~ch were transmitted to all the Lodges and Inspectors of
Districts of our Junsdiction.
The Li?rary of the Grand Lodge has been largely increased during the past
yea~, as will be seen from.the following list of additions to the proceedings of
vanous Grand Bodies in continuation of those already upon our shelves all
· bound in the uniform style heretofore adopted, viz.: Sixty-four volu'mes
proceedings of the Grand Lodges of the United States of America and Canada•

The following report has been received from Suisun Lodge, No. 55 :To THE MosT·WoRSHJPJ'UL GBAND MASTER, OFFICERS AND MEMBERS OF THE
GRAND LoooE oF FREE AND Acc&PTED MASONS or CALIJ'ORNIA.:GBEIITING-Suisun Lodg8, No. 55, Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California, begs herewith to offer its report to this Grand Body in
regard to the payment of the debt to Mr. James McCudden and a~y other
debt the said Lodge may have, and then proceed to disincorporate, as requested so to do by this Grand Lodge.
We are pleased to be able at this time to bring before this Grand Lodge
the following report, which we trust will be in accordance with the wishes of
the said Grand Lodge, and be acceptably received by them.
With and by the valuable assistance rendered us by the committee ap ·
pointed by the Grand Lodge in our behalf, "and we would especially mention
the name of Bro. W. Frank Pierce as one o( that committee who came to us
in the spirit of friendship and good will, and he also went to the representatives of Mr. James McCudden, and, by his able arguments to both, " a settle·
ment was made which is satisfactory to both parties.

1903.J

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

63

By the said settlement we have turned over to the heirs our splendid and
magnificent hall and what money we had on hand at the time of making the
settlement.
And also all other debts have been satisfactorily paid and discharged,
which leaves the corporation entirely free from debt and in a condition to be
disincorporated.
·
Accordingly all lawful steps have been taken as to court proceedin~, and
on the 15th day of June, 1903, the said corporation, known as Suisun Lodge,
No. 55, F. & A. M., through its attorney, Bro. Elmore M. Billings, of Benicia,
did present to the Superior Court of the County of Solano, State of California,
a petition asking for permission to diBBolve said corpora.tion, in accordance
with the wish of the said Grand Lodge.
A notice was given all the members of the said Suisun Lodge, No. 55,
that at the next stated meeting a resolution would be introduced to disincorporate the said corporation, and requesting their presence at said meeting
to vote upon the question; the result was a vote of about thirtei:n-fourteenths
of the membership in favor and not one vote against the proposition.
Therefore, in conformity to said resolution, and from the fact that due
notice of the time set for the hearing of the same and no opposition having
been filed, the Court did, on the said 15th day of June, make and enter its
decree, dissolving tht' said corporation, known as Suisun Lodge. No. 55,
F. and A. M., which, as we now think and wish, places the said Suisun
Lodge, No. 55, Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California, in
favor of the said Grand Lodge of the State of California, so far as we are
able so to do.
All of the foregoing is respectfully subinitted to your kind consideration
and approval by the 11aid Suisun Lodge, No. 55, Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California.
JAS. H. PRATHER,

Worshipful MaJJter.
The above report was adopted by the Lodge at the stated meeting of
August 8th, 1903, in its entirety, and ordered to be forwarded to the Grand
Lodge of the State of California.

In witness whereof, I hereunto set my hand and the seal ·of the Lodge,
this 8th day of Au!llls.t, 1903.
W. K. HOYT,
Secretary.

they are doing their Dest to make the institution what it is intended t:i lie, a
real home where aged Masone, their widows and orph&llll, may be cared for,
and sheltered from the gathering storms of the world.
The expense for maintaining the Home has been about a trifle under $18
for each inmate. This amount ie rather large, but we endeavor to give our
wards at the Home the beet of ev11rything. It will be, however, the desire
and duty of the Board of Trustees, during the next year, to inaugurate any
changes which will render this department more economical, a.e we must
endeavor to take care of many more inmates than we are now doing, without
any increase in the per capita tax.
The day will soon arriv.e when the number of inmates will, no matter how
economically affairs a.re managed, require our entire income for the 'mere
providing of food and clothing. It will then be a very serious question
whether we can care for all the indigent brethren, their widows and orphans,
in this Jurisdiction. There is only one solution poasible for this problem.
We must rely upon donations and bequests to enable us to carry on the good
work. It ie clear from bequests and donations a.lready·received during the
short life of the inetitution, that the charitable brethren will assist in caring
for the Home. As President of the Boa.rd of Trustees, and with' my office
in San Francisco, I am constantly receiVin& communications from lawyers,
both in the city and out of it, asking as to just what name should be given
the institution in order to leave money to it. Thia shows· an awakening
interest in the Home, and that many brethren are' providing for the future
by bequests in their wills and otherwise. In the meantime, the Ba.d of
Trustees will do ~hat it can by cutting down expenses to care for every
applicant.

It will be unnecessary to enter into further detail, as the report of the
Superintendent and the financial report annexed will give all informq,tion a.s
to the receipts and disbursements, as well as the internal management. The
Trustees again ask for the usual per capita. tax of $1.00 for the support of the
Home, and assure the brethren that they will do all in their power to cut
down expenses and keep the Home well within this amount.
The Siminoff Temple will be dedicated on Wednesday, and the Trustees
hope that every member of the Grand Lnd!fe will be present on that occasion.

t.ha We have had to contend, during this last year, with much more
In October, 1902, an epidemic of
D the usual amount of illness,

126

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 13,

_follicular tonsilitis broke out among the children, from which but few
escaped. In December two of the boys were seized with a mild form of
variola, and in that month also sixteen of our children were taken down
with symptoms indicative of diphtheritic sore throat. By the timely
use of antitoxin and other anti-diphtheritic measures, we were able to
abort every case. During January, many of the old people and some
of the children suffered from severe colds. Besides these attacks where
many were affected, there have been several grave individual cases. In .
October, Brother Starkweather was operated upon by Brother Dr. ·E. ·.R
Bryant, of San Francisco, who removed both inf~rjor turbinated b<!n!!S.
from the nose. This was done to improve the hearing. He made a good
recovery from the operation, but in November was attacked with
erysipelas, which confined him to his bed for several days. From this
also, however, he made a good recovery. In" December Mrs. Baxter
suffered a severe attack of la grippe. Another of our old lady i'esidenta, ·
Mrs. Bonham, is afflicted with abdominal dropsy; and frequent tapping
has been necessary. Some of our wards have met with painful accidents.
In November, Brother McGraw, while walking on the county road, was
struck by the hub of a passing cart, which threw him violently to the
ground. He sustained a concussion of the brain, and was confined to his
bed for four weeks, but made a fair recovery, considering his advanced
age. On the evening of January 6th, Brother Comins mistook the rear
stairway leading down from the old men's quarters for an open doorway,
and had a bad fall. Luckily he escaped with no more serious injury than
a very badly lacerated scalp. Many stitches were required to close the
wound; but he soon made an excellent recovery. On March 3d, one of
the boys, Fay Needles, eat his foot under a rear wheel of the bus, with
the result that all the bones in the small toe of his left foot were crushed
and had to be removed. With the exception of a few cases of chronic
infirmity among the old people, all of our wards are now in the enjoyment of good health.
.As has all along been our experience, many of the residents at the
Home take a deep personal interest in all that concerns it, and a good
deal has been done by such, to add to its improvements of a permanent
character as well as to accomplish the diurnal details of its effective
work.
The children continue to attend the public school at Decoto. Three
of the girls are now in the high school (at Centerville).. They are
taken to school and brought back in the surrey, which is driven by
Brother Richard Yates. The _other children walk to and from the ne;rer
school, except in rainy weather. From reports received from the
teachers, we learn that our children are doing well with their school
work and are making a creditable record both · for themselves and. for
the Home which they represent.

The Boys' Band continues to make good progress, although t he de-

Their excursions during the past year have been as fol-

lowl: On October 24, 1902, they played at a political meeting at Decoto,

128

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 13,

receiving twenty dollars for their work. On November 14th they went to
San Francisco and played at the celebration of the fiftieth anniversary
of California Commandery. On January 16th last they played at an
entertainment given by the Congregational Church at Niles. They
played also at the laying of the corner-stone of the new Siminoff Temple
at the Home on .April 22d. On May 30th they went to Oakland and
played at the Memorial Day exercises at Mountain View Cemetery. For
this they received twenty dollars above all expenses. On June 6th the
Band left the Home, in charge of Brother George Bennett, for a concert
tour of the central and northern part of the State. They received $350
for the time they were out. They played at twenty-one cities and towns,
and were everywhere royally welcomed and .entertained. We feel very
grateful to the Masons throughout their itinerary and to the ladies of
the Eastern Star for the interest they took in the boys and the many
courtesies and kindnesses ei...tended. On .August 19th the Band went to
San Francisco and played in the G. A. R. Parade. They received twenty
dollars for this, above expenses. On September 7th they went to Oakland and played in the Labor Day Parade, receiving like remuneration.
Much credit is due Brother John King for his untirini patience in teaching the boys~ Their success is his honor and his reward.
The Home has welcomed over a thousand visitors during the past
year. On .April 22d a large number of Masons flocked hither from all
parts of the State, the occasion being the laying of the corner-stone of
the new Siminoff Temple. The Grand Lodge was in attendance, M. W.
Grand Master Orrin S. Henderson officiating.
On the evening of May 23d Brother Samuel .Adelstein, a member of
Pacific Lodge of San Francisco, came out to the Home and entertained
the residents with selections on the mandolin.
We have been honored on several occasions by visits fro~ the M. W.
Grand Master Henderson. On .August 10th he paid his official visit to
the Home, inspected it throughout, · held friendly converse with the
wards of the Fraternity and made them a masterful address before lea"Ying. He has throughout the entire year manifested the liveliest interest in the Home and its welfare.
The members of the Board of Trustees have also frequently visited
the Home, and have at all times exerted themselves cheerfully and
promptly in the furtherance of its interests.
Our corps of servants remains the same as a year ago. .Additional
assistants would have been required, owing to the extraordinary amount
of illness at times prevalent at the Home, had it not been for the help
rendered by many of the Brethren, who volunteered to wait upon and to
sit up with the sick; services of which I am glad to make grateful
acknowledgment.

laundry plant at the present time, but to hire help from the Valley and
have laundered at the Home all the plain pieces. We hope by so doing
to reduce our laundry bill at least twenty-five per cent.

"I admonish our brethren to remember that the secrecy of the ballot must

Upon the conclusion of the routine bus~ess of Grandi Lodge, The
Right Worshipful Sir James Creed Meredith, Deputy Grand Master,
delivered his Annual Address.
The AddTess was a most interesting one and of more than passing
interest to American Masons. For Instance, In speaking of the one
hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the initiation of George Washington and Its observance by the Grana. Lodge of Pennsylvania, he
said:
"Many of the Officers of this Grand Lodge were invited to . be
pre11ent upon this occasion, and I much regret that none of our body
was able to attend the ceremony. · It was only this morning that J
received a volume-I have not had time to do more tlian glance at
It- which contains · a full account of the address delivered by our
Brother James M. Lamberton, a distinguished American Mason, upon
the occasion of the celebration to which I have referred. The wellknown organ of the Craft in Philadelphia, " 'The Keystone,' of the
8th November, Is a paper which I am quite sure, will be read with
interest by Masons far distant from Pennsylvania. It gives a very
full .and, I understand, a perfectly. accurate account. of that celebration.

1903.J

•

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

197

"The celebration was very interesting in many ways to '1S
Irish Masons, because I find-or rather the researches made for me
by my B.r other the Senior Grand Deacon-have shown that this
Grand Lodge had taken sympathetic note, In the year 1800, of the
Masonic career of George Washington. It Is recorded In the minutes
of this Grand Lodge, of the 5th June, 1800, that we received 'a
communication from the Grandi Lodge of Pennsylvania announcing
the death of their Grand Master, our B.r other George Washington,'
and upon the 7th August in the same year a resolution of condolence
with our American Brethern was adopted by this Grand Lodge, and
was duly forwarded to Pennsylvania. It Is of interest sometimes to
look back upon these records of the past, of more than a hundred
years ago, and to find that a man who played in his day such a very
Important part in the history of the world as George Washington did,
was himself one. who was bound to Masons by those ties by which
we are bound on to the other.
"~d It is Interesting, too, to know that upon the occasion of the
celebration of the hund·red and fiftieth anniversary of his Initiation,
the present President of the United States of America went to Pennsylvania to take part in that ceremony as a member of the Masonic
body, and to render his tribute to that Illustrious American citizen.
"From Illinois I have heard during the year more than once from
our dls~ngulshed Brother General John Corson Smith. Many of
you have met him upon those occasions, far too rare they are, when
he has come over here to visit the Irish Brethren. Many of you
have heard his genial speeches, and I am quite sure should he come
to us again next year, when he Intends. to visit England, that you
will receive him with a hearty welcome."
The address is a most interesting one and our only regret Is not
being able to spare the space to give it entire for the benefit of our
.American readers.
At the conclusion of the address Grand Lodge closed with the
satisfaction of having duly honored the Pat~on Saint of Freemasonry
St. John the Evangelist.

calling their attention to the absence of the loved ones who commenced the journey with them but had been overta.ken by the heat
and burden of the journey an1t' passed1to eternal rest. His tributes
to these" beloved Brethren are mod:eJs of mournful eloquence and will
be preserved! In the archives of the Grand Lodge of Kansas with
pride and satisfaction.
The Grand Master reports, with evident pride, that the growth of
Masonry in Kansas for the year just closed has exceeded that of
any former year, and• the conditions Improve as the years pass by.
He devotes a number of pages to the consideration of intemperance
and the legislation of many Grand Jurisdictions on the liquor question; he argues with earnest feeling in favor of individual In lieu
of Organized Charity and is in no sense an admirer of the Wisconsin
plan; he recounts with pride also the record and success of the
Home at Wichita. The general use of the miserable ciphers in so
many Jurisdictions excites his indignation and brings to his mind
that some general action on the increasing evil is necessary.
He makes an earnest appeal for the general recognition of St.
John the Baptist Day, by the Craft, and! its rational obs\)rvance by
the Lodges. The address is an interesting and instructive one and
we wish it could be read by all Masons but especially by the Masters
·
of our Lodges.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Past Grand Master Willj.am M. Shaver seems to be the handy man
of Masonry In Kansas; he does the official work of three of the
Grand Bodies, which in that growing, "strenuous," jurisdiction is
no sinecure, does duty as Grand Organist, blowing his own ·b ellows,
sings at funerals and puts in his spare time writing reports on correspondence and seems to be contented; for Instance in opening his
present report, he says: "If our effort to condense into a couple of
hundred pages the information glea·ned from fifty or sixty volumes,
aggregating several thousand pages, Is sufficiently appreciated to
secure examination from any considerable number of the progressive
:Masons of Kansas, we will be content." Brother Shaver you're a
Christian-In his conclusion he explains why we e-et left in his
present discourse. He says: "Our belated report of last year enabled us to clean up the entire year's work, but as this review, in
accordance with the custom of our Grand Lodge, must be in print
and ready for distribution at the Annual Communication, we- are
obliged to go to press before the proceedings of Arkansas, California,
· Colorado,. Georgia, Indian Territory, Montana, Nova Scotia;. New
Mexico, Texas, and W•est Virginia have reached our table. And yet
he has reviewed 45 American and 10 foreign jurisdictions In a report
of three hundred pages.

The Committee on Necrology presented a mournfully eloquent
report devoted to the memory of Brethern "at rest." The Committee,
Bro. Herman C. Duncan, Chairman, close their report with the
following deserved tribute to Bro. Josiah H. Drummond·:
"Josiah H. Drummond, our Representative near the Grand Lodge
of Maine, was one of the most profound Masonic students of this or
any age. Well equipped by a collegiate training and the study of the
civic law, he came in his youth to the Lodge. Zeal to search for truth
animating him, he rapidly obtained accurate knowledge of the
philosophic principles of the Fraternity, of its traditions and its laws,
and stood well prepared for the burd~ns of Masonic office. Very soon
he was called to place and station, and right well he filled them all.
Logical and keen of perception, he became an honored judge of disputed Issues,' and a counsellor frequently sought on all questions.
where sound advice was needed. For over a quarter of a century he
has been a writer of Masonic books, and in charge of the Foreign
Correspondence Reports of his Grand Lodge. A great pillar of the
Masonic Temple fell when he died, and we know of no one who can
fill his place. The Masons of Louisiana feel his loss as a personal
one, and join our tears with those of his more immediate Brethren as
they weep. Without exception all pay him honor, revere his memory
•
and deplore his loss.
"Your committee submit the following resolution, and ask its
adoption:

With a hearty and fraternal welcome to the old and new faces

Referring to the missing faces he paid the following tribute t o a

"The untiring Reaper has 1tgain been .at work in our Grand Lodge
and has called to his reward our,esteemed Brother, · Past Deputy
Grand Master Geor'ge L. McCahan, who passed away Wednesday
morning, July 30th, at Glyndon Park, Baltimore County, after an
1llness of nearly eleven months.

[Oot. 19;

. "During this long period of suffering he was cheerful and composed, at times sanguine of recovery, but ever resigned to the will
of God and at the close, when he fully realized his approaching dis"
solution, he expressed to .those about him assurance of that resignation.
"He was born in Frederick, Md., February 5th, 1838, and removed
to Baltimore with his ·parents when quite a boy. His father dying
soon after, the responsibility devolved upon him of aiding his mother
to raise and educate the other children, all younger than himself.·
Like all the duties of after life this service was rendered with
'scrupulous fidelity.
"Few men in Maryland have rendered as valuable service In
Freemasonry as Brother McCahan. He was made a Mason In
Union Lodge, No. 60, July 12th, 1860. After six terms as Worshipful
Master he served nineteen years as Treasurer. For nearly forty ·
years he has been a conspicuous figure in the Grand Lodge, serving
as Junior Grand Warden in l869-70 and as Deputy Grand Master
in 1885-6. He has freqttently served on various important Committees and has been a member of the Board of Managers ever since
Its organization in 1870.
"He organized our Masonic Veter!ln Association In :J,892 and con- .
tlnued Its P:i:esident till his death, maintaining a large correspondence with kindred! Associations throughout the country."
And noting the absence of the Veteran Bwther, the Chairman of

exceedingly that our Chairman of Correspondence, Brother E. T.

and forwarded to Brother Schul~ and his good lady. On 'your behalf I had the pleasure of sending him a memento of the regards of
his brethern of the Grand Lodge."

The twenty-seventh Annual Communication was held in the city
of Calgary, District of Alberta, June 11, 1902,-M.".W.".Bro. R. S.
Thornton, Grand Master; R.'.W.".James A. Ovas, Grand Secretary.
Forty-four Lodges were represented. Three Past Grand Masters
and fourteen representatives of other Grand Jurisdictions were in
attendance.
The Grandi Lodge was opened in Ample Form with prayer by the
Chaplain, Bro. J. Hinchliffe.
The Mayor of the city accompanied by the clerk, delivered an
address of welcome to the Brethren which was responded to by the
Grand Master.
The Grand Master then delivered his Address.
With a hearty welcome to the Brethren, he expressed on their
behalf, the thanks of Grand Lodge to the .All-Wise Providence for
His care and protection during the recess. He paid a glowing tribute
to the late Most Worshipful Brother, the Reverend Dean O'Meara,
whose virtues would be placed of record by a committee appointed
for that purpose who 'would report to Grand Lodge during the
session. But little business outside of the usual routine had been·
transacted and he closed his address in the following words:
" The year has been one of steady and quiet progress, with little
to record. Carlyle says: 'Happy the people whose annals are blank
In history books,' and a similar remark w!ll fittingly describe the
present condition of Masonry in this Grand Lodge jurisdiction. Our
present meeting at CaigB;ry, with the large representation of western
members, is a significant index of our growth. The territory which
we cover has entered on a period of unprecedented activity and de-°
velopment, and our institution is keeping pace with it, diffusing its
principles of Brotherly Lovi:, Relief and Truth."
Detailed reports were received from the District Deputy Grand
Masters of the twelve Masonic Districts, giving the conditions and
prospects of their respective districts. The dispensations of three
Lodges were continued for the coming year.
The report of the Committee on Fraternal Dead-R.'.W.'.Bro. R.
Hill Myers, Chairman, is an eloquent though mournful tribute to the
virtues and Masonic character of those exemplars of the Masonic
profession, our illustrious Brethern W!lllam McKinley and James
Dallas O'Meara.
The Grand Master elect named the appointed Grand omcers and
all were installed by M.'.W.'.Bro. Thomas Tweed, M.'.W.'.Bro: D.
J. Coggin acting as Master of Ceremonies.

seven Past Grand Deputies and twenty-seven Past Grand Wardens

The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form with prayer by
Wor. Reverend Charles A. Skinner, Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master proceeded to deliver the Annual Address.
Having served three years in the Grand East of this venera ble
Grand Lodge the Grand Master found much foodl for comment on
the continued progress and prosperity of the Craft in Massachusetts,
After an expression of his thanks to Grand Lodge for their confidence
and support during this, by their partiality, extended term and his
declination of farther service, In speaking of the present disturbance
of the Masonic peace prominently forced to the attention of the
Grand Lodges of Massachusetts and Ohio he cautioned the greatest
care on the part of examination committees and in the admission of
visitors upon the avouchment Of newly made Brethren, he added:
"I have dwelt on this matter at some length for another reason:
the State of Ohio had a few years ago the same unfortunate Cerneau
difference that has troubled• us during the past year. The matter
was taken to the civil courts there and the Grand Lodge was sustained, the demands for recognition being refused to the Cerneau
people. Without going into details, it is sufficient to state that a
~landesUne, unrecognized Grand Lodge, so-called, was formed by
those disappointed in their attempt to disobey the Constitutions of
their Grand , Lodge. This irregular Grand Lodge got out a civil
charter from the State of Ohio, as any three or four men can do for
any fraternal purpose; and although limited to the State of Ohio
in their un-Masonic work, they have the audacity to issue their
spurious authority to unprincipled men in Boston under our jurisdiction. I menUon these details only as an object lesson of what is and
must be the inevitable result of a divided responsiblllty, and disobedience of the highest law of any organization, and what dissensions might have arisen here had not our Grand Lodge acted as it
did. The action of our Grand Lodge in unanimously sustaining its
own Constitution and Regulations can thus be regarlled as having
sustained the wisdom and good judgment of the framers of our
legislation of twenty years ago. United and prosperous in our good
old Commonwealth, let us stand closer together to discountenance
all impostors and such as are not genuine Brethren."
He announced the death of Past Senior Grand Warden Cha~les
H. Norris and paid afl'ectionate tribute to. his memory.
H~ noted the Special Communications and the ,pu1pose for which
they were called.

been expressed? She Is counted among the galaxy of Sister Lodges

and Massachusetts,-Phlladelphia and Boston,-WllUam Penn and

have produced descendants who . meet as Masons in this presence and
around a common board, with Friendship, Morality and Brotherly .
Love."

Grand Master of Maso~s in Massachusetts, and invoked the blessing

Grand Master, rising from the Oriental Chair, made the ancient response: "May the Grand Architect of the Universe pour down His
blessings on this Society, and enable me to discharge the great trust
reposed in me, to the honor of His name and the royal art. And may
there never be wanting such to fill the Chair who shall promote
Masonry and the good ot"'"mankind, so long as the world endureth.
Amen."

At fifteen minutes after six o'clock p. m. the Craft were called
from labor to refreshment and proceeded to the Banquet Hall, where
the Feast of Saint John the Evangelist was celebrated in due and
ancient form, after the manner of Masons. The new Grand Master
presided at the Feast and at the close of a clever introductory
welcome said:
" Brethren, I wlll ask you to rise and join with me in honoring the
sentiments which lt is our custom to· propose at these festivals before
proceeding to the ordinary business of the evening. I propose to you
the first toast, To the memory of the holy Saints John; may their
examples be our guide and may we reverence their virtues.
(The toast Is drunk by all the Brethren, standing.)
" I propose to you the second sentiment, To the memory of our
Illustrious Brother, George Washington."
(The toast is drunk by all the Brethren, standing.)
" I propose to you the third sentiment, To the memory of our
departed Brethren who have passed on through the dark valley to
the home beyond.

Past Grand Master Frederic Speed sald:"Last year we were inconsolable because of our own great loss
ln the death of our best beloved, the great hearted and incomparable Power, and stood as it wer~, in the very presence of the
grim Messenger and could hear the very rustling of his garments.
To-day we bewail a world-wide loss In the departure of the greatest Mason of his age, to whom death came like a thunder-bolt from
a clear sky. In the morning, . to all appearances, Josiah Hayden
Drummond, not of Maine, not of the United States, but · of all the
Craft universal, was, In the full strength of a hale and hearty old
.age, which had impaired none of his mental and but little of his
physical vigor, but soon after noon, on the 25th day of October,
he was dead- gone, like a fiash of lightning- gone. And yet, not
wholly gone, for his influences and the efl'ects of a good example
survive him, and the work of his hands continues and is lmperlsha ble. The mightiest pillar of our mystic temple had fallen and
that which was material had ceased to be. His friends stood aghast
.and appalled as they beheld the ruin which could never again be
raised to ornament the mighty ·fabric and support the noble edifice
<>f Freemasonry. But now that the first rude shock is over and we
ean think cal~y and reason clearly, we know that It is better so, for
there was no wasting a way of the physical strength or decay of the
mental powers, none of the weakness of a long and· agonizing sickness, but simply the ending of a noble career; a passing out into

"To me, Brother Drummond's departure comes with a sense of
personal bereavement, for from earliest manhood and during aU my
Masonic career, I haCL known him, honored him, loved him, and
had felt and enjoyed his kind and genial nature. He had been to
me more than a friend in the ordinary sense. At the first Masonic
function I attended he presided, and ~he Impression of his greatness
and goodness received then never departed. For years we maintained a frequent personal correspondence; and his letters will be to
me an invaluable legacy, bearing witness to an unbroken friendship
which endured from youth to age.
"To Freemasonry he rendered for more than half a century,
services of the highest order and, to my mind, stood without a peer,
as the greatest exponent of its laws, usages and customs. Others
there have been, who have rendered invaluable services and died
mourned and esteemed· for their labors, but In his own chosen field
as a jurisprudent and enterpreter of the fundamental principles
upon which the superstructure of Masonry stands, he was without
a rival. For this service he was equipped with much and rare
learning and to it was added his indomitable industry. He was
great in all he undertook, but especially was he strong and unyield. ing in his defense of the ancient plan of Masonry and the designs
laid down upon the trestle-board by the fathers, and no one has
ever written more forcibly or clearly upon the history, growth and
development of the Masonic idea than he, and as the champion of
the ways of the fathers he was Invincible; and to say that he was
first amongst his equals, whenever and wherever there was service
In the cause of the Craft to be rendered, is not the extravagance of
eulogy, but simple and absolute justice to the greatest of American
Masons, yea the greatest of all Masons.
"I borrow the following biographical sketch, written by his
friend and my friend, Brother Stephen Berry, who had known

HJ03.J

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

229

Brother Drummond, · well and intimately, for more than forty
years:" 'He was born in Winslow, Maine, August 30, 1827. His father
was Clark Drummond, a descendant of Alexander Drummond, one
of a colony of Scotch-Irish Presbyterians ·who settled near the
mouth of the Kennebec River In 1729. His mother was a Cynthia
Blackwell, an estimable woman, from whom he inherited many of
his admirable traits. He was named · for Colonel Josiah Hayden,
the father of his paternal grandmother, who had been a Major in
the Revolutionary Army.
" 'Brother. Drummond graduated at Waterville College (now
Colby College, of which he was a trustee and president of the
board), in 1846. During his student days he taught school and was
principal of both China and· Vassalborough Academies. After
graduating, he pursued the study of the law until his admission to
the bar, when he went to California in 1850. After a brief stay
there, he returned to Waterville in l&il, and became successor to the
firm of Boutelle & Noyes, his late preceptors. He continued the
business with much success until 1860, when his growing reputation demanded a larger fiE>ld. He then opened an office In Portland,
where he continued to do a leading and prosperous business until
his death. He had held the position of Attorney-General of the
State, and City · Solicitor of Portland, and Solicitor for the Maine
Central and other railroads, as well as General Counsel of the Union
Mutual Life Insurance Company.
" 'Brother Drummond entered political life as a Democrat, but
in 1855 .assisted in organizing the Republican party in Maine, and
was always one of its most prominent leaders. He became a member of the House, and In 1857 was elected Speaker. In 1860 he was
elected to the Senate, but resigned before the end of his term to
take the post of Attorney-General,· to which he had just been elected.
To this position he was annually re-elected until 1864,_ when he
peremptorily declined, in order to devote himself entirel.v to his
increasing professional business. In 1868, however, he was again
Induced to accept the nomination and election as a Representative
in the State Legislature, and was again chosen . Speaker of that
body.
" 'Brother Drummond married Elzada Rollins Bean, a daughter
of Benjamin Wadleigh Bean, on December 10, 1850. They had four
children, three daughters and one son, to grace the family circle.
The son, named for his father, was his partner in business.
" 'Brother Drummond, although widely known in politics and the
law, became still more distinguished in Freemasonry, partly by

230

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 13,

reason of the eminent stations he has held at the head of the Sµpreme Council of the Northern Jurisdiction, the General Grand
Chapter, the General Grand Council, the Royal Order of Scotland,
as well as in all the Grand Bodies of the State of Maine, but still
more l_>y reason of his Masonic writings In every department of the
Order, which placed him as authority on all subjects of Masonic
Jurisprudence. His reports on Correspondence were eagerly sought
at home and abroad, and his Masonic Text-Book was everywhere
received as high authority. His various works In historical research
respecfing Masonry, are also held in high esteem by the Brotherhood.
·~·Brother Drummond was initiated in Waterville Lodge, Waterville, Maine, January 1, 1849, of which Lodge he continued a member. He was Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Masons of the
State of Maine, in 1860, '61; and '62, and became Chairman of the
Committee of Corresponde~ce in 1865, which post he continuously
filled until his death. He was Grand High Priest in 1866 and 1867,
and took the Correspondence in 1865, which he held until the end,
with the exception of 1873 and 1874, when he was at the head of the
General Grand Chapter. He was Grand Master of the Grand
Council In 1868, and took tl;le Correspondence of that body in 1865,
which he gave up to Brother Chase In 1895.
" 'He was Grand Commander of the Grand Commandery of
Maine in 1878 and 1879, and ·correspondent from 1865 to 1873,
Inclusive, when he resigned.
" 'In 1871 he was elected from the floor to the head of the
General Grand Chapter of the United States, and in"1880 was Grand
Master of the General Grand Council of the United States, holdin~
each oflice three years. It was largely due to his exertions that the
General Grand Council was formed, and he was deservedly selected
as its first Grand Master. ·
" 'Brother Drummond received the degrees of the Scottish Rite
in 1861 find 1862, and In the latter year was made a Thirty-Third.
He was Immediately elected Lieutenant-Grand Commander, was
re-elected in 1863 and again in 1866. In 1867, upon the union of the
Supreme Councils whlCh previously existed, he was elected Grand
Commander of the United Supreme Council, and was re-elected in
1870, 1873, and 1876, but declined further service In 1879. Throughout the trying days of the- Northern Supreme Council he was Its
leader, and under his able and wise administration the organization .
was triumphantly conducted to a condition of prosperity and power.
"'The funeral was at the ·old First Parish Church, Tuesday,
October 25th, and was largely attended by the Fraternity from all

over the State and abroad, as well as by the Cumberland Bar, and

" 'Maine has had many e~inent men in its Masonic ranks, but
no one so able and so widely known and admired as Brother Drummond. And, while he was so much esteemed abroad, the best test
of his character was the universal love and esteem In which he was
held at home by those who know him Intimately, as did all the
Masons of Maine. He was peculiarly kind and genial to all who
approached hini, and, as his first Impulse was to grant any aid or
assistance asked of him, he not only obliged a great number, but
convinced even those whom he was unable to serve that he strongly
regretted his Inability.
"'We have nau: many, arso, whose memories are cherlshedfor
· their goodness and eminent services, but no other who will be remembered so long and so fondly, not only by the present generation
who have listened to him in Grand Lodge, but by the coming generations, who will refer to his decisions and discussions of Masonic law,
and observe how he not only filled the places of the eminent lawgivers who bad preceded him, but had far exceeded them In ability;
and not long, but more fondly, by his old associates who have faithfully followed and loved him, and who will miss his kindly greeting
and cheerful companionship, and who will find none to fill his
place.'"

"Oh blessed hope, which we believe will end 1n fruition. That.
somewhere we shall cease our mournings and lamentations for the
qead, and our skies be no longer overcast with clouds, and tp°e sun
shall shine forth in the perfect day . . Here, alas, we no sooner put
oft the habiliments of mourning ere we are again alarmed at the
approach of the messenger of death, who comes stalking out of the
dai:kness and seizes our best beloved and carries them through the .
door between the seen and the unseen and leaves but a memory,
precious and dear, and so forever after there ls a void In our lives. ·
We yearn with exquisite pain for those we love and have lost, and
would fain follow them into the shadows and bring them back Into
the light and sunshine of our lives, !lS if we ourselves were immortal
and not destined to go to them and not they come to us. We cannot
look upon the face!! of dead friends and philosophize; reason is
staggered, and the senses confounded. Bewildered by the awful
enigma of death, we stand in his presence as helpless as little children, and the stoutest quail beneath his dl'ead stroke and draw back,
as If it were possible to fiee from the awful shadow, which Is always
pursuing us.
"We never come up to this General Assembly of .the Craft, but
our pleasure at clasping the hands of the living is shocked by the
cold hands of the dead, which are extended to us. Must it ever be
so? Must there always be sobs Intermingled with our laughter?

"It Is my sad duty to report that In the list of the missing ones
are the names of R.'.W.'. Bros. P. P. Ellis, District Deputy Grand
Master of the Twenty-sixth District, and A. J. Coleman, District
Deputy Grand Master of the Nineteenth District, whom God· In His
Infinite wisdom has seen fit to remove from us. These brethren
have endeared themselves to the Fraternity by long and faithful
service, and will be greatly missed, not only by the brethren of
their districts, but also at the Annual Communications of this Grand
Lodge. Due referencE\ to these Illustrious brethren will be made
by the Obituary Committee."

The Grand Lodge of Montana held three Special Communications
during the recess.
•
The first at Helena, October 20, 1901, for the purpose of placing
the corner-stone of the First Unitarian Churcl;l.
The second at Butte, October 29th, to place the corner-stone of
the new Masonic Temple, and the
Third at Great Falls to place the corner-stone of the Cascade
County Court House. The ceremonies were performed in accordance with the time-honored usages of the Craft.
The thirty-eighth Annual .Communication was held in the City
of Butte, September 17, 1902, in the new Masonic Temple recently
erected in that city,-M:.w:. George T. Slack, Grand Master; ·
R:.w:. Cornelius Hedges, Grand Secretary. Forty-eight Lodges
were represented, together with twenty-six other Grand Jurisdictions. All the Grand Offi~ers, with ten Past Grand Masters, were
In attendance.
A portrait of Grand Master Slack appears on the opening page.
The Grani;l Lodge was opened in Ample Forin with prayer by
R:.w:. F. B. Lewis, Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master appointed the several committees and proceeded to deliver his Address.
He said, "Let us give thanks to the Grand Architect of the
Universe for his goodness in protecting and providing for us during
the past year."
With a glowing tribute to the principles and purposes of Freemasonry he passed to the consideration of the business transacted
during the recess. The corner-stones of four public buildings had
been placed. A Dispensation had been granted for ~he for_m ation
of a new Lodge at Malta.
.
The decisions reported were governed by the laws of the Juris- .
diction. He visited several Constituent Lodges, but was prevented
by business reasons from visiting all.
The R. · .W. ·. Junior Grand Warden reported his official visitations of the several Lodges located In that part of the State in
which he resided.

prosperity emphasized strongly by a net ~ain in membership in the

Hosmer, the all-round Mason whose reputation needs no avouch. ment in the three Jurisdictions of Ohio, Montana, and California.
A fine chemi-litho-gravure of the new Masonic Temple at Butte
is a feature in this number of the Journal.

suitable pages be set apa_rt in the Journal devoted to the memories

.
Grand Lodge decided on placing of the lesser lights near _the
Altar that all three should be placed on the south side of the Altar
so th~t one will be at either end and the third placed so as to form

.

tender mercies of M.'.W.'. Bro. Wheeler and he proceeds to look

We wish the · committee to understand thoroughly our amendment to Regulation 11, concerning Physicial Qualifications. That
regulation as amended now reads, "The person who desires to be
made a Mason must be a man; no woman nor eunuch; free born,
being neither a slave nor the son· of a bond woman; a believer in
God and a future e.:dstenc~; of moral conduct; capable of reading
and writing; having no maim or defect in his body that may render .
him incapable of learning the art, and physically able to conform
literally to what the several degrees respectively require .of him."
The only change in the regulation was to strike out the words
neither "deformed or dismembered," which would seem to have been
placed in the original only to be violated and disregarded; for the
loss of a toe would be a dismemberment and many features, out of
sight and of less consideration, might, under the microscope, be
termed a ~formity.
We think the amendment consistent and in no particular a weakning or compromise of ·the landmark requirements in regard to
physicial qualifications. We salute the new Nebraska firm of correspondents and wish them abundant success.

NEW MEXICO.
21 Lodges
1133 Master Masons.
The Grand Lodge of New Mexico held its Twenty-fifth Annual
Communication in the Oity of Santa Fe, October 20, 1902,-M:. W.·.
.Arthur H. Harllee, Grand Master; R. ·• W:. Aipheus A. Keen, Grand
Secretary. Seventeen Lodges were represented, together with fifteen
other Grand Jurisdictions. Six Past Grand Masters and four Past
Grand Wardens were present.
Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with prayer by the Grand·
Chaplain, and proclamation was made thereof by the Grand Marshal.
The Grand Master announced the committees and proceeded to deliver his Address.
He extended a hearty welcome and a brother's greeting to the
brethren who had come up to attend the Twenty-fifth Anniversary of
the life of the Grand Lodge of New Mexico. After a brief reference
'to the history of the Grand Lodge and its present standing, he directed
the attention of the brethren to those who, with them for years in
sunshine and storm, had passed to rest, quoting the appropriate poem
of Bro. Albert Pike:

•

To the past go more dead faces,
Every year;
As the loved leave vacant places,
Every year;
Everywhere the sad eyes greet us,
In the evening's dusk they greet us,
And to come to them entreat us,
Every year.
He read the names from the death roll, and said, "Let us pause and
with bowed heads reverently pray to their memory. Let us also
bow in reverence with our brethren of other Grand Jurisdictions who
have sustained the loss of distinguished members during the pa.st year,
and who are now at rest."

•

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

249

Referring to Mexican Masonry, or Masonry in Mexico, he submits
his conclusions of the situation:
"Brother Seamon has also kindly submitted to me a copy of a
report which he will file at this time upon the subject of Mexican
11\(asonry, being one of a series of valuable contributions by him upon
this subject. It is not only a matter of concern to us, by reason of our
rproximity and business relations with Mexico, that we be informed
from time to time upon a subject so volatile as Masonry in our sister
Republic, but other jurisdictions as well cannot but appreciate en[ilightenment from such a source. I think it will be conceded that no
one is better qualified to speak intelligently upon such a subject than
Brother Seamon, by reason of the breadth of his views, his powers
of research, his contract with the people of our sister Republic, and his
fhorough familiarity with the genius of its people. I deem comment
upon -said report unnecessary further than to say that it seems to me
that Brother Seamon ha.s offered seasonable s.uggestion for the bringing of harmony and rinity out of the chaotic condition now existing
in Mexico as regards Masonry. I am persuaded that the suggestions
froposed by Brother Seamon o!l'er not only a natural .aolu.tion of existing difficulties, but one in its nature entirely feasible, the same being
a question, however, over which we have no control.
"In view of the existing conditions, I have to recommend that this
Grand Lodge take no further steps looking to the recognition of any
of the various Masonic bodies in Mexico. .A'ny such step, ln my opinion,
Would tend merely to complicate the situation and defer the solution
of existing difficulties."
•

REl'oBT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Bro. W. H. Seamon, as Chairman of Correspondence, reviews the
doings of the Grand Lodge of California in ita Fifty-second .Annual,
being the administration of Grand Master Foshay. He is favorably
impressed with the Grand Master's opinions and rulings, except in
this :-Grand Master Foshay says: "The Master of a Lodge has the
right to refuse a committee to a person applying to visit his Lodge,
if such person cannot furnish receipt for dues or other documentacy
evidence to show that he is in good standing and is a Mason. The
Master possesses the power of determining who shall visit his Lodg!I
or sit therein." The answer of the Grand Master referred to a person
of doubtful standing, and the remedy suggested by Bro. ·S eamon of
"branding with a mark under the seal of the Lodge" has no application.
We of California believe that the Master of a Lodge has absolute
control within his Lodge. None may enter without his perm~ssion,
and he may refuse admission to any at his discretion.
When you question the power of a Master of a Lodge of Freemasons,
you are picking holes in the foundation.

The Grand Lodge was opened in .Ample Form at the September
Quarterly.
The Grand Master,. reporting his official acts and the evidence of
progress in the Juris~iction, in his Address he referred to the crime
against humanity, the assassination of the good President. He said: .
".Animated by such feelings, I ask you to authorize me to transmit,
in the name of his brother Freemasons in New South Wales, the assurance of our heartfelt grief at the sufferings of President McKinley
of the United States of .America, coupled with a hope that the Great·
Architect of the Universe may spare his life, and prolong it for many
years among the people to whose service it has been devoted."
The proposals of the Grand Master were unanimously approved,
all the brethren standing to order.
The Grand Master .stated that he would cable the purport of their
vote to .America; but he also requested the Representatives of Sister
Grand Lodges there to ·forward copies of it in due course to their
respective Grand Secretaries.
The business considered was mostly routine, and Grand Lodge
closed at 9:15 P. H. ·
The Quarterly of Deecember 11th was held in the same place, the
M:. W. ·. J. C. Remington presiding. There was the usual good
attendance.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, and the Grand
Master proceeded to deliver his .Address, mostly devoted to a
"dissension" between Cambrian Lodge and the Grand Lodge of England,
in which we have no interest.
In closing his .Address, he said to the brethren:
"It now only remains for me to congratulate you upon the pros·
perous condition of our Grand Lodge at the end of the first year of
the Twentieth Century. In an experience of over thirty years in the
Craft, I do not remember a time when it was more happy, harmonious,
and progressive than it is to-day in this Territory. Happy is the
Grand Master who meets with such loyal and enthusiastic support."
On the nomination of the M.·. W.·. Grand Master of Maine,' I
have issued a Grand Representative's Commission to R:. W.-. Bro.
James E. Parsons, of that Grand Lodge, to represent New South
Wales.

and money for the good of the Craft ought to be generally appreciated.

REPORT ON CoRRESPONDENCE.

Bro. Herbert S. Thompson, Chairman of this Committee, submits a
review of our proceedings for the Fifty-second Annual, the administra·
tion of Grand Master Foshay. The Grand Master's Address is quoted

The Grand Master sounds a note of warning to careless members of
the Craft, reminding them of neglected duties to the great injury of
the Fraternity. We quote his words:
"I cannot permit the occasion to pass without calling the atten·
tion Of all Lodges to the laxity apparent in the investigation of ' ca.ndidates for the degrees in Masonry; It is popular to be a Freemason and
it is natural that every profane or questionable reputation should desire
membership• with us. The time has come when drastic measures must
be adopted, and I submit, harsh as it may appear, that a brother proposing a candidate for the degrees in Masonry should be held responsible for the worthiness of that candidate. If such responsibility ho.d
heretofore been placed upon the proposer of a candidate, the. disgrace
brought upon the Craft in the recent past would have been impossible."

• The Grand Master, in response to an inquiry, said: "I deprecate
the use of Masonic clothing outside the Lodge rooms on any occasion
other than the laying of foundation stones. I do not see how we can
a.void its use on such occasions, as we a.re then combining operative with
speculative Masonry. I go further, and say that where any brother
has, in dying, made a request that he should be buried Masonically,
the proper clothing on such occasions is nothing more than a pure
white a.pron for every brother."
We think the reply of the Grand Master an appropriate one, and
can only produce the best results in these days of fuRs and feathers.

The Grand Lodge of North Carolina held its One Hundred and Fifteenth Annual Communication in the city of Raleigh, January 13, 1903,
-M:. W:. H. I. Clark, Grand Master; R:. W:. John C. Drewry,
Grand Secretary. Two hundred and sixty-eight Lodges were represented, together with the Representatives of twenty other Grand Jur·
isdictio~s. Eight Past Grand Master.a, a Past Junior Grand Warden
and two Past Grand Secretaries were in attendance.
The portrait of W •·• A. A. Marshall, D. D., Grand Chaplain, who '·
died in office, appear& on the opening page.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form at 7:30 P. M. and the
Grand Master delivered hi! .Address.
Extending a hearty greeting to the brethren, he referred to the
• rapid passage of time and its inevitable changes, marking with joy or
grief our lives as individuals. For the many blessings we have received,
he eaid: "Let us render thanks to the Most High God, who doeth all
things well, but before proceeding to consider the matters that have
brought us together, let us pay the tribute of silent prayer to' those
who have passed to rest." .And he added~
·
"While old friends are greeting .each other with. a hearty handshake
and welcoming the new faces with a bright fraternal smile, yet there is

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

261

a tinge of sadness pervading our meeting and all is not joy. For since
our last meeting in this room the brother who so charmingly enter·
tained us as Grand Orator, by giving his sublime conception °as to
'What is Masonry,' has been called to the Celestial Lodge above. His
life-work has been tested by the square of the Great Overseer, and he
is at rest. The soul of Grand Chaplain Marshall left its earthly tabernacle as the sun was setting behind our western hills, on God's own
day, Sunday, and on wings invisible soared aloft to join the noble band
who preceded him. .An eloquent preacher, a loving, father, a devoted
husband, a good man, the world was better by his having been in it.
The last words I ever heard him utter should be an inspiration to us all:
" 'Mason, may the eagle flight ever be thine,
Onward and upward, true to the line.'
"His remains were laid to rest on the following day under the
auspices of the Grand Lodge, Past Grand Master Nichols officiating."
In speaking under the head of the Fraternal Dead, while mourning
the loss of one hundred a.nd ninety-six of their own·kindred and brethren, members of .their Constitutional Lodges, he referred in sympathy
with Sister Jurisdictions to the many eminent brethren mourned by the
whole Fraternity. He said:
"The loss of these brethren, illustrious as they were in their own
Jurisdictions, was keenly felt, but when the dread su=ons was issued
for the Senior Grand Master of Maine, one of the brightest lights in our
Masonic world faded out."

He ext;nded to all a cordial and fraternal greeting and congratulated them upon the results of a prosperous year. Under the head of
Necrology, he said:
"The official cirCle of our own Grand Lodge remains unbroken, but
elsewhere among our Sister Jurisdictions the shadow of the wings of
the Death Angel ha.a fallen with crushing weight and many of the
ablest and most illustrious members of the Craft have passed to rest.
"Among our own Constituent Lodges forty-eight of the members
have died during the year, and, with the fraternal ministrations of
their brethren, have been consigned to that narrow house which awaits
us all. I append a detailed. list herewith. Let us not forget the widows
and orphans who are left without a husband's and father' s care and
companionship, but dedicate ourselves anew to the alleviation of their
sorrows and of the increased hardness of their lot in life. Finally, let
this subject soften our own pride, increase our charity and sympathy
towards all mankind, make us remindful of the evanescent character
of all human ambitions .and enable us to meet with cheerful equanimity
our own rapidly approaching dissolution, for-

The Grand Lodge of Oregon held its Fifty-third Annual Communica·
tion in the city of Portland, June 10, 1903,-M.·. W.-. William F.
Butcher, Grand Master; R.-. W.·. James F. Robinson, Grand Secretary.
Ninety-six Lodges were represented. Seventeen Past Grand Masters, two
Past Grand Wardens and a Past Grand Secretary were in attendnnce.
Forty other Grand Lodge Jurisdictions were represented.
A handsopie portrait of Grand Master Butcher appears on the open·
ing page.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, after prayer by t'.oe
Wor. and Rev. J. R. N. Bell, Grand Chaplain.
The Representatives of other Grand Jurisdictions were received and
welcomed by the Grand Master.
The Grand Master then delivered the Annual Address.
A cordial welcome to members and congratulations on the progress
and prosperity of the Jurisdiction and a few words pertaining to the
precepts and principles of the Fraternity-and he alluded to the subject
never absent or strange, the passing to rest of kindred and brethren.
He reported the death roll of the year upon which was inscribed the
names of ninety brethren, members of the Constituent Lodges, and
among them many faithful and prominent workers in the Masonic
Vineyard.
The official circle of Grand Lodge was represented in the death
column by the R.·. M :. F. H. Alliston, Grand Treasurer, taken in the
prime of life before reaching the high twelve of his manhood. His loss
was marked and sorrowfully impressed upon the Fraternity in Oregon.

The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form.
The R:. W .-. Bro. J. B. Tresidder presented his credentials and was
received and welcomed as the Representative of the Grand Lodg of Maine.
The Grand Master then proceeded ·to deliver his Address.
While giving the brethren assembled in Grand Lodge a hearty wel- ·
come, he could not but notice the vacant seats and the missing brethren
who were present at the last .Annual. The records bore testimony that
fifty-one of their own tribes and families had passed to rest. .Among
these were the well-known Right Worshipful Brethren James .Addie
and William Patterson.
In speaking of the brethren of Sister Jurisdictions, he said:
"Our Grand Lodge has been further bereaved in the loss of M.-. W :.
Bro. Josiah Drummond of Portland, Maine, one of the most distinguished Masons of his own or any other age. No more eminent Masonic
jurist than Bro. Drummond ever live,d. He was Chairman of the Committee of Foreign Correspondence Of the Grand Lodge of Maine, and
was recognized by all his confreres of the Masonic corps reportorial,
as a most wise and Excellent Master among them. From almost the
formation· of this Grand Lodge Bro. Drwµmond represented it with conspicuous aiility near the Grand Lodge of Maine."
Speaking of the condition of the Craft, he said:
"Harmony and peace have generaly prevailed throughout the Jurisdiction during the last year. It is because the causes of dissention
among us are so few, and the exceptions. to the general rule so rare,
that they stand out so conspicuously whenever they do occur, against the
clear, bright background of harmony and brotherly love."
We think the illegitimate concerns like the .Ancient Landmark, mentioned herewith,' will get small comfort in the pominion. He says:
"Notice having been received from the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts of the establishment within its Jurisdiction of an illegitimate
. body, calling itself '.Ancie~t Landmark Lodge, No. 1,' age.inst the mem·
bers of which the brethren of our Sister Jurisdiction have been duly
warned, and it having been further stated that some of the parties_concerned threatened to institute a so:called Lodge in this Province, I
caused a circular to be issued to all the Lodges of our obedience, warning them against any Masonic intercourse with members of the illegitimate body. .A copy of this circular is appended to this address."

SCOTLAND.
The Grand Lodge of Scotland held Quarterly Communication in
Freemasons' Hall, City of Edinburgh, on the 7th of August and the
6th day of November, 1902,-M.·. W :. James Hozier, Grand Master
Mason; Brother J . D. G. Dalrymple, Acting Grand Master on the Throne;
Brother David Reid, Grand Secretary. There was a full attendance of
Grand Officers, Past Grand Officers and visitors at the Quarterly of
August 7th.
Grand Lodge was opened in Full Form, and with solemn prayer,
after which the Acting Grand Master said :-Brethren, my first duty
is to express my great regret that I find myself in this position in
consequence of the absence of our very much respected Grand Master.
This is the :first occasion on which the Grand Master has failed to
attend a Quarterly Communication during the three years of his
reign, and it is only in consequence of the serious illness of Lady
Mary Hozier, who has, he mentions in a letter, in consequence of
a severe chill, been confined to her bed for several days, that he
has been prevented from coming ·to this meeting. I am sure we all
regret very. much his absence, and sympathize with him in the cause
for it, and all hope that Lady Mary may soon be completely restored
to health.
Grand Lodge resolved to recogiilze and exchange representatives with
the Grand Lodge of Costa Rica.
Referring to the approaching Coronation of the King, the Acting
Grand Master said:-! am sure, brethren, that we are all gratified
that the ~loud which recently hung over the country has been lifted,
and that His Majesty the King has regained so much of his wonted
health, as to go through the trying ceremony of the Coronation on
Saturday. I have, on behalf of the Most Worshipful the Grand
Master, to ask you to grant authority to him and to the Grand Secre·
tary to draw up and present a further address to the King and Queen,
congratulating the King on his restoration to health, and both their
Majesties on their Coronation.
This was unanimously agreed to.

GB.AND LoDGEB OF DENMARK: AND HAMBURG.
The Committee resumed consideration of the application of the
Grand Lodge of Denmark to declare as illegal and irregular the
Lodge Christian Zum Palmbaum, which was erected by the Grand
Lodge of Hamburg at Copenhagen, and no satisfactory replies haying been received from the Grand Lodge of Hamburg in answer to the
recent letters from this Grand Lodge to it on the subject, on the
motion of Brother William Officer, seconded by Brother Alexander
Bruce, the Committee recommended Grand Lodge to pass the following resolutions, viz:- ( 1) "That a Body calling itself 'Lodge
Uhristian Zum Palmbaum' or 'Lodge Christian til Palmatrmat,' and
meeting in Copenhagen, having been declared illegal and irregular
by the Grand Lodge of Denmark, all Masons under the Grand Lodge
of Scotland are hereby warned that they cannot visit such irregular
Body, nor can any Lodge under this Jurisdiction admit as a visitor,
or affiliating member, any member of such irregular Body, without
respectively incurring the penalty attaching to a grave Masonic offense."
And (2) "That a copy of the foregoing resolution be transmitted to
each Grand Lodge ' with which this Grand Lodge is in communication,
and to .t he Right Worshipful Masters of all Lodges holding under the
Grand Lodge of Scotland; each such Right Worshipful Master being
hereby instructed to cause these resolutions to be read at the first
meeting of his Lodge after the receipt thereof, and to direct that
they shall be entered on the Minutes."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

The books of the Grand Secretary show that returns have been received
from every subordinate Lodge, and that all dues have been paid in full, and
while this is no new condition in this jurisdiction it demonstrates the con·
tinned zeal of the membership and the sound financial condition of the Lodges,
The returns made this year show no improvement over those of 1902, in
fa.ct the number of Lodges marked perfect are the same as last year, viz.: 224.
The number of Lodges whose returns were required to be sent back for cor·
rection has increased from 31 in 1902 to 33 in 1903, and the number of Lodges
whos11 returns were transmitted later than the time required by the Consti·
tution has increased from 16 in 1902 to 20 in 1!}03. The number of Lodges
which were not transmitted within the required time and which had to be
returned for correction was 7, which is the same number as in 1902. From
the above showing we would again urge upon ·the Masters and Secretaries the
importance of sending the returns of their Lodges within the time prescribed
by tbe Constitution, the correct spelling of names and the transmittal of the
proper amount of dues. A little extra ca.re and diligence upon the part of
the Secretaries who have been delinquent would remove the cause for criticism,
a.nd would greatly facilitate the work of the Grand Secretary's office.
We recommend that the. Grand Secretary notify the Inspectors when he
·ha.a forward:d blanks to the various Lodges, and tha.t it shall become the duty
of each Inspector when so notified to advise and urge the Masters a.nd Secre·
taries in his District to comply strictly with the law and the instructions
of the Grand Secretary.
Your committee finds tha.t the returns and reports a.re properly preserved,
and that their contents a~e conveniently and handsomely tabula.tad and
recorded in the books of the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Secretary and hie Assistant have earned the thanks and appreciation of this conimittee for their efforts in presenting in a. concise and avail·
a.ble manner the facts and statistics necessary for this report.
All which is respectfully submitted.

W. P. JEFJ'BIES,
E. MEYBEM,
E. J. Lours,
E. C. BONNER,
W. W. SEAMAN.

The Grand Lodge was called on at nine o'clock, the Grand Master
presiding.
After mnsic by the choir, and prayer by the Grand Chaplain, th;e
minutes of the sessions of yesterday were read and approved.

reported the following 11.dclitional officers of chartered Lodges, and

brethren, to fill vacancies in committees : Bro. TH<]MAS J. KIRK on the Finance Committee.

Bro. JAMES W. ANDERSON, from the Special Committee, to.whom
had been referred the Address of the Grand Master and Report of the
Grand Secretary, presented the following reports:To the M. •• W. •, Grand Lodge of California :-

BRETHREN :,-Your Committee to whom was referred the Addres~ of the
M.·. W.·. Grand Master have ca.efully examined the same.
Nothing could more forcefully testify to the energy, the zeal and the
efficiency of our worthy Brother in the discharge of the onerous and responsible duties imposed upon him by your suffrages, than does the exposition of
his work as set out in this excellent paper. If he does not rejoice in the fact
that his year of arduous work is near its end, we feel sure that the partner
"of his toil, his fortunes. his fa.me," and of his love, certainly does. Instant
in sea.son, he has executed the authority with which, one year ago, you

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

.,

[Oct. 15,

invested him in such· manner as reflects credit upon you, and npon the great
Institution in which for many years he has so faithfully labored. He has
reared for himself a monument based in the ap-preciation, respect and love of
his brethren throughout this great jurisdiction. It needs no words from us
saying to yon that he has heeded the behest of the stern arbiter. To him
nothing has seemingly appeared so fair as the smile upon the face of duty.
Flowers with tlieir fragrance seem to have greeted him as he trod the paths of
dnty. He has richly entitled himself to your gratitude, to your love. He
has honored you ; he has made himself worthy of all honor.
All Lodges should be represented at every Annual Communication. That
they were is "a consummation devoutly to be wished." The resultant effects
would prove of great benefit to the Lodges and to the Craft. Were the
Lodges represented the stakes would strengthen and the cords that bind the
Lodges would be lengthened.
We join with the Grand Master in expressions of sorrow-sorrow in that
we are deprived of the able counsels, the benign presence, and the delightful
and elevating companionship _of Past Grand Master PREl!~ON.
" Death's rough ca11
Unlooses all our favorite ties on earth;
And well if they are such as may'be answered
In yonder world, where all is judged of truly."
If excellence of character, if exalted manhood, if piety avails, then, indeed, may we rest assured, that our loved brother has entered upon a new, a
brighter and a better life, in blessed companionship of the great and good,
m:1der the benignant care of Him who doeth all thin!Jll well.

" Do they miss me? 'Twoi{ld be an assurance most dear
To know that some loYed were saying
I wish you were here."
We all say so; and, yet, with becoming reverence we say, "Thy will be
done."
We concur in the recommendation of our Grand Maste!' relative to the
matter of paying proper resp!'ct to the memory and worth of our beloved
brother, recognizing that he has himself written his own epitaph in our hearts,
"Passing away" is written upon every thing. The stalwart form of Past
Grand Treasurer NATHAN WESTON SPAULDING lies prostrate in death. Ripe
in years, after a life of usefulness. death has dimitted him from the earthly
Lodge to the Lodge on high. We are reminded by his departure that another
of those who did so much in laying deep and broad the foundations of Masonry in California has ceased from his labors ; and we do well to honor his
memory. Brother SPAULDING entered this Grand Lodge in 1864, when Senior
Warden of Mission Lodge. After serving that Lodge for two years as its
Master, he dimitted, and became the first Master of Oakland Lodge, and with
it remained until called to join the Lodge above.
