'Ve join with Grand Master HENDERSON in expression of tribute to the
memory and worth of brethren of our own and of sister jurisdictions who have
been called to the other side. Particularly do we feel the loss to the Masonic
~orld of M. •. W. ·• JOSIAH DRUMMOND, the last of the great triumvirate....'...
ENGLISH, MAUKEY, DRUMMOND, are joined in fellowship in the land of light.
We commend most heartily the zeal displayed by the Grand Master in the
matter of visits to Districts and Lodges. It requires but a moment's reflection
to form a proximate estimate of what a wonderful influence for good these
visits wield over the Lodges, and the brethren individually in the Lodges.
The Grand Master visits· with the sanction of the Grand Lodge, hence the
potency of his presence in the inspiring of increased energy and renewed life
in the great work of the Fraternity. Grand Master HENDERSON set a pace
fOr future Grand Masters in this jurisdiction worthy of all praise. Had he
done nothing else he has rendered service to the cause of Masonry commensurate with the honor this Grand Lodge conferred upon him. Your committee
opine that this is one of the chief duties of a Grand Master, and right worthily
has the present one discharged it. His flesh, as well as his spirit, seems to
have been very able to accomplish a vast amount of work, and he appears not
to have lost much flesh in his arduous work. The brethren visited must have
so appreciated his visits that they took good care of him and gave him good
encouragement in his work. Particularly are visits from the Grand Master,
or other Grand Officers, appreciated in the outlying districts of the State, and
here they are most needed. We are not !l.t all surprised that he had no
decisions to report. The influence of his presence made decisions unnecessary.
We heartily concur with the Grand Master in the opinion he expresses
relative to thQ importance of quality of material as compared with quantity.
In these days there is danger of boom in Masonry ; it is becoming immensely
popular to be a Mason, and many without litrle character, or not proper
character, are seeking entrance to our Lodges that they may possess them·
selves with the semblance of character. The Grand Master rightly discountenances everything of this nature in our Lodges, and the brethren should
tollow his su~estions in this respect. He put it right in saying that the petitions of unworthy and objectionable persons should never be presented in a
Lodge. There is much good sense in the expression, " Do not let us become
too lax in regard to whom we accept."
\Ye commend the judicious care exercised by the Grand Master in the
matter of issuing dispensations for various purposes, particularly in relation
to granting dispensations for the formation of new Lodges and for reballoting
on rejected applicants.
The recommendation regarding the establishing of a Lodge at the Siminoff
Temple meets with our approval. The name suggested is an appropriate one
The rule adopted by the Grand Master in the matter of granting dispensa·
tion to reballot on rejected candidates is an excellent one, one that should be
observed by every Grand Master ; and we are in accord with him in what he

330

PROOEEDINGB OF THE

[Oct. 15.

says relative to Committees of Investigation. Too often these committees
shift the responsibility from themselves by reporting favorably upon candidates, thus misleading the members of the Lodge, and opening the door for
the admission of the unworthy.
We endorse all that the Grand Master says regarding the episode at Santa
Rosa. He rightly administers a just rebuke to parties inimical to Masonry
who interfere to stir up discord.
We congratulate Bro. HENDERSON on being privileged to lay the corner·
stone of the High School in Stockton; not often does so happy a coincidence
occur. We trust that hie watchful eye will e,iie to it that the superstructure
is made to comport with the corner·etone. May this Alma Mater prosper and
send out more future Grand Masters like unto him.
The Grand Master gives just mede of praise to the Inspectors and Grand
Lecturers. This is as it should be. The interest manifested throughout the
jurisdiction is greatly attributable to the faithful and efficient services of these
officers, and this increased interest,' in the opinion of your committee, would
justify proper remuneration for such services. The positions, it is true, are
honorable, but honor is not enough.
The recommendation of the Grand Master regarding the time of reporting
by the Inspectors is deserving o( careful consideration by the Grand Lodge.
Mirabile dictu I For the first time, we believe, in the history of this
Grand Lodge, no decisions are reported. Paet Grand Master ANGELLOTTI a.nd
hie confreree on the Jurisprudence Committee. ought to rejoice; and so ought
we, a.II of us. Thie is a healthful indication. Masters of Lodglls are waking
up to realize that something more than the ability to mouth the ritual is
required to constitute one a capable and efficient Master.
We concur in all that the Grand Master has said relative to the dues in
Lodges ; the insurance on Grand Lodge property, the allowance for Grand
Master's traveling expenses, and the expenses of subordinate officers and
brethren when occupied in Grand Lodge work.
We endorse fully the Grand Master's senti!llente .on the matter of affilia·
tion fees ; and we think hie enggeationa in reference to the Home should be
carefully considered. The Jurisprudence Committee should direct immediate
and careful consideration to the matter 'nf incorporating the Honie, if such
ac.tion can be had without infringing upon the control that the Grand Lodge
must continue to exercise over that institution.
All honor to our noble Bro. SIMINOFI!' ! Humanity will hail him bleaeed,
Abon Ben Adam-like, he loves hie fellow men. May the Temple erected by
hie munificence not only serve to perpetuate hie name, but may induce others
with like nobility of character to go and do likewise.
Your committee sincerely trust that the membership of this Grand Lodge
will endeavor to acquaint themselves with the character of the great work
that is being accomplished by the various Boards of Relief ; were they to do

Resolved, That the Finance Committee of this &rand Lodge be and is
hereby inatructed to purchase a suitable testimonial to be presented to our
retiring Grand Master, M. •. W. •• ORRIN S. HENDERSO'!, in lieu of the usual
Past Grand Master's JewelBegs leave to report that, in view of the fact that our retiring Grand Master

Master's Jewel, and another form of testimonial would be appropriate under the
circumstance, we recommend the adoption of said resolution, with the follow.

suitable Jewel, the cost not to exceed $200; an investigation develops that
owing to the general advance in prices of material said sum is at present inadequate, and we therefore offer the following resolution a~d recommend its
adoption:-

Resolt1ed, That the incoming Grand Master and his successors in office, at
the expiration of their respective terms, be presented by the Grand Lodge
with a testimonial, the cost of which shall not exceed the sum of 530Q.

distribution of the Grand Lodge proceedings, we offer the following resolution
and recommend its adoption :

Re&olw.d, That after this year only two copies of the Grand Lodge proceedings be sent to each Lodge of this jurisdiction.

Bro. JULIEN E. PARDEE, Chairman of the Committee on Charters,
presented the following report :your committee, to whom were re.ferred the petitions for charters of the
eight Lodges which have been· organized under dispensation since the last
Annual Communicatio n of this Grand Lodge, respectfully report as follows : The dispensations for said Lodges were issned as follows : Cavite Lodge, October 18, 1902;
Palestine Lodge, October 21, 1902 ;
Sunset Lodge, February 11, 1903;
Pinole Lodge, February 12, 1903 ;
. Hollywood Lodge, April 21, 1903 ;
Presidio Lodge, May 7, 1903;
Mill Valley Lodge, July 17, 1903; and
Buena Park Lodge, September 2, 1903.
We have carefully examined the records and papers accompanying said
petitions and find that in most particulars the records of these several Lodges
conform substantially to the requirements of the Constitution and General
Regulations, and that each of said Lodges is shown to be in good financial
condition, clear of indebtedness.
While it is much more vleuant to commend than to critidse, still we fe~l
that it is onr duty to call attention to certain matters appearing to us from
those records, which we believe are not entirely in accord with the expressed
will of our Grand Lodge, but trust that our suggestions will be received in
the spirit of kindness in which they are offered.
General Regulation No. 57 permits the expenditure for refreshments of a
sum not exceeding ti ve per cent. of the total revenue of a Lodge for the p1·eceding Masonic year. It therefore neceBB&rily follows that a Lodge, wot'king
under a dispensation issued after the first of January of a given year, has no
authority to expend any of its funds for that puttpose during that year.
"Pinole " Lodge and "Hollywood " Lodge are the only ones to which this
criticism applies ; and your committee suggests that it would be well for the
brethren of these Lodges to see that the amounts so expended are returned to
the Lodge treunries, so that Lodge funds may remain intact, subject to duly
·
authorized Masonic uses.
The Secretaries of " Cavite," "Palestine," " Pinole," "Hollywood" and
"Mill.Valley" Lodges are deserving of especial commendation for the excellence of their work. ·Their records are clean and handsome and cannot fa.ii
to prove an "endearing record, not only to their praise, but also to the welfare of their respective Lodges."
Nearly all the Secretaries of these eight Lodges have closely followed
the forms contained in the minutes of the proceedings· of "Example Lodge,"
and while so guided it is impossible that a brother Secretary can materially

1903.]

GRAND LonGE OF CALIFORNIA.

339

err. But in one particular your committee is of the opinion that "Example
Lodge " forms ought to be amended, viz.: with reference to the present&·
tion and payment of bills. The fonn now given is as follows : "The Secretary presented the following bills, viz. : of •...•• etc., all which were referred
to the Auditing Committee and ordered to be paid if found correct."
In the opinion of your committee no bill should be ordered paid until after
the same has been reported upon by the Auditing Committee ; and the minutes of the order for its payment should show the exact amount for which it
is audited and for which a warraut is authorized to be drawn. We therefore
recommend that the formula of "Example Lodge," in that particular, be·
.
&mended to read as follows : "The Secretary presented the following ·bills, viz. : of ...... etc., and, it
appea.ring that the same had been examined and approved by the Auditing
Committee, it was duly ordered tha.t warrants be drawn for their payment."

In this connection we beg to say that in the judgment of your committee
the records of &Lodge ought to show, in every instance, for what a bill has
been contr.scted-w hat senice has been rendered, or what supplies furnished
to the Lodge, as &basis for the charge made-in order that it may affirmatively
appear that the expenditure is such as is B&Ilctloned by our Laws and Regula.
tions. lo some ins~ances the Secretaries of the Lodges under dispensation
have failed to specify for what purpose the expense was incurred.
With reference to "Buena Park " Lodge, we call attention to the fact th&t
its dispensation was not issued until September 2, 1903; its first (and only)
meeting thereunder having been held on September 4, 1903. At \hat meeting
five petitions.for 'he degrees of Masonry were received and duly referred to
Committees of Iuvestigation. These committees cannot report until the ned
stated meeting of the Lodge, consequently it has been impossible for the
Lodge to do any degree work. Our Constitution provides (Part III, Art. I
Sec. 1), " * • and no charter shall be granted to any Lodge until it shall
have WORKED & time under dispensation, aod shall have exhibited to the
Grand Lodge satisfactory evidence of Ma.sonic capability." If the word
"worked" is used in this section of the Constitution in its ordinary Ma.sonic
eense-i. e., as referring to the conferring of degrees-it will at once appear
that " Buena Park" Lodge is not entitled to & charter. If, however, the
word is to be given a more general meaning-as referring to general Lodge
work---0pening, transacting business and closing-we do not see that ii
would necessarily follow that "Baena Park" Lodge would be entitled to its
charter ; for the phrase "shall have worked a. time under dispensation "
must, under all rules of interpretation, be held to mean .aome~hing-not to
have been ueed by the law-makers loosely and for no reasonable purpose. As
your committee is in doubt as to the proper interpretation to be given to this
provision, we ask that the question be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence for their opinion, with the request that they report thereon at the
~liest poBBible moment.

Your com:rittee, to whom was referred the transcript of t~e trial record
in the case of JoE D. YEAGER, suspended by "Russian River" Lodge, No.
181, on October 18, 1902, for unmasonic conduct, beg leave to report as
follows:The proceedings were conducted in regular manner, and the tri~l record,
as shown by the transcript, is in proper form. The charge con~ms three
specifications, viz :First-" That he had left his family and is, or has been, living with
another woman not his wife."
Second-" That he has maintained undue and improper intimacy and relati~ns with one May Hopper."
Third-" That he has practised fraud and deceit upon a. brother Ma.son, by
introducing to them in Los Angeles the said woman, or some other woman, a.s
·his wife, when his lawful wife was continuously resi:ling in Windsor."
The accused was duly summoned, but did not appear at the trial. He,
however, sent a letter to the Secretary, saying that he would not attend, and
for the Lodge to do as it pleased and fix matters to suit themselves.
The Commissioners found the accused " guilty " on the first and third
specifications contained in the charge and of the charge of unmasonic conduct,
and fixed the punishment a.t "suspension."
·
On the second specification the-Commission find-" not guilty."
Your Committee is of the opinion, that the crime having been proved, the
name of the particeps criminis is immaterial. Robbery is none the less such
because the party robbed be unknown. Rape is none the less flagrant because
the name of the innocent Yictim be unknown. And unlawful cohabitation is
none the leBS such, simply because her name is involved in obscurity.
" Stolen Sweets " a.re just as sweet by whatsoever name they may be called.
The Committee is of the opinion, that, the offense having been proved, the
Commissioners were warranted iu imposing the extreme penalty. Desertion
of wife and family, unlawful intercourse with another woman, and her introduction to brother Masons a.s his wife, surely desen-es the severest penalty
known to Masonic law.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the judgment of "Russian River" Lodge, No. 181'
rendered on the 18th day of October, 1902, whereby Joe 'D. Yeager was suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and :he same ~s
hereby rev.ersed, and the said Joe D. Yeager be and he hereby is, by this
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, expelled from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry.
Respectfully submitted.
J. F. BOLLER,

This being the hour for the special order, as ordered by the Gre.nd
Lodge Tuesday, the Grand Orator, the W.". Bro. EDWARD H. HABT,
delivered the Annual Oration before the Grand Lodge, as follows:MosT WoRStUP FUL GBAND MA~TER
AND BRETHREN OF THE GRAN D L OD GE : -

"LIBERTY, EQUALITY, FRATERNITY."
"The number three," we are told, "alludes to the three creat
Lights of Masonry, the th.ree Degrees of Masonry, and the t nree
principal Ofllcer>1 of the Lodge."
·I n Masonry and in the universe the D(Umller "three" has a fa.r
deeper signif1oance, and on a.II sides do we encounter the mystic triune quailititcs of three m one. Nature itself is made up of the mineral,

M. ·. W. •• EDWARD MYERS PRESTON, Past Grand Master of
Masons of California, has been called from labor to eternal rest and '
peace. Th11 summons came in the evening of the 24th day of .April
1903, .kand to us all, unaware of the seriousne88 of his brief illneas, .i·t'
was .l l _e a .s~aft of lightning from a clear and cloudless sky. The
patnotic 01tize.n, the wise counselor, the honorable man, the exemplary M~on, is dead. The Masonic Fraternity of our great State
m~urn his loss, and to-day join in paying the last official and personal
tnbute of respect, friendship, brotherly love and affection to his
memory.
"'!e can no .longer lonk to him for counsel and advice or be guided
by his clear mmd and sound judgment. He has passed away, but hi!

works endure. The rich legacy of lessons and influences of the life ~f
this good, brave, honorable man remain to us and will bear perennial
harvests which death· cannot destroy, and which may in some measure
tend to assuage our grief and temper our sorrow. We may find
much that will profit us in a review of the life, services and character
of our beloved brother.
EDWARD MYERS PRESTON was bcfrn in Freedo111, Washtenaw
County, Michigan, on the 4th day of May, :f841. He was educated
in the public schools of his native town and at the Michigan Agricultural College at Lansing, graduating therefrom in November,
1862, with the highest honors.
Early in the year 1863 he left his home for California, ariving in
San Francisco on June 6th, and soon after went to Nevada County,
where for several terms he taught in its public schools, then engaged
in the drug business at Nevada City until 1876, when he assisted in
the organization of the Citizens Bank at that place, bec~me one of its
Directors and was elected its first President, which office he held to
the time of his death.
On November 8, 1870, at Nevada City, he was united in marriage
with Miss Maggie H. Hinds, who died on June 2, 1889,leaving him~
young son, Myers .A. Preston, now grown to manhood. That union
was a most happy one, and if the story of.their wedded life and home
in Nevada City were told it would be ".A sweet savor wherever
happy homes are recognized as the. citidal of virtue and the hope of
the world." Her death was a severe blow and tinged the remainder
of his life with sadness; yet with high courage, fidelity to duty, and
a heart full of love, he took up the burdens, assumed the additional
responsibilities, and devoted his life to the rearing of the motherless
child, maintaining to the end that home: once warmed and brightened
by the dear wife and mother's love, and presence-wherein the memory of her, who h~d passed away, was ever cherished and held sacred.
While always taking a deep interest in affairs of State and in all
public matters, the turmoil of political life was not to his liking, yet
he was called upon to serve the people in public stations, being twice
elected Supermtendent of Schools of Nevada County, and in 1888
elected to thu State Senate, serving in the legis!ati ve sessions of 1889
and 1891.
His public duties were marked by zeal and devotion to the inter·
ests of the people. His great love of children led him to consider
their welfare at all times and to encourage ,and support any measure

1903.J

GRAND LODGE OF 0ALIFO~.

359

having for its object the education and. betterment of the youth of
our country. He was the author and advopate in the State Senate of
a bill to establish a school of industry, to which boys under the age
of eighteen years, convicted of any criminal offense, could be committed, there to receive such discipline and education as would fit
them to go into the world, earn an honest living and become good
men and citizens. Upon the fi_nal passage of this bill in the Senate,
there was paid to Senator PRESTON the .highest of .:ompliments, in
that the bill was unanimously amended by designating the institution as the "Preston School of Industry," in.honor of the author of
the measure. Upon the organization of the school, Senator PRESTON
was appointed one of its Trustees, was immediately elected President
of the Roard and served as such to within a short time of his death.
Brother PRESTON was initiated an Entered Apprentice Mason,
passed to the degree of Fellow Craft, ~nd on May 4, 1863, raised to
the sublime degree of Master Mason in ;, W ashteuaw" Lodge, No. 65,
at Dexter, Michigan. He dimitted therefrom and affiliated with
"NeV'llda" Lodge, No. 13, at Nevada City, in 1873. He served this
Lodge as Senior Deacon and Treaeurer, was elected Worshipful
Master in 1880, served as such for two terms ; and in 188i he was
again elected Treasurer, holding such offi.re continuously up to the
time of his death.
·
He was appointed antl served as Senior Grand Deacon of our
Grand Lodge ill 1889-90, elected and served as Junior Grand Warden
in 189'2-3, unanimously advanced through the several stations, and at
the .Annual Communication in 18£15 was elected Most Worshipful
Grand Master of Masons of California.
Brother PRESTON came to the Grand Lodge in 1889, after an
absence of several years, animated with the desire to be of some
1erv1ce to his fellow man, particularly to the unfortunate orphans of
our deceased brethren, determined to advocate and espouse the cause
of the widow and the fatherless and to establish a Widows and
Orphans' Home for their use and benefit. This matter had be~u preaented to the Grand Lodge at a previous communication and had been
fl-approved by it; Brother PRESTON, however, took up the work
where it had been abandoned and on October 9, 1889, offered a resolution, '' That the Grand Lodge take such measures as may be deemed
proper to establish and foster an institution for the care of destitute
Orphan children of Masons; and that a committee of five be aJ>pointed
by the Grand.Master to report a plan therefor at the next Annual
1
•tr1Diunt - 0.11, " which resolution was adopted. He was appointed

by the Grand Master, the chairman of such committee, and at the
Annual Communication in 1890 be presented a report in .which it was
recommenderl "That there be established within this jurisdiction a
home for the nurture, and intellectual, moral and physical culture of
the children of deceased Master Masons of the State of California,
and a temporary asylum for the sick and indigent widowa of such
deceased Freemasons." This report was, after due· consideration,
rejected, and the matter was again referred to the committee, with
instructions to report at the next Coinmuaication of the Grand Lodge.
At which time the report of the committee was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence; which last committee reported that it had
not the time to complete a scheme for the establishmelit of the home,
but that it believed the establishment of such an institution was the
unanimous wish of the Masons of this jurisdiction, and recommended
that a committee of nine be appointed to organize such an institution,
as such committee might deem best ; which resolution was adopted
by the Grand Lodg~, a:nd th~ Grand Master appointed Brother
PRESTON as chairman of such committee. During the year the plan
was completed and organization perfected, all of which was approved
by the l.:l:rand Mas~r and ratitied by the Grand Lodge at the Annual
Communication in 1892, and the work was immediately commenced
and carried on under the direction and control of the Board of
Trustees, of whom Bro. PRESTON was one, serving as its President up
to the time of his election as Grand Master, when he resigned the
trust which had been so faithfully executed by him.
It was peculiarly fi ttii;g that the last official act of Grand Master
PRESTON should be the laying of the corner-stone, on October 14,
1896, of the institution for which be bad labored so 1011;g and zealously.

Let us ever remember, brethren, that it is our duty to foster and
support this grand institution, which was made possible through the
energy and untiring efforts of Past Grand Master PRESTON. As has
been well said, "The Preston School of Industry at Ione and the
Masonic Widows and Orphans' Home at Decoto are monuments of
State and of M&aonic pride and glory in the redemption and blessing
of humanity, spanned by Heaven's own prismatic arch, the keystone
of which is Charity, on which will ever appear the name of Eow ARD
MYERS PRESTON."
On Octoher 16, 1897, upon the death of Past Grand Master
CURTIS, Brother PRESTON was appointed Chairman of the Committee

on furiaprudence, which position he filled with honor and satisfaction to the day of bis death.
The spirit of a good man has gone to God who gave it ; the
pa.ge of bis life was clearly written without blot or stain-a good
ma.n, a good citizen, a zea.lous Mason, a.nd a loyal friend.
We miss his genial presence, the sound of his cheerful voice, the
warm grasp of his band. He sleeps the sleep that knows no waking,
bot he will live with ns all in memory 'f orever.
He was at all times dignified, kind and courteous, with the same
sunny smile and cordial greeting for one and all. He made friends
and kept them.
His career has been a sweet and wholesome example in right
living, high thinking and unselfish service in public and private
walks of life, and bis memory will ever remain an inspiration to those
'
who loved him living and mourn him dead.
It was our sad privilege to attend his funeral services at his home
in Nevada City, and we shall never forget the impressivenesi5 of that
ecene, for it seemed that every ~an, woman and child in his home
city, and indeed for miles a.round, came to do him honor .and pay a
tribute of respect to bis memory. · All were moved with pity and
prow-the highest evidence of sincere a.nd genuine affection for their
honored dead.
As the sun slowly sank to rest beyond the western horizon on
that beautiful April day, we stood about the open grave, high up in
the foothills of the Sierras, overlooking the pretty mountain town
where for almost forty .years our beloved brother ha.d lived, revered
anrl honored by all. With the impreesive ceremonies of our Fra·
fAlrnity, which he loved so well, we gently bid him away by the side
of her who did so much to. surround his life with a happy environment and to crown his da.ys with joy.
The tliought then came· to .us that no marble shaft was necessary

to Illa.rk his resting plll.ce or to perpetua.te his memory, since there
had been erected in the hearts of his fellowmen for Enw ARD MYERS
PaBSroN a. monument far more everlasting and enduring.

The following was also presented by that committee:At the last Communication of this Grand Lodge, Bro. JAS. W. ANDERSON
proposed an amendment to Section 1 of Article IX of the 'Uniform Cope of
By-Laws, the object of which was to aliow any subordinate Lodge to proride
for life memberships. (See Proc. of 1902, p. 1040). Your committee then
reported against th~ adoption of the amendment, but the matter was , ~e-re­
ferred to this cominittee, the understandinR bei~g that the committee should
report some plan by which a Lodge might, at its option, establish life memberships. The question of life membership bas been before this Grand Lodge
many times, and, as has before been said, appears to be a difficult one to
arrange in any satisfactory manner. The Committee on J nrisprudence in 1888
said, through Bro. BELCHER, its chairman: "If there be any good plan at all
in regard to life membership, it would be to grant such exemption only upon
payment of a sum of money which the Lodge shall judge to be at least a fair
equivalent for the monthly dues; and that the money S9 received should in
all cases be securely invested as ~ distinct fund, of which only the income
should be used for current or even extraordinary expenses. That fund should
stand in the place of the member himself for the payment of dues. If extraordinary expense is at any time incurred, it should be met by an increase of
the dues of the members of the Lodge, and a life member should no more be

19(13.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

375

uempt from such increase than one who had maintained his standing by the
monthly payment of his dues."
We entirely concur in what was said by Bro. RKLCBER as to the necesaity
of including in any plan for life membership the features stated in his report.
Every Lodge member who is able to do BO should at all times bear his portion
of the common burden, and no Lodge should be allowed to impair its ability
to do the work for which it is instituted by releasing any of its members from
auch obligation. The necesaity of preserving intact the sum paid for a life
membership and using only the interest for current expenses is obYious, and
is recognized by thA framer of the proposed amendment. The proposed
amendment does not, however, come up to the standard set by Bro. BELCHXR
lo the report from which we have quoted, and we are unable to recommend a
departure therefrom in any respect. It does not provide for the protection of
the principal sum paid for a life membership; it does not insure that a suffi·
cieot aum will be charged ; it does not provide for the contingency of an
increase of dnes.
We therefore recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.
In obedience to what we consider to be the desire of the Grand Lodge, as
intimated by its action in re-referring the proposed amendment for further
_,01ideration, we submit, without recommendation, a proposed amendment to
Section I of Article IX of the Uniform Code of By-Lawll, which will allow
life membel'llhips upon certain terms and conditions. The terms and c_onditions are such that we do not believe it would be harmful. .At the same time
we cannot see that any useful purpose would be subserved by its adoption.
The proposed amendment is a.a follows, viz.:Rte0/11ed, That Section I of Article IX of the Uniform Code of By-Laws
be and hereby is amended to read as follows, viz.:SBCTION 1. The dues of each member of the Lodge shall be ....•.•...••
. . • . • • . . . • . • . • • _••.•••• ., payable quarterly in advance; provided that t~is
Lodge. by the adoption of a standing resolution to that effect, which resolu·
tion shall not be acted upon at the stated meeting at which it is introduced,
nor until notice in writing thereof shall have been forwarded by mail to' every
member, may provide for a system of life membership, which shall forever
exempt the life me.mber from the payment of dues therein, unlesa the dues of
the members of the Lodge be increased, in which event ea.id life members shall
pay ae dues the amount of the increallll quarterly in advance in the same manner as.other members pay their dues. Said resolution shall provide that no
life membership shall be granted except upon the payment of a sum of monev
named therein, which sum must be sufficient te produce at the current rate of
i11tereet paid by savings banks an amount per annum equal to the annual dues
of the Lodge, and shall further provide that all amounts paid for life member1bip shall be invested either in reputable banks of deposit, or in bonds of the
United States, State of California, or some county, city and county, city or

GRAND LODGE:

As representatives of more than twenty-nine thousand Masons under
the iurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California, I desire to extend to
7ou ·a. car.d ial welcome to its Fifty-fifth Annual Communication.
The past year has been one of unusual activity among the Craft, and
will show, by the Report of the Grand Secretary, a larger gain in membership than any previous year during the existence of Masonry in California. Nothing bas happened to mar the good-fellowahip that exist.a
among the Fraternit7, and everything points to the fact that this con·
tinued growth and activity will redound to the best interests of our
St.ate. By the Constitution it is incumbent upon me to ·give you a resum6
of the dutiea performed by the Grand Master during the last year, but
before entering upon a detailed statement of these duties we must :tint
remember those brethren in our own and other jurisdictions who have
passed from their earthly labors.

During the year, so far as my limited time would permit, I have
endeavored to come in personal contact, through visits, with as many of
the brethren of the Jurisdiction as possible, and, in addition to these
official visits, I have participated, by invitation, in the celebration of
the Fiftieth Anniversary of two Lodges"Union" Lodge, No. 58, at Sacramento;
"Live Oak" Lodge, No. 61, at Oakland.

On invitation, I installed the officers of " Dunsmuir" Lodge, No. 297,
and "Sisson" Lodge, No. 310, and also the officers of the five Lodges situated in Sacramento. These social reunions have been among the most
pleasant of the many pleasant experiences of the year.
Brother Sidney Espey, W. M., "La Fayette" Lodge, No. 126, being
disqualified, at his request I appointed Brother Lawrence H. Wilson,
W. }.{., "Russian River" Lodge, No. 181, to preside at a trial in "La
Fayette" Lodge.
DEQISIONS.

Many inquiries regarding the Masonic Law Ji.ave reached me during
the year. Most of them, however, required nothing further in answer
than a reference to our written iawe. The following, however, 1 consider of sufficient importance to bring to the attention of the Grand
Lodge:
A Junior Warden y;as instructed by a Lodge to prefer charges against
a brother for un-Masonic conduct. He was afterward elected to and installed as. Senior Warden of the Lodge.
QuesUon: le he still the accuser and prosecutor in the case!
Answer: The Junior Warden eontinued to be the accuser, notwith~ standing his election and installation as Senior Warllen.
QuesUon: · Hae a Lodge the right to suspend a mentally incompetent

brother?

Answer: You have no right to suspend a brother who is mentally
incompetent.
Question: Must Lodges under dispensation contribute their per
capita to the Masonic ·Boards of Relief!
Answer: Lodges under dispensation are Masonic Lodges for all purposes, and under the same 'iaws, rules and regulations governing chartiired Lodges.

QuesUon: The propriety of receiving the petit ion of persons under
indictment by a grand jury. (This communication came t o me, signed
by the officers and members ·of a Lodge, they being extremely anxious t o
have these persons as members.)
Answer: Replying to your corumunication of January 15th, signed
by yourself and other officers and members of the Lodge, referring to the
reception of petitions for membership in your Lodge, will say that I
am of the opinion that it would not be good policy to receive these petitions until after the charges against such parties are cleared up in
Court. I have no doubt, from what you say, that these charges are
malicious; at the same time, if, after receiving t hem into your Lodge,
the charges should be maintained, it would put your Lodge in a posit ion
that Rt least would not be pleasant.

" Hawaiian" Lodge, No. 21, was incorporated under the laws of that
kingdom in 1858,' and they write for my advice as to what t hey shall do
in the matter. My reply was that they should at once take the necessary
steps to dieincorporate, and I referred them to the history of the disincorporation of "Suisun" Lodge, No. 55, in the Proceedings of 1903.
In answer to this I received a communication stating that this matter
had been referred to a Committee consisting of the Master and Wardens, with instructions to report at the next regular meeting, since wliich
time I have heard no further from t hem.
Have received various communications from the Masonic Club at
t he Soldiers' Horne in Los Angeles Count y. This Club has a membership
of about one hundred. The Government will not allow the formation of
a Masonic Lodge in the Home, and these old brethren desire the privilege of having Masonic burial. My answer to their various inquiries is
n.e follows: The Masonic Club has no right to use the Masonic burial
services at the funeral of a member. If the brother be in good standing
at the time of his death, it would be proper to ask some regular Masonic Lqdge to conduct the funeral services. If, in the case under consideratjon, the burden would be too onerous on t he Lodges conduct ing
the ceremonies, I think probably that the Grand Lodge would relieve
them of some of the expense. A Mason not in good standing has no
right to Masonic burial, unless his Lodge sees fit to accord him the
same. pt case of the death of a Past Grand Master, t he officers of the
Club should notify the Grand Secretary of this Jurisdiction. The Grand
Honors cannot be given at a funeral, unless it is conducted by a Lodge
after being regularly opened. The desire of these old brethren seems to
be to have a Masonic funeral at their death. In my opinion, they deserve some consideration, and, if possible, an arrangement should be
made with "Santa Monica" Lodge, being their nearest Lodge, to conduct
these funeral ceremonies.

POLITICS A.ND POLCTICA.L METHODS IN THE GRAND LODGE.

This subject I approach with some trepidation, as I fear that my intentions
may be misconstrued; but the fact that the use of these methotls has graduaUy grown until it has become patent to all who have eyes to see, makes it
incumhent on some one to bring it to the attention of the Grand Lodge, and I
cannot help but think that this unpleasant duty falls upon the retiring Grand
Master. Caucuses have been held for the purpose of influencing the election
of Junior Grand Warden ; letters have been written to the representatives of
Lodges who will attend the Grand Lodge, as well as letters to persons outside qf the fraternity, a.eking them to ·use their influence ID behalf of aspirants for this place; and whisperings have come to m1i that combinations
have been formed parcelling this office out to various sections of the State
for the next few yeard. Now, brethren, this is all wrong. There is no room
in Masonry for the use of these methods; nothing will so surely mar our
usefulness or more certainly strike a death blow at the very foundation of our
Institution.

MASONIC HOME.

The officers •elected to serve this Grand Lodge should be the uninfluenced
choice of a majority of its members. Consultations as to the best material
are perfectly proper; but consultations having the least semblance of t!Jose
methods so notorious in political conventions should be 11voided.
This is all-it io only DPcessary to call attention to these things and the
overwhelming majority of. Masons, recognizing the danger, will formulate a
cure for the evil.
RECOMMENDATIONS.

To the q~est.ion of Life Membership I have. Siven a great deal of
thought during the past year, and it is my opinion that it would be for

811

the best interests of the Fraternity in California if some system of Life
Membership could be adopted by this Grand Lodge.
Investigations made at my request seem to indicate that the Masonic
life of Masons is limited to about ten years, and a sum that would be
fair to the brethren and fair to the Lodges could be fixed upon. This
sum should be regulated in the different Lodges by the amount of dues
paid. Where the dues are $12.00 per year, $200 would seem to be about
a fair amount, and where the dues are $6.00 per year, $100. These
amounts should be placed in a separate fund, known. as the Life Mem·
bership Fund, and invested in undoubted securities, and only the interest
thereof should be drawn upon for the current expenses of the Lodge.
This fund ;would then belong to the Lodges in perpetuity. Though
the brother might lose his membership, by death or otherwise, this
sum would continually pay into the Lodge a certain amount of
dues as long as the Lodge existed. Nearly all the Grand Jurisdictions
have some form of Life Membership, and I have heard of no instance
in which it worked a hardship, either to the individual brother or fo the
}'raternity. This subject, in my opinion, deserves the earnest considera·
tion of the Grand Lodge at this time, and I hope that some method may
be devised that will work satisfactorily.
"Rose's Bar" Lodge, No. 89. The annual returns were not received
until September 21st, and at the present writing (October 7th) no Grand
Lodge dues have been received. I recommend that the affairs of this
Lodge be referred to the Committee on Charters for investigation.

Affiliation :fee shall he small, or none at all, and r respectfully suggest
t_hat at .this time the Grand Lodge formufate its policy by fixing a maxi·
mum Affiliation Fee.

During the early part of the year the Grand Master spent almost two
weeks of his time in looking over the affairs of the Masonic Home, and
came to the conclusion that, if time be given, everything in connection
therewith would be worked out to the perfect satisfaction of the Craft.
There seemed to be no indication why he should arbitrarily inferfer.e
with the present management. The Board of Trustees were Masons of
undoubted standing, good judgment, with the best interests of the Home
at heart, desirous of doing everything that would make this institution
what the Masons of this Jurisdiction desire it should be. A weat many
questions were looked into, and, while there was a great deal of talk,
there was no evidence on which to base an intelligent decision.
Dr. Aikin and bis wife have continued to preside over the Home during
the year, and their administr&tion has been satisfactory to a majority
of the Board of Trustees. Everything has been very carefully watched,
and nothing has occurred to mar the usefulness of this, our greatest institution. Brother Charles L. Patt.on, President of the Board of Trustees,
and to whom more tba.n any one eliie we owe the present satisfactory condit.ion of the Home, ea.rly in the year informd me that he could not, on

1904.]

account of bueinese engagements, serve for another term as Trustee, and
it will be neceeeary that the incoming Grand Master appoint a eucceeeor
to him. The Fraternity in the State owe theie Trustees not only their
beet wishes and earnest support, but their sineers tha.nks,' that they, at
the expen~e of a great deal of time and trouble, have devoted themselves
to the carrying out of our idea~ in the establishment of this Home. We
all know that the Home is not_ doing the work that we anticipated at its
inception, but the problem is being gradually worked out, and in time I
hope to see provision made ·that will accommodate every deserving appli·
cant.
Within a short time Dr. Aikin and his wife have resi~ed their posi·
tions as Superintendent and Matron, and the Boe.rd of Trustees has
unanimously elected Dr. Rucker, of Merced, Pe.et Grand Master of thi.s
Jurisdiction, as Superintendent, and Mrs. Rucker as Matron. The gen:
ere.I trend of the management has been in the right direction, and as the
years go by we will able to point with pride to this, the greatest monu·
ment of Masonic charity ever established on this Coe.st. Numeroue donations have come to the Home, a detailed acoount of which will be found
in the Report of the Board of Trustees.
Brethren, we have come to the end of another Masonic year,' and,
while perhaps the anticipations of none of us have been fully realized,
still we should be .satisfied if we have done our 'best.
Masonry is not only the oldest, but the most conservative of institutions in the affairs of men, and we should endeavor to preserve it as it
has been handed down to us from time immemorial. Its dignity should
never be lowered. by any act of ours, and we should endeavor so to con·
duct ourselves as to be pointed out for the peculiarities of our lives and
walks. Proud we should be that we are a part of an institution that in
all a.gee of the world has attracted to its -membership men pre-eminent
in all walks of life, and that he.a ever exercised an influence toward the
uplifting and upbuilding of human character of which we can have no
conception, but, after all is said and done, what Masonry has been in
times po.st, what it may be in the future, is of very little use to us in·
dividue.lly, unless we at the present time weave its principles·and teachings into the warp and woof of our daily lives.
What we do ourselves, as Masons, is what will be of use to ue, but,
unless we so conduct ourselves that the places in which we reside shall
be made better from the fact that we have po.seed fhis way, our member· .
ship in the Lodge ~ll be of no avail. Unless we relieve the distress of
some needy brother, unless we take by the hand and support some s,truggling member of the Order. unless we take some weakling among our
ranks and place him upon his feet, and direct him in the right path,
and support him until .he is able to stand alone, Masonry, with all its

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

813

grand history, will be of no specie.I use to us. In other words, the practice.I application of thie frame-work of moral le.we to our daily lives is
what is essential to the individu~l Mason, if he desires to get those benefits which accrue to eveey pian because of the fact that he has lived an
upright, moral, genteel and kindly life. The kind deeds that we do
will, after all, be the only thing that will be left for us when we come to
make that great change that is decreed for all men.
It will -not matter at that time what positions we have held, how
much of this world's goods we have a~cumulated, or whether, in the common 11enee of the word, this life he.a been a failure or a success, but if
we ha.ve done some kindly deeds on our journey, if we have soothed the
unhappiness of some on~ who needed it, if we have stretched the helping
hand to raise a fallen brother, if we have whispered good counsel and
good cheer in his ear, if we have in any manner made the lives of those
among whom we walk pleasanter and better, and more manly, then we
have accomplished . all there is in life, and these deeds will be something
that we can hold on to when earth is slipping away from ue.
This year hae been a peculiarly pleasant one for your Grand Master,
and while he has fallen far short of what he intended to do Me.sonically,
be assured that his best thought and best efforts have been given to the
furthering of the interests of our gr and Fraternity; and in bidding you
farewell, and in again a.ssuming a position on the :floor of the Grand Lodge,
T desire to return to you my sincere thanks for all the kindnessee and all
the helpfulness, and all the part,iality, you have sliown me through this
last Masonic year.
Respectfully submitted,
CHARLES W. NUTTING. Grand Master.

.
Lodge.
On.the 13th January, 1904, two thousand two hundred a.nd fifty copies of
the proceedings were distributed, or reserved for future binding, in the customary manner, viz. : one copy to each of the present Grand Officers .; one
copy to ea.ch of the elective Pa.st Grand Officers; three copies to each of the
Grand Bodies, American and Foreign, with which we are in correepondence ;
one copy to each Inspector, and four copies to each of the Lodges of our
·
jurisdiction.
Th!! proceedings of all the Grand Lodges of the United States, for the
year, h~ve been received and placed in the ha.nds of the Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence, with the exception of Arkansas, Rhode Island a.nd
North Dakota, as have also those of Canada, Costa Rica, Ouba, England,
Scotland, Irela.nd, New Brunswick, New Routh Wales, Nova Scotia, Prince
Edward Island, Quebec, Victoria and Western Australia.

The Trustees are plea.sed to report that the affair3 of the Home are pro. greasing satisfactorily, and that the number of inmates have increased during
the past year. .They now have in the Home 124 inmates, of which 48 are
men, 29 are women, 20 girls· and 27 boys.
The changes are fully set forth in the Superintendent's report, which i1
1ubmitted herewith.
It is with the greatest pleasure we report that during the past year we
have lost none of our children by death. The children made most excellent
progress at public school during the past year, all gaining promotion, and three
attending high school at the present school session. '
The Trustees repeat the suggestion made in former years that members of
the Craft make frequent ·l"isits to the Home in order that they may come in
personal contact with our great charity, and at the same time demonstrate to
the residents their interests i~ their behalf.
Religious services have be~n held every Sunday, consisting of Sunday
school in the afternoon, with song services and sermon in the evening. These
serricea afford much comfort and enjoyment and are generally a~tended by
those in the Home, and our thanks are due to the Rev. Dr. Priddy, of HayW&l'ds, for services rendered.
LATES'r ADDITIONS.

Siminoff Temple,· embracing Lodge-room and eighteen rooms for men, two
cottages of twelve rooms and sick ward, and nineteen rooms for women, over
dining hall. These we feel will be about all we can take care of with the
present per r.apita. Our extra expenditures during the year have been very
large, and we submit a list ~bowing how it was used. It will be many years
before it will be necessary to make like purchase&.

The Home is open for visitors an!1 those who desire can visit any inmate
at all times during the day. Among the visitors during the past year have
been many members ot' the Fraternity who have shown special in~rest. in
the Home methods, and the impression derived therefrom must be cond~c1ve .
to the best interests and growth of a work which is rooted in fraternal fnend-ship and obli~ation.
· We desire to place on record a recognition of the generosity of the various
Ma~onic Bodies near and out of S&n Francisco at the holiday season in their
remembrance of the inmates of the Home. May this spirit become general
at Christmas time.
Care of inmates will range from $200 to $220 per ca.pita per year, as we
1urllish everything from toothbrush np. The comforts and blessings. which
the Home afford ought not to tempt the application of those who can hve out
of it by their own exertions or the. aid of their friends and r~latives. T~s
work is a work of absolnte charity and must continue so to be if the work is
to be successful and accompliah its object.
Brethren: The Home has been in active operation for ' the period of six
years. Its light has not been hidden under a bushel, but it has stood out in
the .open, seen and observed by all. It has proved that it is not experimen.tal
or sentimental. lt has proved itself to be practicable and capable of bemg
-conducted· upon the suhlimll principles of Masonic charity, and also upon
·s ound business principles, without which their labor would be in vain.
·
· With a total membership in the State of approximately 29,000, for every
thousand members, we are caring for lees than five, including Masons, their
wives, widows aud children. This is certainly not a serious draft upon our.
-charity. We feel that we ought to caution Lodges to use the i:rreatest cBre
before recommending applications for admission to the Home, and thus save
.applicants the mortification of rejection and the Board the disagreeable duty
-of declin.ing"admission. None who a.re worthy and in actual ·need of a home
sh;uld be refueerl; but business principles, upon which alone the Home can be
maintained, require that all who do not need its protection should be ex-duded a.nd not permitted to consume its resources.
Electricity has been. installed through all the buildings of the Home
·during the past ye£.F. Though costing m(}re per year, it is a better and safer
light.
Our worthy Superintendent and Matron, Brother and Mrs. Aikin, after
"!ix years ser,•ices at the Home, resigned September 15th, 1904, the Doctor

To the for.,going report the President desires to add the following :
From the close of the Grand L odge Sessi_on up to, and including the
present time, the President's health has been such that he could give little .
attention to the Home. He regrets to state that, for the first time in nine
yea.rs, it has been necessary for him to learn the condition of the Home,
principally from the reports of · the Trustees and Superintendent. Those
repor ts, however, must unquestionably be gratifying to the members of the
Grand Lodge. They show that, with the increa.se of years, this great cha.ritabll' institution has increased the scope of its beneficent work.
Within its protecting walls more and more of the agerl brethren and widows,
weary from the storm-tosserl -ocean of life, have found peace and rest, and
more and more of the orphans have received that. attention, educat;on and
care necessary to fit them for the battle of life.
The Home to-day stands as an enduring monument to show that Masone.
practice charity, a nd proves that the present generation has not lost the Great
Light which for ages has shone upon all who have reflected on the grand moral
lessons taught in the Masonic Ritual.
The Presiden t is indeed gratified that he has been permitted to contribute·
from his time and means toward the upbuildini and successful -operation of
this institution, and in closing his term of office would say that all the Trustees from its inception have assisted in making the Home what it is.
He remembers with gratitude, and records with pride, that it may b&
acknowletlged by the Fraternity during all the yea.re to come, that,
not alone to the Trustees belongs the credit for the success of this vast undertaking, but that, through the years of effort at session after session of the
Grand Lodge, in spite of opposition by some, the members ha.Ye strengthened
the efforts of the Trustees and contributed liberally from the means of the

•

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

841

Grand Lodge to establish this Home. Grand Master after Grand Master has
drawn upon his store of experieni:e to the same end. All have joined in making the Home a. real home, and all have rejoiced together at its success.
In the report of the Snperintendent will be set forth the details of the
management. Doctor Aikin and his wife have resigned as Superintendent
and Matron, and now remain only until the new Superintendent shall take
charge.
The Trustees have officially, by vote, ·thanked Doctor Aikin and his wife
for their labors. The President, on behalf of himself and the Trustee:f,
desires to say that their,management of the Home has been admirable from the
first. That Doctor Aikin and his wife have shown a capacity to deal with
the difficulties incident upon the management of an institution of this kind;
that as the increasing demands of the work grew, so, to a like degree, the
efficiency of the Superintendent and Matron seemed to increase. It wa& with
regret their resignation was accepted.
On behalf of the Trustees, we wish both Doctor Aikin and his wife Godspeed.
• The Trustees, in September, elected Past Grand Master Doctor Hiram
Newton Rucker, Superintendent; and his wife, Matron. No better s"lection
could ha.ve been made. The Trustees were unanimous in requesting Doctor
Rucker to accept the place. He is well known to all the members of the
Grand Lodge. He has served, since retiring as Grand Master, for the benefit
of the Craft in general; and, as new members of the Grand Lodge have come.
and gone, Past Grand Master Rucker has oeen one toward wb,pm the attention, love and regard of all have ~een directed. The Fraternity is indeed
fortunate in acquiring the ripe experience of Doctor Rucker, both as a physi·
cian and as the manager of public institutions, for the purpose of guiding the
future destinies of the Home. He will devote hie entire time to bettering
every part of our work.
The President cannot give any of his time to work outside of bis business
for many months to come; in fact, under his physician's advice, he is now
residin~ outside of San Francisco. Last January he asked Grand Master
Nutting to accept hie resignation, but at the earnest solicitation of the Grand
Master, consented to serve out this term- ill health, however, continuing, he
a.sks that some other brother be appointed with the hope that the mant le of
President shall fall on worthier sh~ulders than his own.
In closing his participation with the active labors of the Home the writer
asaures the Grand Lodge that his experience has served to increase his.confidence in its necessity, efficiency and future, and he pledges hie support and
assistance to the T rustees and Superintendent in extending the sphere of usefulnesa for the Home.
CHARLES L. PATTON,
Pruident.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

Considerable dental work has been done for th~ children by Dr. Eaton of
Centerville, at a rate much reduced from the regular charge for such services.
Our thanks are also due again to our brother, Dr. E. R. Bryant of San
Francisco, whose surgical skill has been gratuitously rendered in bebalf of
some of our warde.
ACCOMMODATIONS.
The splendid temple presented to the Home by Brother·Siminoff was dedicated on October 13, 1903; Brother Orrin S.Henderson, then M. ". W." Grand
Master, conducting the services for the Grand Lodge, and fnlly three thousand
visitors witnessing the ceremony.
The qld men who occupied apartments OTl'r the dining room were given
rooms in the Siminoff Temple; and the rooms formerly occupied by them were
renovated and fitted for occupancy by the many women who had been elected
to residence by the Board but who had not been admitted because we had no
place to put them. Several men were also on the waiting list; and to make
room for them, two more cottages were built on the grade, in line with the
thriie that had previously been erected. The upper' floor of the fifth cottage
was left as one large r!Jom, to be used as a lwspital. This room is sufficiently
large to accommodate six beds; and a stationary wash-bowl and toilet adjoin
it. This will prorn a. great convenience in the care of our sick and bedridden
brethren; for by having all the sick in one room, they can all be cared for by
one attendant to better advantage than when they are confined to their own
chambers, with as many nurses as th!lre are sick.
SOCIAL DIYERSIONS AND INTERESTS.
On four occasions ~faster ·Masons' lodges in cities of this connty have conferred the third degree of Masonry in the .Jodgeroom of the Siminoff Temple.
(4) Our aged brethren, most of whom are too infirm to travel several
miles at night to attend Masonic lodges, have appreciated and enjoyed these
visits beyond expression. And we earnestly hope that other lodges will, from
time to time, make similar use of our beautiful lodge-room during the coming
years .
The Girls' Mandolin and Guitar Club, nnder the able instruction of Mr.
Baker of Oakland, has also become a proficient music-maker. Owing to the
absence of some of the girls during the school vacation of the summer months,
the Club disbanded during June' and July.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 11,

The Boys' Band, under the patient tutelage of our Brother John King, has
continued steadily to progress, in spite of rearrangements rendered nedessary
by the departure of some of the boys from the Home. So well known have
they become, a.nd so well·recognized their ability a.e musicians, tba.t their
services have been in freq)lent demand a.t Masonio, patriotic and other celebrations-not a. little to their pecuniary advantage. (5)
Our Thanksgiving and Christmas dinners (the latter again the gift of Brother
F. G. Horner of Centerville) were, a.s formerly, memorable occa.eions. The
Christmas presents, purchased with funds subscribed by the Ma.sonic bodies
about the Bay, were both immerous a.nd useful.

The sewing-room under the supervision of the Matron and with the assistance of the seamstress and Miss Keller and the older girls, have made 26 new
dresses for women, 8 wrapper~, 3 skirts and 10 waists, and for the children
50 dresses, ·u skirts, 15 night ~resses, 14 pairs of drawers, and 9 aprons.
We still send our starched olothes to the Contra Costa Laundry in Oakland;
but all our plain washing is done in onr own laundry at the Home, completed
la.st June ; this plain washing being done by contra.ct for $100 a month. By
this ana.ngement, we will save from $i00 to $600 a year in laundry bills alone.
La.et fall we began to butcher our ·hogs, and in all over thirty were killed
for our consumption. On account of the constant increase in the size of our
family, more and more meat is used at the l!ome; but by raising hogs for
winter use, our meat bills are kept within moderate proportions.
Our poultry farm has proved adequate to supply us with eRge; and our
seven cows furnish us with an abundance of milk.
For several months we hi~ed a baker to come over from Centerville twice a
week and bake our bread. His product was genera.Uy unsatisfactory, and we
decided to try buying bread in San Francisco. We find that we can get better
bread, and at less cost than what we expended for material, fuel a.nd wages
when we had the baking done at the Home.
During the latter part of last year and the fi,rst of this, all the vege·
tables used a.t the Home were raised on our own grounSs ; but a.s we could
never get enoug~ of any one thing to serve all the tables, we began to buy
from the San Francisco markets. In this instance also, we find that we can
procure an abundant supply of fresh vegetables at less cost than when we
hired a gardener and raised our own. Our foreman has, however, raised a
quantity of sweet corn, sufficient for our table use, besides a goodly supply of
early potatoes and a large patch of watermelons.
Durinii ihe early pa.rt of .the year, a number of fruit trees were purchased
and planted in the orchard, to take the places of those that had died. Neither
our orchard nor our vineyard, how.,ver, has as yet begun to yield largely.
But both are growing splendidly, a.nd in another year or two will be very
productive. Last October we were able to dispose of five tons of apricots
and seven tone of wine grapes. This year the yield of the vineyard ought to
be at lea.et forty or fifty tons. Our p1·une crop this year was heavy, but the

IMPROVEMENTS
The appearance of the grounds is, of cou·r se, constantly improving with the
growth of the trees and shr11bs that have already been set out. More flowering plants have, however, been added from time to time ; and Bro. Haelke,
our gardiner, assisted by Bro. Bettes, has worked steadily to beautify our
environment.
The main drive was regravelled in the early •pring, and the roads were
kept in good condition during the summer months by sprinkling.
The lower platform or landing in front of the main building became so badly
cracked that it was decided to remove it and to replace it with new concrete
and cement. A concrete walk has also been laid between the kitchen and the
servants' quarters.
Many improvements. and repairs have been made within· doors. In October
the dining.room and kitchen were recalcimined, as well as the halls and rooms
of the ma.in building. Bro. Hagerdon repainted the floors of the dormitories
and the kitchen, placed new rubbers on the rear steps of the main building,
and repainted the floors of the rooms above the dining-room. In the hall
over the dining-room Bro. Eli Smith erected a. se\•en·foot partition, thus
affording twelve rooms there for women and se\•en for men, with a separate
bath and toilet for ea.ch compartment.
Bros. "Vilson and Herring donated to the Home and placed in position a
large window of colored glass, enclosing a. portion of the front porch on the
ma.in building, thus sheltering it from the strong afliernoon winds. Bro.
Wilson also donated the brick and labor necessary to wall in an exposed
sewer·pipe in the girls' basement.
Fire extinguishers have been placed iJ). the two new cottages ·and in the
Siminoff Temple. Radiators were placed in each room in the new cottages.
The old steam boiler was enlarged and a. new smoke-stack pul on. The remodeled boiler is of sufficient capacity to heat all five of th.e t<>ttages. A
steam boiler was also installed in a pit back of the Siminoff Templ~. to furnish
heat for that building. A new bath heater was placed in the basement of the
rear building, :;.s the old one had worn out in five:years' constant use.
In the Siminuff Temple a partition was erected on the third floor, thus providing another bedroom. A handsome new pipe organ of 350 pipes, donated
by Bro. Siminoff, ha.a been installed in the lodge-room of the Siminoff Temple.
It is so constructed that it may be opera.lied automatically by an electric
motor.

New roller curtains have been placed in the dormitories; a flight of winding stairs has been built to the cupola of the main building ; picture molding
has been placed by Bro. Eli Smith in all the rooms on the second floor of the
ma.in building and in the rooms over the dining-room ; new bowls have been
placed in all the water-closets; all the hair mattresses at the Home, packed
and hardened from five yea.rs' use, have been remade; and an infinite number
of minor improvements and repairs have been ma.de.
Bro. Sanderson's labor of love in making headboards for the graves of our
dea4 who rest in Cypress Cemeliery, Decoto, has been finished, and the boards
placed in position.
During the first part of the year, our water supply got dangerously low, and
all our plumbing was carefully gone over and repaired. It will probably be
necessary to install a. pumping plant over the spring by the boys' playground.
This spring flows some five thousand gallons a day ; and by using it as au
accessory feeder for the reservoir, we could always be assured of a. supply of
water sufficient not only for household use but for fire protection as well. '
Wi~h this report, I bid farewell to the Home where I have lived and worked
for nearly six yea.rs. Though still young and with all my life as an independent practitioner tOlook eagerly forward to, it is not possible to leave surroundings with which I have been so long familiar and to part from those with
whom I have been so closely associated, without many a heartache. To my
successor in office I wish Godspeed; to the Home I wish continued prosperity
and success. And I wish to express to the members of the Board of Tr11steee,
-on my own and on my wife's behalf, our appreciation and our gratitude for
their uniforn courtesy and kindness.
Respectfully submitted,

I. R. AIKIN, M. D.

DEAR Srns AND BRETHREN-The Masonic Board of Relief of the City of
Los Angeles presents the foll..,wing report of its labors from October lst,
1903, to Qctober lst, 1904, as follows :

881

Golden State, U. D · · · · ·

•

···· · ····

l

.
Willis Milnor Dixon,
J ~hn Leland Jones.
j oh'n Hill Bean,

The year 1903-04 has been on.e calling for much relief from this Board,
owing in a great measure to the enormous building activity in our city, the
lower rates of transportation and the labor disturbances in the East. This
has driven laborers and mechanics to .the Pacific. Coast. Positions being filled
•before their arrival, the brethren ·w ere left' stranded, relief being necessary.
w~ hue noticed with much sorrow the increase of the impostors, the .
detection of whom is sometimee next to impossible. They are persis~ent and
many times insulting.
Reimbursements from sister jurjsdietfons have been quite good. Just
recently Alabama has made a generous contribution to relieve the distress of
the widow and two children of one of its deceased members.

882

PROCEED INGS OF THE

[Oct. 11,

Funerals.c onducted under the auspices of this Boa.rd of Relief have been
fairly well attended, although a still larger attendance would be appreciate d.
And right here it might not be out of place to state how we secure the good
·
attendance we get.
At the request of this Board of Relief, the Master of each ' Lodge in the
city, at each stated meeting, appoints what is known as a Funeral Committee
whose duty it is to attend all funerals coming under the auspices of the Boa.rd
of Relief during the current month. This they are expected to do either in
person or to provide a. substitute' who will represent them at said funeral.
Lodges havi.iJ.g 100 members or less appoint 3 members; 100 to 200 appoint 5
members ; 200 to 400 appoint 8 members ; above 400 appoint 12 members ea.ch ;
giving r.s a committee of seventy-th ree.
The names and addresses of this committee are furnished the Secretary of
this Board, and on the death of a visiting brother the Secretary of this Board
serves a written notice on each member of the Funeral Committee , by special
messenger, giving him full informatio n as to hour and place of meeting. We
provide a apecial car for use of the Funeral Committee , and generally have it
comfortabl y, and sometimes uncomforta bly, filled. We have found the foregoing method quite satisfactory .
The following is a list of funerals which this Board of Relief has been
called upon for burials <luring the past yea.r:Member ot Lodge.

ALABAMA.

This Grand Lodge held its Eighty-third Annual Communication
tu the City of Montgomery on the first and second days of December, 1903,~the M:. w:. Robert J. Redden, Grand Master; the R.".
.w:. George A. Beauchamp, Grand Secretary. Three hundred and
fifteen Lodges were represented with twenty-five other Grand
Jurlsdlctlons. Two Past Grand Masters were vresent.

892

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 11,

The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form with prayer by
the Reverend Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master delivered his Annual Address.
He presented to the Grand Lodge a practical business paper,
embracing, it seems to us, everything of importance and interest
to the Grand Lodge of Alabama. Of his decisions he tells us:
"Many questions Involving Masonic law have been submitted to
me during the year. The majority of these were so distinctly covered by existing edicts, that I only directed the enquirers to the
particular edict covering the case in question for its solution."
He is an earnest advocate of the establishment of a Masonic
Home, although not confident of its immediate adoption by Grand
Lodge-as the question had been submitted to the Lodges, and the
returns indicated in favor of the proposed Home, 159 with 220
against the proposition, it would have required 259 to pass the
measure. In the enactment of so great a responsibility, we would
"make haste slowly," as the brethren of Alabama have .resolved in
this matter.

The following Is a Decree by the Grand Master:
"1.- That the Freemasons of this Jurisdiction are absolutely prohibited from taking part in any way in the formation, In this Republic, of Craft Lodges other than those which may be established
under warrant of the Grand Lodge of Oosta Rica.
"2.-Those Brethren who assist in the formation of such L-Odgee
thereby commit a Muson1c crime of the gravest d<escription (see
Article No. 286, Paragraph 3, of the Code), and render themselves
liable to the penalties provided in Article No. 209 of the Code.
"3.- Any Lodge In Costa Rica, warranted by a Bodiy other than
the Grand Lodge of Costa Rica, is hereby declared Clandestine (see
Articles Nos. 12, 13 and 78 of the Code), and its members also Clan-destine.
"4.-It is forbidden to all Masons of this Jurisdiction to in any
manner hold Masonic relations with Clandestine Lodges or their
members.
"I hereby comm8.Ilid that the above Decree shall be read by the
Worshipful Master, or the occupant of the Chair, of each Lodge in
this Jurisdiction, at each of the four meetings following the date of
its receipt; the fact of it so being read shall be placed on the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

911

The Master of a Lodge in Buenos Ayres having addressed a com·
munication to the Grand Secretary requesting a Warrant of Constitution for his Lodge (in view of the Masonic entanglement existing In the Argentine Republic), the Grand Master answered that the
Cuban Grand Lodge exercises jurisdiction over the Island of Cuba
only, and that solely with the object of establishing in another coun,.
try, of as yet unoccupied Masonic territory, a sovereign Grand
Lodge independent of Supreme Councils or other high bodies, could
this Grand Lodge grant temporary warrants to three or more Lodges
in such countries (as was done some years ago in t he case of
Mexico), so that such Lodges rruight at once proceed to form their
own Grand Lodge. In this manner only, that ls to say, provisionally and passingly, could the Grand Master of this Grand Lodge
recommend the admiss1on of Lodges founded in the Argentine Republic; not for the purpose of exercising jurisdiction over that t erritory, but in order to give it the benefit of a Sovereign Grand Lodge,
whereby perhaps the organl?..ation In that Republic of Masonry in
regularly acknowledged form miglit be achieved thus completely
doing away with hybrid organizations, in whose shade the Ancient
Fraternity of Free and Accepted MasoDS can never thrive.
According to the statutes of the Grand Lodge, ordinary soldiers
cannot be initiated in the order, and the Grand Master therefore
ruled that simple guards, corporals and sergeants cannot be admitted.
This decision is in harmony with the former rules of the Grand
Lodge and of the Committee on Juris.prudence, rendered on the subject.
Various copies (Volume II, Nos. 11-18, 1903) of the official
periodical entitled "El Ideal Mas0nlco," published in Sancti Spiritus,
have reached us and we gratefully acknowledge the courtesy. They
contain Lodge reports and other Items of Masonic news, and are
issued by authority of one of the constituent Lodges called "Amor
y Verdad."
'
The previous Grand Officers have been re-elected, a good proof
that the old-fashioned Masonic platform upon which the present
head of the Cuban Craft stands is thoroughly endorsed by the leading members of this Jurisdiction. We rejoice at the f1ourishing
condition which our Masonic brethren on the Island of Cuba enjoy
to such great extent.

This report is by Past Grand Master G. W. BaJrd, and is a most
excellent practical review of the transactions, virtual!~, of the
Masonic world, with conclusions Fendered in a paper of 145 pages.
Bro. Baird reviews California in its Fifty-third Annual Session
under the reign of M. ·. W. ·. William S. Wells. He commends the
Grand Master's report of duties performed in matters of official
visitation and the discharge of official duties.
In noting our mention of the case of Holmes in last year's report,
.be says: "The true version is this: Holmes, an officer in the"U. S.
Navy, was made a Mason in a Scottish Lodge at Nagasaki; a · negro
member of the Lodge was present. When Hobnes's ship vJ..s ited
Canton he essayed to visit a Lodge there, but, on discovering that
two firemen from his ship (who happened to be·negroes) were already

916

PROCEEDINGS qF THE

[Oct. 11,

in the Lodge, he refused to go in and sit with them because they
were members of a clandestine Lodge in Brooklyn, N. Y.; a Lodge
.which descended from Prince Hall. The purpose of Holmes m
writing to our Grand Lodge, where be now belongs, . was to advise
that some means be taken to inform the English Lodge at Oanton
which were the legitimate and which the illegitimate Lodges in the •
United States. There is a pressing need for such information all
over the world."
