The Grand Lodge held its One Hundred and Seventeenth Annual
Communication in Masonic Temple, Macon, commencing October
27, 1904,-M:. w:. Max Meyerhardt, Grand Master; R.'. w:. W. A.
W:olihln, Grand Secretary. Four hundred and thirty-nine Lodges
were represented, together ·with fifty-six other Grand .Turisdictions.
Two Past Grand Masters, one Past Grand Deputy Grand Master, a
Past Grand Treasurer and a Past Grand Warden were in attendance.
Past Grand Master W .. A.. Davis. introduced several visiting
Brethren from other Jurisdictions, who were received and welcomed.
The (}rand Master then delivered his Annual Address. With
thanks to the Great Creator for His continued favors extended to
the Masons of Georgia, the Grand Master, in eloquent words,
addressed the Brethren. The force and power of words to impress
a great truth will not be denied. To be able, not only to commun1cate but to explain the mysteries of Freemasonry is a priceless gift
and a fitting qualification for one called to preside over the "Sons
of Light." We quote his opening words·, rather than mar their
beauty by attempted description. The Grand Master said:
"My Brethren: In the harbor of New York stands a magnificent
statue, holding with uplifted hand a flaming torch. This statue was
presented by the Republic of France to the Republic of the United
States, and ls called 'Liberty Enlighten~ the World.' Its illuminating rays are seen far out at sea and shine brightly in the darkest
night. Beautifully does u· typify the sacred light of Freedom for
which our great Republic stan&.
"Uncounted thousands who have left their native lands in the old
world to carve out a new career under the American flag have beheld
with delight the statue of Liberty as they neared our shores. Its
flaming torch was to thein a symbol of the new life upon whlch
they were about to enter. In the old world they left darkness,
persecution, and despair. In the new world they found light, liberty,
nnd hope. What pen can describe the thrill of ecstasy that animated
the hearts of these unnumbered hosts when their eyes fell in raptureupon this splendid statue of 'Liberty Enlightening the World'?
"My Brethren, Freemasonry has erected no statue of brome or
stone to symboliize its beautiful truths. But on the brow and in the
heart of every true Mason ls written in letters of living flame the
glorious fiat, 'Let there be light!' In the darkness of ignorance; in
the shadow of persecution; under the lowering clouds of hate; even

1904.]

GRAND LODGE OF 0ALIFOllNIA.

925

in benighted lands, Masonry has ever. proclaimed, 'Let there be
light!' In the face of kingcraft and of priestcraft, which would
fetter the mind and dwarf the soul of man, Masonry still bravely,
nobly declares, 'Let there be light.'
"And so it is that in lieu of statues and monuments, in lieu of
codes and creeds, Maso:Qry inscribes upon her banners the one grand,
creative word 'Light.' That word has converted ignorance into
knowledge, evil into goodi. It has d.issipated the forces of fanaticism
and unrighteousness. It has broken down the barriers of sect and
creed. It has shattered the clariklng chains of oppression and despotism. It has guided men from out the blighting realms of hate
into the beautiful Kingdom of Love.
"With this same banner floating proudly above us, with 'Light'
for our motto, with love for our guiding-star, we meet once more
in this Temple erected to God, to enter upon th.is, our One Hundred
and Seventeenth Annual Communication. Never in all our splendid
history has such a gathering assembled upon our tasselated floor.
You have come' in magnificent Ilillmbers to represent right worthily
the 25,000 tried and true Masons of Georgia. You have come with
purest motives and most unselfish purposes to gather about our
Altar and offer up to the Great Architect of the Universe the sweet
Incense of your loyal devotion. With a heart overflowing with
grateful thanksgiving, I greet you, my beloved Brethren, with tidings
of good cheer.
"The past year has been one of rinparalleled prosperity to
Masonry in this Jurisdiction. The surph1s in our treasury ha.s increased to wonderful proportions. Not a single charter has been
forfeited. Three dispensations for new Lodges have been granted
and a number of charters will be granted at this Communication.
'l'here has been a substantial increase in our membership. Our
peace and harmony have not been disturbed by any untoward event.
And, above all, our Brethren are an.imated by fervency and zeal,
and by the genuine spirit of Masonry.
"Truly and thankfully let us praise God, whose mercy endureth
forever.''
Again in most eloquent words did the Grand Master pay Fraternal and affectionate tribute to the Brethren who during the past year
had put on immortality, not forgetting those who had worked in
the qualTies of other Jurisdictions. With earnest words he urged
continued and renewed efforts. in strengthening and upbuilding of
the Georgia H~me.
His visitations were many, requiring more than 3,000 miles of
travel, which enabled him to "look into the faces· of more thaD
four thousand Georgia Masons.''

Of the Grand Master's Decisions, they are so plain and COlllprehensive that ·w e are prepared in advance to note their approval

·of "Give Us Men:"
"Brethren, the crying need of this age is men-men of thought,
men of deed, men of conviction, aggressive, stalwart men.
"In this day we do n.-0t want weaklings, moral cowards, trimrucris,
without backbone, without stamina, ready to bend to every breeze,
willing to s'wim with the popular current, n-0 matter where that
current may lead.
"In Church and State, in politics and society, and. above all, in
Masonry, we need earnest, upright, God-fearing men. We have no
room for him wb-0 places money above booor, selfishness above
righteousness, passion above virtue, power and place above manhood and iilltegrity, Mammon above God. We have no room for
those who worship the golden calf, who bow down before the idols
of pleasure and frivolity, who waste their God-given talents in
idleness and dissipation. We need t()-day men -0f pure hearts, men
of clean lives, men who are willing to sacrifice all upon the altar
of truth, who are willing to live for it, and, if need be, to die for it.
"We need men like Abraham, who shattered his father's idols,
and who, when God called him, exclaimed: 'Here am I!' We need
men like Moses, who dared. to say to· the mighty Pbaroab, 'Let my
people go free!' We need men like Isaiah, who, with burning zeal
a~d fiery eloquence, denouniced the sins of bis people. We need men
like John the Baptist, who passed like a flaming meteor through
the land, proclaiming to a sin-steeped world, 'Repent! for the Kingdom of God is at band!' We need men like Judas Maccabeus, that
great hero who fought with bis bands while be prayed unto God
with his heart. We need men like Mordecai, who prostrated-not
himself before Haman, and who would not bend the knee to unrighteous power. We need men who dare to rebuke iniquity in high
places as well as in low, who dare to cry aloud against the sins
of the nation and spare not.
"Brethren, you who preside over the Craft, you who are the
leaders and teachers of your people, to whom they look for light
and guidance-upon you devolve great duties and serious responsibilities. Purge your Lodges. Purify your membership. Raise high
the standard of Masonry in your communities. Do your duty manfully and bravely, without fear and without favor. Scrutinize
-closely the character of those who seek to enter .your inner door.

<loes not measure up to the full standard of a man. Keep out no

The Grand Lodge· held its Sixty-fourth Annual Communication
in the city of Chicago, convening October 6, 1903,-the M.". W.".
George M. Moulton, Grand Master; R.". W.". J. H. C. Dill, Grand
Secretary. Seven hundred and fifteen Lodges were represented,
together with forty-one other Grand Jurisdictions. Nine Past Grand
Masters were in attendance.
After prayer by the Grand Chaplain, the Grand Lodge was opened
in Ample Form.
The Grand Master delivered his Annual Address. He gave frat ernal welcome to the Brethren, and congratulated them upon an
increased roll of membership, which at the close of the year represented sixty-seven thousand good and true Free and Accepted
Masons.
But, with his congratulations, he referred to the ever-present
death roll, upon which was r ecorded the names of ten hundred and
two of their late associates in the. Constituent Lodges of the Juris-diction-an army of the dead. After paying fraternal tribute to
several of the elders whose names were inscribed thereon, he said:
"From the reports filed by our Lodges with the R.". W.". Grand
Secretary we are advised of the demise of ninety-six of our Brethren who have presided in the Oriental Chair by election. These
chosen of our Brethren have joined the elect in the Celestial Lodge
above, where our Supreme Master fo,r ever presides. Let us reverently attend to the reading of their names."
His reported Decisions were few and none require comment.
Although not as much affected by clandestine Masonry as our
Brethren of the "other side of the river,'' we believe his action in'
the issuance of his encyclical letter of sufficient interest to warrant
the re-publication here, and we quote:
"FBOM THE EAST OF THE MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND LODGE OF ANCIENT
FREE AND ACCEPTED MASONS OF THE STATE OF ILLINOIS.

"To the Wor8hipful Master8, Warden8, and Brethren of the Oon8tituent
Lodges of our Jurisdiction:
"Brethren: Certain advertisements have recently appeared ·In
the daily papers of Chicago, and circular letters issued by one J. E.
Furniss, the purport of which is to induce applications from the
unwary to become charter members or otherwise, of an alleged
Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons under the 'authority of

932

PROCEEDINGS 011' '!.'HE

[Oct. 11,

the Grand Lodge of Ancient,. Free and Accepted Masons of Ohio,' of
which one Justin Pinney claims to be the Grand Master. The principal
illiducement offered seems to be a reduction in fees, although even
the minor sum acceptable to this degree-monger far exceeds the
value of his wares, the worth of which is merely represented by the
gratification of a morbid curiosity to know something of the forms
and ceremonies of our institution.
"The organization referred to, which is engaged in the reprehensible practice of violating the traditions, obligations and regulations
of Ancient Craft Masonry, although permitted to have a corporate
existence by the laws of the State of Ohio, from a Masonic standpoint is clandestine and irregular, and the Masonry which its emissary seeks to Impart is spurious. The so-called Grand Lodge which
he represents is originally composed. entirely of seceders from the
regularly organized and duly recognized Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of Ohio, who from pique, disappointed
ambition, mental weakness, or other unworthy motive, have deliberately violated their obligations, and shown utter disregard of
the landmarks of Masoil!l'Y. Their dupes may be objects of pity,
but their mission is too contemptible to be adequateiy characterized
In words.
"All genuine brethren will discountenance these dissenters from
the original plan of Masonry and their work. Should aey of your
friends inquire of you regarding the solicitations and efforts of these
disturbers of harmony, warn them of the illegitimacy of their organization, and that no genuine brother or regular Lodge of Ancient
Craft Mallonry, will accord them recognition as 'Masons; neither will
any of the recognized organizations of the Masonic system, Chapter,
Commandery, or Scottish Rite admit them to their membership.
"Until otherwise ordered, all Lodges will require from visiting
brethren who are not regularly vouched for, In addition to the usual
'strict trial and due examination,' competemt documentary evidence
that they are members of, or have regularly withdrawn from, some
regular Lodge working under the authority of, and In obedience to,
some Grand Lodge which has received fraternal recognition from
our M:. W/. Grand Lodge, before admitting them to the Communications of the Lodge.
"The pamphlet enclosed gives a list of the regular Lodges of the
several Graoo Jurisdictions. Examining Committees will in-variably
assure themselves that a visiting brother gives convincing proof
of being or having been a member of one of these regular Lodges
before recommending his admission to their Lodge.
"A copy of this encyclical was mailed to every individual Mason
affiliated with the Lodges in Cook County, and I feel assured that

materially aided in exposing the nefarious workings of these

"We begin our review of the Proceedings of the various

" 'Where the spirit of mortal may worship
In the freedom of Unwritten creeds,
Hearing many and joyous responses
In the music that comes from the reeds;
And where in my fancy I've pictured
A temple that's builded so high,
It reaches In grandest proportions
From the beautiful.lake to the sky."

The Grand Lodge being in order, the Grand Master proceeded

With a few words of pleasant comment upon the early summer
weather, the existing peace and prosperity with the work of the
year as applied to Grand Lodge bus~ness, he proceeded to co~ider

Decisions reported, being governed by the local law, we presume to
be according to Iowa laws and usage. He reported the placing of
two corner-stones, of proposed school houses, by the Craft at Garden
Grove and at Bloomfield.
"One of the pleasantest parts of the year," he says, "has been
that devoted to visitation."
His tribute to the Fraternal Dead of the year, with his conclusions, was both feeling and eloquent.

Fraternity, the names of Brothers Woodbury, of Colorado; Staton, of

Pennsylvania; Horton, of Vermont; and Bouck, of Wisconsin-their
names are as pass words of the Fraternity. We quote the closing
-Of. this timely and appropriate report:
"Quite too soon this annual gathering will close; hands· will be
dasped in farewell, and good-byes be spoken-with some for the·
last time. Yet shall we part in hope, and with courage undaunted
go to our work, though knowing full well that some will weary and
fall out by the way ere again the June roses bloom and the Grand
Master's gavel calls the Craft to labor.
"But the wearied workers who 'rest from their labors' are not
forgotten, neither do they forget. They abide with us-do we not
.abide with them? The break in the ranks· is but temporary. They
'who _have gone are in detached service, but they are still of the

[Oct. 11_.

army. Their valiant service here we cherish as a holy memory to
incite us to better and nobler living; ls not that memory also a ground
of confideuce that they who were true and valiant here will be no
less true and valiant wherever they are? If there be a doubt, let it
be of ourselves, and that only as a spur to more heroic endeavor
to prove ourselves worthy of the noble companionships which have
made life so richly worth living. So shall we best honor the deadwho yet live; so shall we best do our part to cheer the world, and
make its burden lighter while we stay, and ·win the love which will
keep us in sacred remembrance when we pass to rest and reward."
"It sometimes happens that two friends will meet,
And, with a smile and touch of hands, again
Go on their way along the noi~y street,
Each is so sure of all the friendship sweet,
The loving silence gives no thought of pain.
And so I think those friends whom we call <lead
Are with us. It may be some quiet hour,
Or time of busy work for hand or bead,
Their love fills all the heart that missed them so,
They bring a s~eet assurance of the life
Serene, above the worry that we know;
And we grow braver for the comfort brought.
Why should we mourn because they do not speak
Our words that lie so far below their thought?"

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE,

Bro. Joseph E. Morcombe, the author of the present report,' writes
a paper full of life and vigor. The one before us reviews Qalifornia
for the Fifty-fourth Annual, the administration of Grand Master
Henderson. The Grand Master had a busy year, as Bro. Morcombe
discovered, by his reported work fully accounted for. Referring to
our comment last year upon the question of the right of avoucbment,
he says :
"Evidently our intended sarcasm was of too· dull a point. But is
it not likewise true, Bro. Davies, that members .of a Lodge are not
supposed, as such, to have knowledge of any other of the concordant
orders? It might be possible to imagine a case where one qualified
to sit in Chapter or Commandery was nevertheless ineligible to
participate with his Brethren in the Lodge."
Not in California,. Bro. Morcombe. There has been no time in
the history of the Grand Lodge of California when a Mason, of
however high degree, could sit in Chapter, Council, or Commandery
unless he were a Master Mason in good standing; we were built
upon the lirn~s of dependent membership. Bro. Morcombe's report
is a fine one and worthy its place in the handsome book it is a pa~t
of.
M.". w.·. Sumner Miller, Grand Master; R.'. w:. Newton R.
Parvin, Grand Secretary. Correspondent, Bro. Joseph E. Morcombe,
Cedar Rapids.

W.'. Alex L. Van Arsdall, Chairman of the Committee ou

We quote the following from the report of the Committee on
Ritual as a matter -of general importance to the Craft:
"At the last Annual Communlcation a motion was made to change
the Grand Honors of this Grand. Jurisdiction, and the question was
referred to this Committee for report at this time. As full Investigation as possible has been had, with the result that the members of
the Committee believe and recommend that the Grand Honors, except
f-0r funerals, be changed. As a result of research and personal Inquiry,
the Committee feel justified in ·saying to you that the Grand Honors
of Masonary are three, viz.: private, public, and funeral. The private
Grand Honors are the signs and dueguards of the three degrees.
The public Grand Honors are given by striking the palms of the
hands together 'three times three,' as now used for the private
Grand Honors in this Jurisd.iction. The funeral Grand Honors are
a.s they are now used in this Jurisdiction. The Committee recommended that you specify and adopt the foregoing as the Grand
Honors of this Grand Jurisdiction."

Master's Jewel, by Grand Master Fitch, as a testimonial from
personal friends.
The Grand Master named the committees, and the Grand Lodge
was closed in Ample Form, with prayer by the Grand Chaplain.
REPORT ON Co:imESPONDENCE.

Past Grand Master William M. Shaver represents the Grand
Lodge of Kansas in the matter of Correspondence,. and we .learn
with some surprise that there should have been any kicking at his
report. We learn, however, from himself that "such things have
been." As Bro. Shaver says In the number before us:
"Our previous efforts have been criticised as 'too lengthy.' The
only answer that can be made to such a criticism is that consclentlously 'to review and report upon' the Proceedings of fifty American Grand Lodges, as well as a number of representative foreign
Jurisdictions, in this ctay of action, requires space. However, as we
believe the criticism is a just one, we shall endeavor to keep this
report 'down.' The only way in which this can successfully be
accomplished, as we view it, is to eliminate excerpts as much as

1904.J

GnAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

947

possible. This we will strive to do. Whether it wlll improve or
Injure the report remains to be proven. We shall still aim to present
a comprehensive view of the 'doings' in the Masonic world of to-day,
and for this reason bespeak your careful attention to the report
which follows."
And, as thus amended, Bro. Shaver submitted a report of 345
pages, and it's good matter, every page of it. He reviews our
Fifty-third Annual and the administration of Grand Master
Wells. His review ls full, complete, and not uncharitable in comments.
He demurs to the location of our report in the bowels of the
Journal, but that is a matter to settle with the Grand Secretary.

KENTUCKY.

The Grand Lodge of Kentucky, under the escort of "The Masonic
Home Drum and Trumpet Corps,'' on the 20th of October, 1903,'
marched to the site of the new Masonic Temple in Louisville,
whereon the "Masonic" had been erected and was declared ready
for dedication to the uses and purposes of Freemasonry.
The scene was unique and. beautiful. The childxen of the
"Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home" were seated on the large
stage, the .s eats being elevated like steps upwards towards the rear;
at either side, in front, the Grand Officers were seated-an Altar and
'
Great Lights in the center.
The children sang "Hail, Universal Lord," and the President of
the Home, Bro. T. L. Jeft'erson, addiressed the Grand Master, presenting to the Grand Lodge the 245 happy childxen of the Home.
After an eloquent response by the Grand Master, the children
eang "When the Saints Come Marching."
The Grand Marshal the "daddy" of all the good children in ·
Kentucky, Bro. William Ryan, preseillted to the Grand Master one
of his girls, who, on behalf of the 245 children and the widows of
the Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home of Kentucky, presen-ted to
him a bouquet of beautiful flowers.
Grand Master :M.ndrum received the gift with thanks and kissed
the attractive young miss, and proceed<ed with the Ceremolllies of

The Grand Lodge held its On~ Hundred, and Third Annual Communication in the Masonic Temple, commendng October 20, 1903,M.'. W.'. John W. Landrum, Grand Master; R.'. W.'', Henry B.
Grant, Grand Secretary. Four hundred and seventy-six Lodges
were represented. Twenty-two Past Grand Masters were in attendance.
A portrait of Grand Master Landrum appears 011 the opening
page of the Journal.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, and the Grand
Master delivered his Annual Address. After a fraternal welcome
he said:
"As becometh Masons, we have reverently listened to "the invocation by our Most Reverend Grand Chaplain, and responded. 'So
mote it be.' I devoutly hope that this indicates our hearts' gratitude
for the blessings that have been poured upon the era.ft and our
country, and I pray that the Grand Architect of the Universe may
ever plan and direct the buildirng of our moral and Masonic characters, so that we shall at last meet with his approval."
He, as a first duty to a personal f-tiend and Brother, announced
the death of Past Grand Master James W. Staton, to whose memory
he paid affectionate fraternal tribute, and it remained for the Committee- on Necrology to complete the record for the Grand Lodge
Archives.
The Grand Master also embraced the opportunity to speak a few
kind word•s of a living veteran of Kentucky Masons, Bro. Thomas
Todd. We quote his words:
"In 1853, fifty ~ars ago, our dearly beloved Todd, who Is still
living and with us to-day, was elected Grand Master of the Grand
Lodge of Kentucky. Since then he has been punctual in attendance
upon this Grand Body, performing with wisdom and zeal every duty
assigned, and he stands to-day the honored and oldest living Past
Grana. Master of Kentucky. May he yet live many years and continue in the enjoyment of the honors which he has received and in
the love and reverence of his Brethren."
No important decisions were reported.
After giving a pleasant account of his visitations to his Constituent· Lodges and a few earnest words for the Home, he says,
because he couldn't keep it back any longer:
"And now comes Grant! The good, Christian man; the peerless
Secretary, whose knowledge and skill is so necessary and so ready

for the use of a Grand Master; whose merit is beyond computation,

The following action was had In remembrance of a "good man."
God give him rest:
"Past Grand Master J. Soule Smith, for the Special Committee on
the death of Past Grand Master James W. Staton, presented the following report. Eulogistic words were spoken by Past Grand Master
Bernard G. Witt, Past Grand Master W. LaRue Thomas, and Past
Grand Master J. Soule Smith, and the report was adopted by a
rising vote, viz. :
"To the Most Worshipful (}r(ll/Uf, Lodge of Kentucky:

"Sweetness and gentleness are strength. God works not so much
through His earthquakes and storms, as through the smiling sun,
the gentle dew, the rain which falleth silently. So, in the lives of
men, His word is often known by that which emanates from those,
who, like a star-unhasting and unresting-do what they believe
to be His will. Such was our Bro. Staton. Quiet, courteous, gentle,
calm, yet always firm, in every place he was himself-man, made in
God's own image, an exemplar of God's truth.
"We lose in him a counselor most wise; a man whose learning ·
only could be equaled by his modesty; a Mason brave and free,
inflexible in any trust, as tender as· the violet, as steadfast as the
rock. Fear could not move his soul, nor envy stir his heart, both
were in service to the right. Now, therefore, be it here
"Resolved, That in. the death of our beloved Brother, we have
su1Iered serious l_oss, andJ. Masons everywhere will mourn with. us.
Let these few feeble words be spread upon our records, that those
who shall come after us may know we loved and honored him, and
a copy furnished his family as a testimony of our sympathy.''

The Grand Lodge of Minnesota held its fifty-first Annual Communication in the City of St. Paul, commencing January 20, 1904,M:. ·w:. Henry R. Adams, Grand Master; R:. w: .. Thomas Montgomery, Grand Secretary. Two hundred !UJ,d twenty-three Lodges
were represented, together with forty-one other Grand Jurisdictions.
Ten Past Grand Masters, one Past Deputy Grand Master, and six
Past Grand Wardens were in attendance.
A handsome portrait of the Grand Master appears on the opening
page.
The Grand Lodrg e was opened in Ample Form with prayer by the
Grand Chaplain.
· ·
The Grand Master named the committees and then proceeded to
deliver his Annual Address.
A poetical quotation with a cordial and fraternal welcome were
the Grand Master's introduction to the duties of tlie Fifty-first
Annual Communication. His opening wo'fds were poetically expressed, shadowed, perhaps, by the thoughts that were to follow
under the head of "Necrology." On his reported death roll were
Inscribed the names of 259 Brethren, whom he said "have wandered
upon the shell-lined beach and drunk in the music of the waves
that break upon eternity's shore."

Inspired by his subject, he said: " Brethren, arise and reverently
listen while I recall the names of the permanent members of this
Grand Lodge who have wandered into an unknown land and left
us thinking how very fair it must be since they linger there."
· He paid affectionate tribute to Past Grand Master Royal Hatch
Cove and Past Deputy Grand Master Wm. Tuttle Rigby, who had
put on immortality.
He closed his repl>rt of the Fraternal Dead with these beautiful
lines:

'fhe promise of a gracious God,
That all shall meet among the blest."

The Grand Master announced the committees and proceeded to
deliver his Annual Address..
·
He welcomed the famlllar faces and to old and new members
extended a hearty welcome, and then, as his first duty to the
a.ssembled Brethren, said:
"Before entering upon this work, it is becoming that we kneel at
our sacred altar. and through our Grand Chaplain return thanks
to our Heavenly Father for his watchful care over us, for th~
many blessings He has so graciously bestowed, and to implore His
presence at our deliberatioDS of this annual session."
.
In his consideration of the death roll of the year he commented
with much feeling upon the passing away of Past Junior Grand

Warden Algernon M. Roak and Past Grand Master Joseph Alvah
Locke. Of Brother Locke the Grand Master in part said:
"Joseph Alvah Locke rendered to the memory of one of our late
Past Grand Masters. Little d'id we then. realize that before the year
:should pass, those lips would be silent, and that it would be for
others to speak in testimony o~ the nobility of character and beauty
-0f the life of him who gave us such eloquent words on that occasion;
~t that time he seemed to be in.prime health, with every indication
of being with us to-day. But such are the uncertainties of this life,
that we cannot anticipate what the future has for any of us.
"As his health had become somewhat impaired, accompanied by
his daughter, he went South, In the hope of obtaining recuperation,
but was soon obliged to return home, where, after a few short days,
he passed on to the eternal life on Fast day, Thursday, April 21,
1904, at the age of 60 years, 3 months, 28 days.
"Funeral services were held on Sunday afternoon, April 24, 1904,
in the Chestnut Street Methodist Church in this city, of which he
had been a faithful member for many years.

The Grand Lodge of Montana held a Special Communication
April 24, 1903, for placing the corner-stone of the Memorial Arch
to be erected at the entrance to the .Yellowstone National Park.
Additional interest was given to the ceremonial by the presence of
President Roosevelt on the occasion. The Grand Lodge was opened
in the hall of Uvingston Lodge, No. 32,-M. ·. W. ·. Frank E. Smith,
Grand Master; R.". w:. Cornelius Hedges being Grand Secretary,
and proceeded to the site of the proposed/ Arch.
Upon the arrival of the President at the site, the Grand Master
commanded silence and stated the purpose of the assemblage and
invited all to unite with the Grand Chaplain in an invocation to the
Grand Architect of the Universe. The box having been prepared,
many articles of interest were placed for deposit, among others;
portraits of Hon. N. P. Langford, the first Superintendent, who was
one of the Washburn party of 1870, and Cornelius Hedges, member
of the same party, who first suggested making the present National
Park; the papers of the day, etc..
When the box was closed and ·in place, the Grand Master passed
the trowel to the President, who spread the cement, and then the
stone was lowered to its place with the public Grand Honors.
, The stone was tested by the implements of Masonry and pro-.
nounced well formed, truly laid and correctly proved.
The elements of consecration were then poured upon the stone
and their significance interpreted:.
The working tools were returned to the Chief Architect, and
proclamation made by the Grand Mars·h al.
From a nearby stand the President delivered a stirring and very
appropriate address, setting forth the purposes of the Park, its
dedication to the pleasure and instruction of all the people of all

five thousand people, the Grand Master presented the President
with a handsome gold nugget Masonic cP,arm, suitably tnscribed.
· The weather was fine, the scene rough and rugged, but the

HEZEKIAH LORD HOSMER.

"Born at Hudson, N. Y., December 10, 1814.
"Died in San Francisco, .Oalifornia, October 31, 1893.
"The- sub-joined! is a sketch of Judge Hezekiah ~· Hosmer, the
first Chief Justice of Montana, and for two years (1870-1871) Grand
Secretary of our Grand Lodge, succeeding Past Grand Masters
Sanders and Star in that office, resigning in 1872, when he removed
to San Francisco, during the Grand Mastership of Grand Master
J. R. Weston, who first appointed the present incumbent to that
office, which he has held by successive elections to the present
time. He prepared two reports on Foreign Correspondence which
appeared in our Proceedings of 1871-1872. A larger and fuller
sketch of his life appears in the third volume of the published
transactions of the Historical Society of Montana, 1890, accompanied by a faithful picture.
"Knowing him well but not intimately, we prefer to give the
sketch prepared by his son, J. Allen Hosmer, of the firm of Hosmer
and Paddock, attorneys at law, Hayward Building, San Francisco.
"Judge Hosmer was twice married. A son andi a daughter by
his first' wife, together with his second wife are still living in
California.
"We will only add that Judge Hosmer; both by taste and ex"
perience, was· an elegant and interesting writer, and in Masonry,
especially in the Orders of the Tempi~. which he loved most, was
an accomplished and impressive ritualist. He is kindiy remembered
in Montana by all his old associates and friends.
"C.H."
"Hezekiah L. Hosmer was born at Hudson, New York; on the
10th day of December, 1814, of Connecticut parents. He received
his early schooling at Oxford, Chenango County, New York, and at
the age of sixteen went to Cleveland, Ohio, where he studied law
under John W. Allen, a kinsman, who was then in active practice
in that city. He was adimitted to the bar in 1835, practiced for a
year at Painsville, and in 1836 moved to the Maumee Valley, where
he resided until 1861, for a portion of the time at Maumee Olty, later
at Perrysburgh, and finally at Toledo. During his residence at these
places he practiced law and' devoted a portion of the time to literature and politics. He was an ardent Whig while that party lasted,
and joined the Republican party in 1860, to the principles of which
party he adhered until his death. He was for some years the editor

1904.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

971

and part proprietor of the Toledo Blade, and was the author of the
novel 'Octoroon,' which was published Ln 1859, and upon which
.13<>ucicault founded a portion of his plot for the play of that name.
In 1861 he went to Wiashington andi became the Secretary of the
House Committee on Territories, of which Mr. Ashley, the Congressman for the Toledo District, was chairman. In this ~apacity
he did a great deal of the work which was later used ID legislation in the formation of the Territories of Dakota, tdaho, and
Montana. Upon the making of Montana as a Territory, he was,
through the inftuence of Secretary Chase and Mr. Ashley, appointed
by President Lincoln its first Chief Justice, a position he held until
1868, a part of his official duties being the organization of the Courts
therein. In 1869 President Grant appointed him postmaster at
Virginia City, a position which he held until he IP.ft Montana in
1872, when he went to San Francisco, California, where he resided
until his death on October 31, 1893. During his residence in San
'.Francisco he held positions in the United States Customs service
and in the State Mining Bureau, besides devoting considerable time
to literary pursuits, publlshing in 1887 a work entitled "Bacon and
Shakespeare in the Sonnets," in which he contended that the Sontiets were written as a cypher explaining that the plays attributed to
Shakespeare were written by Bacon.
"Judge Hosmer was made a Mason in W!Ood County Lodge in
Ohio in 1843, and went ten miles into the woods to receive the deirees, the antipathy to Masonry occl!sioned by the Morgan excitement not having abated at that time. He was exalted as a Royal
Arch Mason in Circleville Chapter · (Ohio) in 1845, and created a
Knight Templar in Toledo Commandery, No. 7, in 1847. He fl.lied
the positions of Master of Rubicon J.i0dge at Toledo, High Priest of
:Fort Meigs Chapter, and Eminent Commander of Toledo Commandery, the latter for a number of years. He was Grand King of the
Grand Chapter of Ohio, Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge of Ohio
at its s~sion of 1851, and Deputy Grand Master of the Grand Lodge
of Ohio. Going to Montana he became Master of Montana Lodge,
No. 2. F. and A. M., and was for six years Commander of "Virginia
City' Commandery. In the Grand Lodge of that Jurisdiction he was
several vears Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence and
two yea~s Grand Secretary. He retained his Blue Lodge membership until his death and his Chapter membership in Ohio. At the
time of his death he was Prelate of Golden Gate Commandery,
No. 16, of San Francisco, a position he had held continuously since
the organization of that Commandery thirteen years before. At that
time he was also Grand Prelate of the Grand Commandery of Cali·
tornia, which office he held the preceding ten years."

Brethren, who now rest from their labors; and as we go forth from

The Grand Lodge of Missouri held its Eighty-third Annual Communication in the city of St. Louis, October 20, 1903,-the R.". w:.
William F. Kuhn, Deputy Grand Master, presiding In the absence
of the Grand Master, John Campbell Yocum, who passed to immortality on the preceding April 26th.
The Deputy Grand, before assuming the station, announced the
death of the Grand Master in the following feeling address:
"IN MEMOBI.A.M.

"John Oampbell Yo<;um, Past Grand Master, died Sunday morning, April 26, 1903, after a l~gering illness, aged 49 years.

1904.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

977

"Our Grand Master had been a patient sufferer for several years,
and in the hope of prolongi.Dg his life he went to Arizona; after a
BOjourn at Phoenix for several months he returned to his home In
Kansas City, unimproved. His indomitable energy sustained his
wasted body, until tired nature sank beneath the strain, and his
gentle, lovable spirit winged its flight to 'that House not made with
hands, eternal in the Heavens.' He died resting calmly in a deep,
firm faith in the 'Lion of the Tribe of Judah.' He was a Christian,
a member of the Presbyterian Church, and one whose belief in religion and Masonry was not a convenience, but a reality and a life.
A calm and gentle soul has left its tenement of clay to meet the
rewards of the just made perfect:
"Bro. Yocum was an attorney at law, and had successfully followed Ws profession all the days of his active life; a man with the
culture of the schools, the refinement and bearing of an ideal gentleman, and the integrity of a true Mason.
"He was born in Pennsylvania, April 23, 1854, of that sterling
combination of Scotch and German· parentage. He was married to
Miss Fannie C. Killinger, Annville, Pa., October 28, 1885. She survives him with two children, Louise K., aged 16 years, and Jacob ·
K., aged 14 years.
He was made a Master Mason April 28, 1885, in Catawissa Lodge,
No. 349, Oatawissa, Pa., in which he served as Junior Warden.
upon Ws' location in Kansas City in 1887 he affiliated with Temple
Lodge, No. 299, in which he served as Senior Steward, Senior Deacon, Warden, and then Master in 1893, and for the last five years
as its Secretary.''

The Grand Master then delivered his Address. After a brie:!'
welcome, he proceeded to deliver an account of his official acts.
In mentioning the "Condition of the Craft" he used these plain
·
'
words:
"The returns will show a larger number of initiations than ever
before in our history, and could we be assured that each and every
candidate had first been prepared in ·his heart to receive the lessons
of the Ancient Craft, the addition of more than one thousand earnest
and zealous Brethren would mean much in the future for all that
Masonry stands for. Just so far, however, as they have been
actuated by improper and unworthy motives, they are an element
of weakness rather than of strength.
"Although this apparent prosperity has been well distributed,
we have a number of very weak Lodges, incapable of doing thei_l'
work with dignity and impressiveness, and still worse. by their lack
o:!' harmony and of the true Masonic character, bringing the Order
into disrepute in the community . . These Lodges should either be
purged and cleansed of their iniquity or be no longer suffered to
exist. I am not a believer in human perfection, but there are
mortal sins even in Masonry, and the Brethren guilty of them should
be made to feel the smart and sting of Masonic discipline."
His Decisions are riot many, and no dictionary is needed to determine their meaning. For instance:
No. 1. That a candidate for Masoury must be a complete man,
with all his natural limbs and capable of making all the requirements of an initiate."

The following interesting letter was received and read by the
Grand Secretary. The medal mentioned was delivered to the Grand
'Master to be by him transferred to the oldest Mason in the State of
Nebraska.
OMAHA, NEB., June 8, 1904.
Most Worshipful Grand M<UJter, Wardens, ana Brethren of the
Grand Lodge of N eb·raska.

. "BRETHREN: It becomes my sad duty to inform you of the demise
of my dear father, Isaac Gibson, who was called to the Supreme
Lodge above, from his old home in Tekamah, Nebraska, April 22.
1904.

"He died, as he had lived for many years, with a heart overflowing with love for the institution of Masonry, and as an evidence o{
the love and esteem in which he was held by his lodge, I will state
that they turned out almost to a man, and went in procession to the
cemetery about one mile distnnt through a pouring rain, with their
empty carriages following the procession, and not one of them
would ride.
"I beg to return herewith a medal which he had proudly borne
upon his breast for several years, as the oldest Mason in this Grand
Jurisdiction, and can only hope that it may be as worthily worn and
as highly appreciated by his venerable successors as It was by my
dear departed father.
"Fraternally yours,
"J. S. GIBSON."
Thursday, .lune 9th, was a gala day for the Grand Lodge, for on
that day the members, escorted by Mt. Calvfil'y Commandery of
Knights Templar of Omaha, repaired to Plattsmouth for the purpose of dedicating the Masonic Home of Nebraska.
Four hundred and fifty-one people were carried on the special
train from Omaha. These, with the Freemasons and citizens of ·
Plattsmouth, made an assembly of more than one thousand people.
It was a perfect June day, with just a cloud here and there, permitting God's sunlight to shine upon those engaged In the greatest
and noblest work that man can find to do--dedicating to charity a
Home where may l;>e sheltered from adrverslty, and where their declining years may be peaceful, contented and happy, all those who
may of necessity become resid~mts thereof.

the Deputy Grand Master. We give the opening words of the
Address:
""'·en Beloved Brethren: With but few exceptions, for the past
fifteen years I have been with you In the Annual Communicati ons
of this Grand Lodge, and it is with pain that now, owing to serious
!llness, I must forego the great pleasure of being with you as your
Grand Master.
"With true Masonic pride I have looked forward to that highest
of high honors, the distinction of presiding over my Brethren in
Grand Lodge assembled; but the Supreme Grand Master has willed
otherwise. He doeth all things well I dlare look up to Him and
say, "Deal with me as Thou wilt; I am Thine." Though I cannot
be with you, Brethren, I send you greeting, and rejoice with you
that our Lodges are prosperous and that peace prevails."
. He reported the death roll of the year, and recommended that
pages be set apart in the Journal "In Memoriam" of the deceased
of our own and Sister Jurisdictions.
·
Of visitations, the Grand Master says:
"Owing to severe illness, which has existed during my entire
term as Grand Master, I have been denied the pleasure of visiting
the several Lodges."
In conclusion, the Grand Master said:

1904.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA .

987

"When elected your Grand Master, although at the time suffering
severe illness, I fervently hoped and confidently expected to be
restored to such health and strength as would enable me to properly
Rdminister the affairs of that important office, if not to the entire
satisfaction of the Craft, at least to my own. In this I have been
sadly disappointed, and aiil a consequence have probably left undone
some things which should have been done; but I am not cognizant
of having done anything which should not have been done.
"As this is probably the last time I shall have the pleasure of
addressing you, I wish to express my gratitude for the many honvrs
you have conferred upon me from time to time, and to assure you
that in my he art of hearts I entertain naught but the sincerest
and purest brotherly love for each and every member of our Grand
Body and for the members of our great Fraternity, wh!thersoeve r
dispersed. Brethren, adieu."

NEW SOUTH WALES.
189 Lodges.

9,378 Master Masons.

Thls volume fclr 1903 contains the transactions of the Grand
Lodge of New South Wales, as shown in their Special Communications and four Quarterlies.
New South Wal~s, the oldest State In the Commonwealth of
Australia, covers 309,175 square miles, . and the Lodges are fairly
well distributed throughout the entire area. Those at Broken ·HUl
· in the West, are 850 miles from the metropolis, but are only acces:
sible by a journey through other States of about 1,400 miles.
The Lodge fartherest north is at Murwillumbah, distant 340 miles,
and south at Bombala, 200 miles.
At the first .Special, on the 4th of July, 1902, Grand Lodge was
opened in Ample Form, at 7:15, P. M., and after the transaction of
the preliminary business, proclamation was made of the re-election,
foi: the fourth year, of Grand Master J. 0. Remington, and that he
had been duly obligated and invested. ·
The Grand Master responded with an address, in which American
Masons have an earnest, sympathetic interest. We quote from the
address:

1904.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

999

"By a notable coincidence we meet on a day, the annual recur·
rence of which is celebrated with enthusiasm by the citizens of the
great United States of America, where, I need scarcely remind you,
Freemasonry flourishes on that giant scale which seems appropriate
to that great country.
"On the 4th of July, one hundred and twenty-six years ago, the
American Colonies emerged from their childhood, and boldly cut the
leading-strings by signing the Declaration of Independence. Not
however, till they had exhausted their efforts to otherwise secure
.autonomous government, which they would then have ooen quite
content should oo under the Crown, as that of Australia now is.
"Under what different, happily different, circumstances, did we
<>elebrate, in January, 1901, our coming of age! To quote Lord
~·ennyson again:
"Britain fought her sons of yore.Britain. falied; and nevermore,
Careless of our growing kin,
Shall we sin our fathers' sin;
Men that in a narrower dayUnprophetlc rulers theyDrove from out the Mother's nest
That young Eagle of the W;est,
To forage for herself alone."

The Grand Master in his Address mentioned the flourishing condition of the Fraternity in New South Wales, its increase in numbers and in wealth. He said :
"Such at least is the impression left strongly on my mind after
my recent visitation to some of the Lodges situated between the
\Vestern and Southern railway lines, for which, accompanied by the
Junior Grand Warden and seven other Grand Lodge officers, I left
Sydney on Monday, October 20th. The tour occupied the rest of
the week, and involved journeys aggregating over six hundred and
fifty miles by rail and road.
"At Temora I dedicated the Masonic Hall, lately completed by the
Brethren of Lodge No. 168, according to ancient custom, and installed the Worshipful Master for the ensuing year."

763 Lodges.

126,177 Master Masons.

The Grand Lodge of New York held its One Hundred and
Twenty-third Annual Communication in Masonic Hall, in the city
of New York, commencing May 3, 1904. In the absence of Grand
Master Crandall ; the R.". W .'. Frank H. Robinson presided as
Grand Master; M.". W.". Edward W. Ehlers- being Grand Secretary.
Seven hundred and sixty Lodges were represented, together with
sixty-five other Grand jurisddction~. Twelve Past Grand Masters
and four Past Grand Treasurers were in attendance.
Elegant steel engraved portraits of Past Grand Master I. H.
Anthon, Grand Master in 1870-1871, and R.". W.". Theodore A.
Taylor, Past Grandi Treasurer, appear in this number of the Journal.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with prayer by
the R . ·. W. ·. William S. Carter, Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Officers of the Grand Lodge of New Jersey were
announced as visitors, and were welcomed and received with the
Grand Honors.
The Grand Master's Address was then read. In his report the
Grand Master stated the la~t to be a 1year of unprecedented growth
-but he said "In this life the bitter and the sweet are strangely
blended. No' object catches the sun's light upon its face but a
shadow lurks beyond. No mountain lifts its brow towards the sky
but a chasm yawns beside it."
He directed the attention of the Grand Lodge to the death roll
of the year, on which were inscribed names of many men prominent in the civil and Masonic history of the Empire State.

He reported the holding of fifteen Special Communicati ons for
the placing of corner-stones , constituting Lodges, and installing

of Homes, and attending the centennial of "Albion" Lodge, No. 26.
He issued four Dispensations for the formation of new Lodges,
ai;id recommended that charters be granted to each.
The routine work and business of this Grand Jurisdiction occupied, necessarily, a good portion of the Address.
The receipts of the year by the Grand Treasurer were $104,101.23,
and the expenditures, including $20,000 invested, were $73,912.47.
The report of the Superintende nt of the Home, Past Grand
Master Jesse B. Anthony, is a most interesting report of this famous
charity. We quote from the report:
"The average for the past year equals 300 inmates.
"The current expenses of the Home-embra cing maintenance,
repairs, farm and barn expenses-the $59,729.26, showing a per
ca.pita cost for the year of $199.10. This increase over last year
is very easily accounted for by a comparison with last year's report,
which we present below.
"As the per capita cost is a very important factor, we desire at
this juncture of afl'.alrs, to express the opinion that we have seen
our lowest per capita cost of maintenance. While the expenditures
in certain lines must inevitably increase, nevertheless, we regard
a ratio of $200 to $210 as a fair estimate, predicated on the present
plant, exclusive of extraordinary expenses, which are apt to occur."
The following acknowledge ment deserves a place in our report:
"We desire to place on record a recognition of the generosity of
the Lod·g es at the holiday season, in their remembrance of those
inmates in whom they were especially interested. While we cannot
have a personal knowledge of all such gifts, yet it would appear
to us that there were a greater number of them than ever before,
and (with good judgment) generally of a financial nature.
"May this spirit become general, so that none shall be found
outside the circle of the good will of the Christmastide and the
happiness for the New Year."

w:. Edwin A. Quick, Grand Historian, who occupies one hundred
and four page;i in the present number of the Journal with his report.

The Grand Master opened a Lodge of Master Masons, and appointed the necessary Committees. He then declared the Grand
Lodge of Ohio opened in Ample Forni, and the R:. w:. and Rev.
Clayton A. Smucker invoked the Divine blessing upon the session.
Greetings were extended by the Mayor of Dayton and by the
Grand Orator on behalf of the citizens of Dayton, and by Past Grand
Master Barton Smith on behalf of the Masons of Dayton.
Past Grand Master Melish introduced to the Grand Lodge Sir
Thomas Kite, the Grand Commander of the Knights Templar of
Ohio, who was received with the Grand Honors.
The Grand Lodge of Ohio held twenty-three Special Communications during the year, of which fifteen were for the placing of
corner-stones of public buildings, churches, schools, and Temples;
and the others for the dedication of Masonic Halls.
The Grand Master appointed the standing committees, and proceeded to deliver his Annual Address.
He gave an earnest welcome to the assembled Brethren, old and
new; and we quote from his address the following words:
"Masonry iU: Ohio, and' I might say throughout its domain, has
not taken a step backward. Progress is the watchword everywhere.
While the business world has made unprecedented advancement,
and the minds of men are seemingly wholly absorbed in th!' hustle
and bustle of the twentieth century life, still Masonry is not forgotten.
"The continual growth of Masonry is a fact. More men have
been initiated this past year than ever before in any one year in
its history•in Ohio. Last year was the banner year up to that date.,
with its 3,025 increase. But this year shows an increase of 3,691,
or an increase of 666 over last year's success.
"This is not all. More Masonic Temples and new halls, and
grander than ever before, are now in process of erection, or have
been finished this year than Masonry in Ohio has ever known in any
one year.
"Yes," he said, "Providence has certalnly dealt kindly with our
official famtly, and I take it that there is work yet to be accomplished for all of us."
Oontinuing, he said: "Let us pause a moment in memory of those
of our ranks who have gone before. R:. w:. Grand Chaplain lead
U!! i;11 our thoughts!
"(All join in devotion, led by the Grand Chaplain.)
"And now, for a few moments longer, let us pay a tribute of
respect to the distinguished dead of our Sister Grand Jurisdictions,
and also extend a brother's sympathy to those who mourn."

The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address. The
passage of another year with its blessings resulting in the material
prosperity of . the people which has been abundantly shared by our
great Fraternity causes us as Masons to be devoutly thnkful to
the Great Father for His merciful kindiness therefor. He said "Let
us go forward to the discharge of the duties before us invoking the
continuance of His blessings upon our future etiorts."
In commencing the report of his official acts, under the head of
"In Memoriam," after paying affectionate tribute to their Fraternal
Dead, he mentioned the following sad occurrence:
"On Sunday evening, June 14, 1903, immediately following the
last Annual Session of our Grand Lodge, the beautiful little City of
Heppner· was · overwhelmed and nearly destroyed by a great water
spout in which many homes were swept out of existence and two
.hundred people lost their lives. Six of our brethren of 'Heppner'
Lodge No. 59, were among the lost, and many others lost wife or
children, or both, together with a loss of all worldly possessions.
As soon as I learned the extent of the calamity which had befallen
them, I issued the following order which I trust will be approved:
I

" Office of the Grand Master,
" Eugene, Oregon, June 16, 1903.
"To ;rames F. Robinson, Grand Secretary:
"To assist in relieving the distress of brethren of Heppner Lodge
No. 59, in the terrible calamity which has come upon them, you are
ordered to draw a warrant on our Granti Treasury for $100.00 to be
sent to the Master of said Lodge.
S. M. YoRAN, Grand Master. .

"I desire also to acknowledge a similar contribution sent through
our Grand Secretary by our brethren of the Grand Jurisdiction of
Washington. It was an unselftsh and noble deed, which will bind
more firmly the bonds of love between the Mother Grand Lodge and
Its noble otispring. Many of our subordinate Lodges also responded
promptly in forwarding means for relief."
He reported the issuance of four dispensations for the formation

The Grand Lodge of Quebec held its Thirty-fourth Annual Communication in the City of Montreal January 27, 1904,-M.'. W.'.
John B. Tresidder, Grand Master; R.'. W.'. Will H. Whyte, Grand
Secretary. Fifty-three Lodges were represented, together wlth
thirty other Gtand Jurisdictions. Six Past Grand Masters, a Past
Deputy Grand and four Past Grand Wardens were in attendance.
A handsome portrait, in full regalia, of the Grand Master, appears on the opening page.
The Grand Master proceeded to del!ver his Annual Address. He
extended a Fraternal greeting to the brethren assembled as they
were from all parts of the Province for the purpose of considering
the past and making preparations for the future of the Fraternity in
Canada.
He reported the past year as exceeding any former one in signal
progress and he congratulated the brethren that the condition of
the Jurisdiction, Masonlcally, was better and stronger than ever
before in its history.
He mentioned the Fraternal Dead, reporting that "the death roll
of the past year in our Jurisdiction has been comparatively small in
number, nevertheless there are those who have passed away, who
will be much missed in our ranks, and in the Lod.g e rooms where
they were wont to meet."
In his visits to the Lodges he was always accorded a loyal welcome il.nd was always most hospitably entertained.
Among his rulings we note one on the vexed question of the l"lonpayment of dues. The question asked the Grand Master was:
"Should the non-payment of dues be treated as a Masonic offense'!"

men' and fills them with happy anticipations of the next occasion's

After prayer by the Grand C_haplain the Grand Lodge was opened

The Grand Master appointed the standing committees and then
proceeded to deliver his Address.
He gave the brethren pleasant greeting at the opening of the
Ninetieth Annual Communication. The passage of time had taken
with It the record made during the year, the scroll has passed with
time, and the record must stand as made.
"Life Is but a sheet of paper white,
Whereon each one of us 1fiay write
His word or two, and then comes night;
Though we have time but for a line,
Be that sublime;
Not failure, but low aim is crime."
He passed to the consideration of the death roll before reporting
his official acts. He gives some interesting facts concerning the
last Illness and death of Past Grand Master Bernard Francis Price.
or as he was generally known to the Fraternity, Bun F. Price.
The Grand Master relates an affecting .i ncident connected with ·
the last sad record. The Grand Master writes:
"Feeling the death stroke stealing upon him, but while still in
the full exercise of his mental faculties, Brother Price, with his ·.

which I have tltought it not improper to here incorporate, to sho~ · .
how he viewed his approaching dissolution. It is as follows:
" 'To· the Readers of Shibboleth, Good-by:
'Dearly Beloved Brethren-Greeting: When your eye rests upon
this article the editor, founder and owner of Shibboleth, Bun I'.'·
Price, will be no more. Our mortal remains will lie bl~chlng beneath the clods of the valley In beautiful Elmwood, and our dlsem- .

He recalls to our remembrance "the days of old" by the following

Orator, and we think his Oration as Grand Orator, delivered in
May, 1863, W:ithout a peer. But we give Bro. Diehl's coinment:
"One of the. newly chartered Lodges located in San Francisco is
named Starr King Lodge. How that name .refreshes the memories
of the early 60's! A great man was the Rev. Bro. Starr King. He
was one of the grandest and most gifted orators we ever heard, and
It was he, Colonel Baker and a few other magnetic or&tors who kept
California under the Stars and Stripes. Those were troublous times;
but, thank God, there were strong men at the helm, and it was 'The
Union Forever.' Another new Lodge bears the name of the wise
ruler, brave patriotic and true American, 'McKinley,' the beloved
and martyred President of the United States. The Lodge in Manila,
P. I., has already one hundred and thirteen members, and is only
about two years old." ·
We hope for Bro. Dlehl's complete recovery. .

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Past Grand Master Aldro Jenks, Chairman of the Wisconsin
Committee on Correspondence, presents, as usual, a report abounding in good oldrfashioned Masonic sense in his comments anent
the doings of the Grand Lodges composing the Masonic world in our
day and generation.
He notices California in his report for its Fifty-fourth Annual,
the administration of Grand Master Hendersov.. He follows our
legislation very closely and witli approval, until he runs against the
dictum that a Lodge begins its existence with the issuance of the
Dispensation of the Grand Master. On the subject, Bro. Jenks
says:
"Our California Brethren have been wrestling with the subject
as to when a Lodge begins its existence, and have reached the conclusion that the date of the Issuance of the Dispensation by the
Grand Master should be considered In fixing the date of the fiftieth
or otber anniversary. A couple of years ago the Grand Lodge of
Wisconsin reached the conclusion that the 'Natal Day' of a Lodge
Is when it is constituted and receives its charter, and we think this
is the better rule. Until that time it does not exist as a Lodge, but
is merely a creature of- the Grand Master. It has none of the rights
of a Lodge and can be abolished by the Grand Master at pleasure;
It cannot dimit or affiliate members, elect or install officers, discipl!ne
its members or do any act whatever, except receive petitions, act

1042

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 11,

on the same, and confer degrees. These conditions are such that
until it receives its charter such a body of men is not a Lodge in
fact. For want of a better term we call it a 'Lodge U. D.,' but it
lacks the powers and prerogatives necessary to make it a Masonic
Lodge."
We believe the Wisconsin declaration the cdrrect one-that the
existence of a Lodge of Freemasons commences to run from the
date of Its charter. We believe In the decision mentioned as fixing
the date of birth, that it was a case where a semi-centennial having
been held with all the appurtenances, it was important to fix the
date .thus early to establish the legitimacy of the proceedings
already had.
M.". W.". David H. Wright, Grand Master; R.". W.". William W.
Perry, Grand Secretary. Correspondent, Past Grand Master Aldro
Jenks, Dodgeville. · ,

> The Grand Lecturer p:resented his Annual Report to the Grap.d
Lodge as follows:

To the M. ·. W. ·. Grand Lodge of Oali./ornia :Again a year has passed into the things that were, and we can look back
with pride and satisfaction upon what has been accomplished. Our great
Fraternity has kept pace with our great State in material advancement and
growth. We, as Masons, have grown not only in membership and the power
to exert our inflnE'nce for the uplifting and benefiting of our State, our neighbors anil our families, but we have reached and realized a higher standard of
excellence in our beautiful ritual.
There is now a uniformity in all the work of ·the Lodg~s a~d a pride in its
exactness which excites the admiration, not only of our own brethren, but
also of those from other jurisdictions who happen to visit us. This is the
result of having made the language of our work into a grammatica.l, connected, consistent and complete text; and further, perhaps more, the result is
due to the faithfulness and energy of the Inspectora of the various districts
who, by reason of their annual visits to the Grand Lodge and the schools _of
instruction, are able to keep the correct work fresh in their own memories
and carry it home to their Lodges. By this means the ll10st remote districts
away off in the recesses of our ru~ged mountains and mining regions are
enabled to share equally with the brethren of our great plains and fertile
valleys the knowlE'dge and beauties of our ritual.
Yet, with all these opportunities and advantages, I am pained to confess
that some of our Lodges are officered with those who seem to be quite contented with. being elected to fill the honorable and important office of Master,
but have not the energy or ability to learn the work and fill the office with
credit to themselves-and honor ~ the Fraternity.

It seems to me, for instance, that in the choice of Senior and Junior Deacons the Master should ask himself the question, "Are they such material as
would in the future make good Masters!" If not; do not appoint them, for
they will _surely expect, when the time ·comes for advancement, that they
should go on into the stations above, and will feel that they have been
unjustly treated if they do not get the preferment, and bitterness and lack of
harmony result.
From my experience in the field as Grand Lecturer, I believe that there
snould be established in this jurisdiction some rule or regnlation of the Grand
Lodge making it compulsory upon the officers of every snbordinate Lodge in
each Masonic district of the State to be present at least once a year at a
Lodge of Instruction conducted by the Grand Lecturer or the District Inspector, and that this general Lodge of Instruction should last at lea.st two nights
and a day, but longer if need be. Such a requirement would be of inestimable benefit to mlllly of the districts, and would redound greatly to the
·
credit. of the Grand Lodge.
Many of the Grand Jurisdictions in the older States have such a regulation and it works admirably.
This suggestion is ma.de because it bas been my experience and that of my
predecessors that it not infrequently happens that notice is sent to nll the
Lodges of a certai~ district that on a date, named some two or three weeks in
advance, the Grand Lecturer will he present at some specified central point
in the district for the purpose. of instructing the Lodges of that district, and
when the time a:rrives it is found that some, perhaps a majority, of the
Lodges are not represented and the benefits are, of course, lost to the
absentees.
There should be some re.medy applied to this .condition of affairs. The
Grand Lodge _-is at considerable expense in furnishing transportation and
paying hotel bills and salary that the Grand Lecturer may instruct t he Lodges
in all that pertains to the work and business of the Lodge. Under the present
conditions the officers simply use their pleasure-come or remain a'l'.l'ay. This
can and shonld be remedied by the Grand Lodge making attendance at such '
instruction compulsory.
I believe, too, that the Inspectors ·of the various Ma.sonic districts should
be appointed by .the newly installed Gr!'nd Master immediately after the close
of the Annual Communication, that they may have ample time to visit,
inspect and instruct the various Lodges of their districts and be able to make
their reports to the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer by the let of September, as required by law. I think, also, that the instruction to the Inspectors
should be given by the Grand J;,wcturer during the session of the Grand Lodge
and the Saturday following its close, and not during the four days after its

1050

PROOEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 12,

close, because many of them ,feel that they must leave for home at the end of·
the Grand Lodge ·week and beg to be excused from further stay.
The funeral service of our jurisdiction is not exactly what it should be.
It should be reconstructed so that it would be equally applicable to interment
or cremation, and undergo such changes or additiQUs as would make it correct
whatever be the method of disposing of the remains of a deceased brother.
I wish here to repeat in part, but more explicitly, what was said in my
last report about the dropping of the acacia into the grave of a deceased
brother.
\\'hen the Lodge has arrived at the grave, the Master at the head, the
Senior Warden at the foot, and the Junior Warden at the left and between the
Master and Senior Warden, the Master reads or recites the funeral service until
he reaches the point at which the acacia is to be dropped. He then steps to
the left to a position even with the shoulder of the body and facing the grave
says, as he presses with his right hand the acacia to his left breast : "We
cherish his memory here ; "· then as he points upward with the acacia, he says,
" We commend his spirit to God ; " then, as he drops the acacia into the
grave, he says, " We consign his body to the grave."
The officers and brethren then move in procession,, single file, around the
grave, each one stopping at the point where the Master stood to drop the
acacia, and each brother there faces the grave, repeats the action or gestures
of the Master in dropping the acacia, but omits the words used by the Master. All the bretaren after thus passing around the grave and dropping the
acacia will be in the same position that they were before starting to move.
The Master then proceeds to finish the ceremony.
. · The Grand Lodge sends out its Proceedings, two copies going to each
subordinate Lodge. These copies, as a rnle, are laid away amongst the cobwebs and dust of some unfrequented nook in the Lodge-room, unnoticed,
unknelled and unsung, there to gather their share of accumulating dust and
cobwebs. It should be the duty of every Master at the stated meetings of
his· Lodge to read, or cause to be read, some part of these reports to the
brethren, that the rank and file of his Lodge might become educated in
M~sonry.

The Address ef the Grand Master, his decisions upon points of Masonic
Jaw, the report of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, are all of vital
interest 'to every Mason, and would tend to elevate and educate him in the
principles and groundwork o~ Masonry.
Anderson's Manual has also been sent by the Grand Lodge, four copies
to each subordinate Lodge ; this Manual contains, among other things, the Constitution of the Grand Lodge, the digest of every decision rendered by the
Grand Masters of California from the foundation of the Urand Lodge to the
present, all the forms and ceremonies for constituting Lodges, laying cornerstones, etc., etc. It is an fnvaluable book to every progressive Mason in this
jurisdiction, aDJi its contents should become familiar to all. ,

During the spring months and up to the close of my school term at the
first of June I was suffering considerably from nervousness and overwork,
not having had any real rest for more than five years, and, at the suggestion
and advice of my physician, I took a trip to the World's Fair at St. Louis,
and to the cities of the East. I was away for seven weeks.
To the R. ·. W. ·• E. R. HART, Junior Grand Warden, I am greatly
indebted for assisting me, at many places doing my work far better, perhaps,
than I could have done it for myself, and by reason of his valuable aid the
jurisdiction lost nothing by my enforced absence.
I wi~h again to express my gratitude to the brethren of the State for their
many kindnesses and courtesies extended to me during the year. I also wish
to thank the Grand Master and Grand Secretary for kindnesses received at ·
their hands.
Respectfully submitted.
WM. HARVEY EDWARDS,

Three ca.sea of 1088 by fire suggest the propriety and desirability of Lodges
devoting a modicum of income to the insurance of their property. No Lodge
as well as" No man knoweth what a day may bring forth."
We join wiih the Grand Mastt1r in sympathetic mention of those sister
jurisdictions whom the Dread MeBBenger has summoned on the last ca.JI.
"Their fate is but the common fate of all," and should teach us to "Live
well, how long or short permitting to Heaven."
The Constitution of the Grand Lodge of California has no superior, anrl,
were its provisions studied by the Masters of Lodges as they should be, the
Grand Masters would not be plied with questions that are therein explicitly
answered ; beside11, that Constitution has been, in almost every lineament of
it, fully interpreted in decisions rendered by Grand Masters and approved by
the Grand Lodge. In this connection your committee desire to say that when
members of a Lodge desire to communicate with the Grand Master they
should do so only through the Master of their Lodge. Not to cavil, but obey,
should be the rule. We think that the Grand Master was right in decliniug to
answer questions coming to him through individual brothers, unleBS ~he ea.me
are P"esented to him through the Lodge or the Master thereof.
To canvass the merits and qualifications of parties, aspirants for office. in
the Grand Lodge, is unquestionably the right of every member of tb:e Grand
Lodge. The interests of the Grand Lodge and of Masonry demand this much.
The introduction or exercise of the methods of political tricksters, however.
in either Grand or subordinate Lodge, is unmasonic, and must ultimately
result in irreparable injury. Right-thinking men and Masons will put the
seal of condemnation on anything savoring of the methorls of the politician•
There should be but one ptinciple of action in this important particular, and
that is that the officers should be selected, or rather, callerl, to positions of
trust and responsibility through eminent fitness. "Only tqis and nothing
more." There should exist a strong sentiment among the brethren against
anything that is wrong. Sentiment is all-powerful, and will accomplish
better ends in better manner than anything else.
Aristocracy in Lodges ought not to be countenanced. Character is the
grand requisite. If any Lodge does not desire the affiliation of any particular individual, such Lodge has a means of declining to admit him. The evil
of non-affiliation is grea.1 ly enhanced by the fact that the bar to affiliation is
in the way. The fee, if there be any, should be a reasonable one. We agree
with the Grand Master that the Grand Lodge should a.ct in .the matter, and
devise some method that would 'J>roperly adjust and settle this question which
so often bobs up in our Lodges.
That there is a growing sentiment in favor of a proper system of Life
Membership in our Lodges, ~8 evident. A plan for such membership can be
framed that will work for the benefit and strength of the Lodges and of the
Grand Lodge, and of Masonry in the jurisdiction in general. The matter is,
at least, worth1 of due consideration by the Grand Lodge.

Your committte again congratulates this Grand Body.on the work being
its 1mbordinate Lodge@. We thought
that the p;ains shown in membership in the year 1902 of 1949, and in
1903 of 2343, was high-water mark, but this year shows still greater gains.
namely. 2390.
The returns made this year show no improvement over those of 1902 and
1903; in fact, when we take into consideration the increase in the number of
Lodges, we think a very poor showing of proficiency has been made in 1904.
The rating of Lodges for the last three years is as follows : The number
of Lodges marked perfect for the years 1902-3-4, is 224; the number of
Lodges whose returns were sent back for correction was in 1902, 31 ; 1903,
33, and 1904, 31. The number of Lodges whose returns were transmitted
later th~ the time required by the Constitution was in 1902,"16; 1903, 2();
1904, 17. The number of Lodges whose returns were noi transmitted within the
required time and which had to be returned for correction was 7 in each of
the yea.rs 1902-3-4.
From the above showing we would again urge upon the Masters and Secretaries the importance of sending the returns of their Lodges within the
time prescribed by the Constitut.ion, the correct spelling of names, and the·
transmittal of the proper amount of dues.
"Rose's Bar" Lodge, No. 89, located at Smartsville, Yuba. county, failed to.
send its returns until September 2lstt a.nd its Grand Lodge dues were not
received until Obtober 8th, which wa.s too late to include the amount in the
Grand Secretary's report of this year.
"Mt. Zion" Lodge, No. 114, loca.ted at Grizzly Flat, El Dora.do county, was
very derelict in sendi°ng in its returns. The Master and Secretary left the State·
and made no provision for their returns to the Grand Lodge, and after diligent
efforts by the Grand Secretary the report wa.s secured, a.nd bore the signature of an Actiug Master a.nd an Acting Secretary.
We feel that some penalty should a.tta.ch to officers of Lodges who al"e
negligent of their duties. To obviate, at least, so far a.a poSBible, the recur·
rence of such inattention to the reports to thia Grand Lodge, we recommend.
that the Inspectors of the various· districts be held responsible for the for- .
warding of the returns of the Lodges in their respective districts.

To the M.·. W. ·.Grand Lodge of Oalifornia:Bro. ALBERT S. PARSONS, at the last Annual Communication, presented
the following proposed resolution, which was referred to this committee, viz.:
" Be it Resolved, That before a candidate shall be permitted to sign the
By-Laws of the Lodge in which he is being raised, he shall pass a satisfactory
examination on the obligation of the Master Mason Degree."
The proposed resolution is in conJlict with certain provisions of our Constitution and Uniform Code of By-Laws. By Section 1 of Article I of Part
V of the Constitution, it is provided that membership in a Lodge is acquired
by having regularly received the degree of Master Mason therein; by Section
1 of Article V of Part IV, it is provided that the Secretary of a Lodge shall ·
keep a book of By-Laws "for the signature of the members in the order of
their admission, in which he shall see that each member at once sign his name
in full;" and by Section 3 of Article IV of the Uniform Code of By-Laws, it
is '(lrovided t}u>.! Aver" n"••nn raiaed to the de(lJ"eA of Master Mason shall eign
it. By-Laws.
