A Junior Warden was instructed by a Lodge to prefer charge• against a
brother for unmasonic conduct. He did so and was afterward elected to and
installed as Senior Warden of the Lodge.
The Grand Master was asked whether the Junior Warden continued, under
the circumstan ces, to be the accuser and prosecutor in tbe ca.ae,. and ans.wered
"that he continued to be the accuser, nowithstan ding his election and mstalla.tion as Senior Warden."
We are of the opinion tha.t this answer wa.s correct. A charge of unm~­
aonic conduct ca.n be presented against a Mason only by a Master Mason Ill
good standing, a.nd must be in writing over his own signature. . In ~ccord
with a. time-honor ed custom the Junior Warden of a Lodl(e, by direct10n ~f
the Master or the Lodge, often presents such charges, but when he does this
he does it as a Master Ma.son, and thus constitutes himself the " accuser "
for all the purposes of the trial. The statement conta.i.ned in the cha.rg~ to ~he
effect that he is the Junior Warden, a.nd presents the charge under d1r~ct1on
of the Master or Lodge, is only explanator y· of the reason why he constitutes
himself the accuser.

Under these provisions one who regularly receives the degree of Master
Mason ill a Lodge acquires thereby membershi p therein, with a.ll the rigHs
a.nd privile11es of membershi p, a.nd must immediatel y &ign the By-Laws.
We recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
At the last Annual Communic ation Bro. JULIANE. PARDEE proposed certain amendmen ts to Sections I a.nd 2 of Article I, Part III of the Constitution, which were referred to this committee, to be reported on a.t this Communication . (Proceedin gs for 1903, p. 377.)
The object of these proposed amendmen ts is to place it beyond the power
of the Grand Lodge to grant a charter to any Lodge before it has worked for at
least three months under dispensatio n, the la.w now providing that a. charter
shall not be granted to a. Lodge until it shall have worked "a. time" under
dispen•a.tion, and nil time being specified, it is within the power of the Grand
Lodge to grant a charter to any Lodge that has worked for a.ny time under
dispensatio n.
The effect of these amendmen ts would be to require a.ny Lodge formed by
authority of dispensatio n issued within three months of the Annual Communication to continue to work thereunder until the next succeeding Annual
Communication.
The proposed amendmen ts have been so drawn as to accomplish the
purpose designed.
We ca.n, however, see no necessity for the adoption of these proposed
amendmen ts, and we believe it to be unwise to a.mend our Constitutio n unless
the necessity therefor is apparent.
As the matter now stands it is for this body to determine, in its discretion,
whetlier or not a Lodge to which a dispensatio n has been issued by the Grand
Master furnishes sufficient evidence of its capability to be a useful member
of our family of Lodges. If the evidence is not satisfactor y the charter Iila.y
be refused, or the Lodgl! continued under dispensatio n for another ye~·r . . It
cannot be maintained that in all ca~es a Lodge mut work for three months
under dispensatio n before it can be shown that such Lodge is worthy of a
charter and will be a credit to the Fraternity. This condition may be demonstrated by the circumstan ces existing at the very outset, certainly to as great
an extent a.s it will be at the expiration of three months, a.nd where this body
is satisfied from the evidence submitted to it that the Lodge should be chartered, we believe.it should have the power to issue the charter. In such a.
matter we ma.y rely upon the wisdom of the members of this Grand Lodge
without fixing any arbitrary limit of time.
We, therefore, recommend that the proposed amendmen ts be not adopted.

" The Report ~f the Committee on Application for Membership was presented to the Lodge by the Secretary. He gave names of committeemen and
th~ir i~dividual reports, one of which was unfavorable. The question was
asked me if the Secretary had acted wrong in disclosing the nature of the

The Grand Master reports as follows : "Have received various communications from the Masonic Club at the
Soldiers' Home in Los Angeles county. Thie club has a membership of a.bout
one hundred. The Government will not allow the formation of a Masonic
Lodge in the Home, and these old brethren desire the privilege of having
Masonic burial. My answer to their various inquiries is as follows: The
Masonic Club has uo right to use the Masonic burial services at the funeral of a
member. If the brother be in good standing at the time of his death it would be
proper to ask some regular Masonic Lodge to conduct the funeral services.
If, in the case under consideration, the burden would be too onerous on the
Lodges oonducting the ceremonies, I think probably that the Grand Lod~e
would relieve them of some of the expense. A Mason not in good standing
has no right to Masonic burial unless his Lodge sees fit to accord him the
same. In case of the death of a Past Grand Master, the officers of the club.
shoull notify the Grand Secretary of this jurisdiction. The Grand Honor1
cannot be given at a funeral unless it is conducted by a Lodge after being_
regularly opened. The desire of these old brethren seems to be to have a
Masonic funeral at their death. In my opinion they deserve some consider&·
tion, and, if po11sible, an arrangement should be made with "Santa Monica"
Lodge, being their nearest Lodge, to conduct these funeral ceremonies,"

Answer: The Committee Report is.1>£ record, and the Secretary did no
Masonic wrong.
'' Since making this ruling I am not sure that my decision conduces to the
harmony of the Lodge, and I would respectfully ask that the Grand Lodge
formulate a procedure in these cases."
The report of the Investigating Committee must be made to the Lodge, and,
as has been decided, must be in writing. There is no law requiring that any
portion ~f the report thus made to the Lodge shall be withheld from the
members present at the meeting. a.t. which it is received, a.nd, in the absence
of express direction to the contrary from the Master, we cannot see how
the Secretary could 'be considered guilty of any wrongful act in reading t he
whole thereof to the Lodge. Unless, however, there is a question as to the
cor:rectness of the announcement of the Secretary as to the nature of the
report, fa\"orable or unfavorable, there can be no real necessity for an
announcement as to how each individual member of the committee reported,
and it might be more conducive to the harmOJlof of the Lodge, as suggested
by the Grand Master, that no other announcement should ordinarily be made
than that the committee, or a majority thereof, or one member thereof, had
reported unfavorably. The minutes of the Lodge should contain no further
statement. The reports themselves, so long as they are retained, should be
kept in the secret archives uf the Lodge.

We find no error in any statement as to our law contained in this answer,
except that we are of the opinion that there could be no objection to the mere
reading of the Masonic burial service over the remains of a deceased Mason
by any body of Masons, even though not constituted or opened as a Lodge.
In fact, it has been so decided by this Grand Lodge. (Proceedings, Vol. XIV,
P·. 190.) To that extent, tberefors, the burial service may be used by the
Masonic Club referred to. But such mere reading of the burial service would
not constitute a Masonic burial. Masonic burial can be conducted only by a
regular Lodge, dnly opened for that purpose, and what the members of this
club desire is "Masonic burial " in the full sense of 'that term.

With the limitation first above suggested, we recommend that the Grand
Master'e decision in this matter be approved.

It has come to be a custom with us that a brother elected to the station of
Junior Grand Warden is ordinarily promoted through the intervening stations
to the exalted office of Grand Master.
In selecting a Junior Grand ·warden we ara, therefore, selecting a brother
who will, in all human probability, be called upon to assume the great respon sibility of directing the destinies of Masonry in this jurisdiotion. It is needless to say to Masons that in the relation of one who is ultimately to be our
Grand Master, with all the powers and duties of that great office, personal
• friendship and pride of locality, and other like considerations, should all yield
to the superior one of worth and fitness, and that the brother selected should
be the free choice of a majority of the members of the Grand Lodge, uninfluenced by trade or combination of any kind.

Grand Master upon this subject. The matter is not one as to which legislation
would afford any remedy. His appeal is to the hearts and conscience of all
good Ma.sons. We feel confident, witlc him, that it is only necessary to call
attention to these things: and t?at_ the -overwhelming majority of Masons,
recognizing the danger, will formulate a cure for th~ evn.

.Bro. BRILLIANT, of "Wilmington" Lodge, No. 198 bas propounded forconsirleration and ruling theofollowing question : "What Lodge bas a right to accept
a petition for degrees from a seafaring ml n who has no residence except on boa.rd
ship?" This having been referred to this.committee, we answered, No Lodge.
Section 2, Article III, Part III of our Constitution, provides that no Lodae
shall receive an application unless the applicant shall have been a. resident of
the State d~ring twelve months and within the jurisdiction of the Lodge six
months next preceding the date of bis application except where an applicant
belongs to the army or navy of the United States, it may be received by dispen_sation from the Grand Master. Residence, within the meaning of this
section, baa been held to be the place where the party resides with the intention of remaining permanently or for an indefinite time, and which he leaves on
business or pleasure with the purpose of returning, so it depends largely upon
the intention of the party; if a man selects a. place as a home and acquires
the right to vote there, it is his residence, though the exigencies of business
may keep him moving from place to place. The acts and declarations of a
party may show his intent, one having a residence may remain away for yea.rs
and still retain his reaideu.ce, provided he went and rem!l.ined away with the
intent to maintain it.
A seafaring man who bas never resided within the jurisdiction of a Lodge,
sailing from port to port, who claims or has no residence except the ship on
which be may happen to be employed, remaining iu port but a few weeks at a
time, or only so long as the business of the ship may detain him, cannot make
application to any Lodge.
•
A man must first acquire a residence in a. place; he must b&ve some fixod
place of abode or home before he can petition a. Lodge, and it is not lawful for
any Lodge in this jurisdiction to receive or act upon a petition from such a
person.

enshrined it in the affections of its votaries, and have gained for it the

proven by the altars they have raised and the Temples they have built
wherever civilization has extended among men. · To its shrines have been

and you have borne the inconvenience and discomforts of travel to perform the duties of this Grand Lodge. You have come that you might
"interchange the influence benign of loving eyes." You have come to

the great work our Fraternity is doing for the elevation of man. And
when you consider what Masonry has done, and is doing, in advancing
man upwards to a higher and nobler state, you are justified in your
enthusiasm and your devotion to its institutions.

1904.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

1089

In considering the contributions to human progress which Masonry
has made, the inquiry naturally arises as to what is meant by human
progress ? It is the procession of man through the ages from a debased
and savage to a high moral and intellectual condition. It is the upward
movement of humanity, arising from the unsatisfied yearning in the
heart for a nobler and a better life. Progress consists in, and is, man's
moral and intellectual development. This is the purpose of man's existence on earth and the goal towards which he is ever struggling. It is
the pathway that leads to the :final perfect state.
If there be those who doubt that the uplifting and ennobling of
humanity is the purpose of man's existence on earth, let them "sit at
the feet of history and trace her footsteps back over the night of years."
Let them observe the gradual unfolding and development of moral and
intellectual ideas as man has come from the darkness of ignorance, into
the light of knowledge. Let them note that there has been an unceasing
movement of the race from a savage state to it s present exalted position.
When contemplating this truth in the history of man the mind is led to
the inevitable conclusion that man's upward progress is the result of a
purpose, and :Qot the result of accident, or chance. We know that all
things' are governed by law and that there is a divine order in the universe. Therefore, we believe that man's moral and intellectual dev~·
opment on earth, like other "facts of Nature, are the result of design;
that this development is the purpose of his existence on earth and is
the fulfillment of a divine plan.

And how, and by what means, has this advance of man been made?
It has been accomplished by the struggle and conflict between right and
wrong in the world and the victory of right. And this explains the
reason why these two antagonistic principles of good and evil are in
the world. It is through this conflict in the nature of man and in the
world, and by the defeat of evil, that man has come up from the savage
state.
Lincoln, whose moral intuitions were perhaps superior to those of
any other man of the century, clearly grasped this elemental truth. In
his debate with Douglas on the slavery question, he said: "It is the
eternal struggle between these two principles-right and wrongthroughout the world; they are the two principles that have stood face
to face from the beginning of ~ime and will ever continue to struggle."
Every advance that man has made has been by the triumph of good
over evil ; by the victory of the moral and spiritual forces in the nature
of man over the animal and the material. In this contest right has
always ultimately triumphed over wrong; the moral and spiritual forces
have always finally subdued the animal and the material.

1090

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 13,

Froude, the historian, says : "History is a voice forever sounding
across ·the centuries the laws of right and wrong. Justic~ alone endures
and lives. Injustice and falsehood may be long-Jived, but doomsday
comes at last to them."
Out of this conflict between right and wrong have come the great
examples of heroism, of self-sacrifice, of unfaltering faith in the right,
of exalted character, and of steadfastnes.s to duty, which glorify our
human nature. Out of this contest came the example of the ~elebrated
architect whom 1\fasons are charged to imitate. These examples are the
"Great voices
Heard in the breathless pauses of the fight,
By truth and freedom ever waged with wrong,
For the uplifting and the enn~bling of man."
.An~ why has man chosen the good rather than the evil in this
unceasing conflict between the forces in his own nature and in the
world T It is because of the impulse implanted in the soul of man by
the .All Wisi:i Creator that man might fulfill the purpose of his existence
on earth, which, as I have stated, is his moral and intellectual development. It is this impulse in the heart of the race that is forever lifting
humanity into higher and nobler fields and giving it a wider and a
grander outlook. This impulse in the heart of every man, urging him to
do the right, we call the voice of conscll!nce.
·

One of Washington's rules of conduct, in his boyhood days, was,
"Keep alive in your breast that spark of divine fire which· men call conscience." Beethoven, the supreme master of harmony .among men, recognized this voice in the soul. When his deafness shut out for him the
melody of external numbers, in the secret chambers of his soul, he heard
and interpreted to men the divine harmonies of the Invisible. .And in
one of his great compositions he endeavored to express in music, "the
voice of God in the soul pleading with man to lead a higher life."
It is this voice in the soul that in the hour of temptation and doubt
leads man to choose the good, the beautiful, the true; that keeps him in
the path or duty though it leads to suffering, and sacrifice and dea.th;
that sustains the statesman in the hour of his country's need; that
nerves the martyr in the hour of approaching dissolution; and that
strengthens and supports the great and good wlio give their lives a
sacrifice for their fellow-men.

· This voice in the soul forever cries for the ideal. It is the inspira·
tion of all art and all literature. It i~ the cause of the great moral and
intellectual movements of the race.

1904.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

1091

The great teacher, Delsarte, said that ".Art is the tendency of the
fallen soul towards its primitive purity, or its final splendor; or, in one
word, it is the search for the eternal type.''
In the gr.eat moral movements of the race this voice in the soul
becomes what Lowell has so beautifully expressed as
"That spirit which doth ever brood
In patient calm on the unpilfered nest
Of man's deep heart, 'till mighty thoughts grow fledged
To sail with darkening shadows o'er the world,
Filling with dread such souls as dare not trust
In the unfailing energy of Good,
Until they swoop and their pale quarry make
Of some o'erbloated Wrong-that spirit which
Scatters great hopes in the seed field of man
Like acorns among grain, to grow and be
A roof for freedom in all coming time."
This divine voice in the soul is incarnated in the Institutions of
Masonry, making it a mighty influence in advancing human progress.
For the direct . object of Masonry is to vitilize, to develop, and to
strengthen the voice in the soul that is ever pleading with man to lead
a higher life.
We are taught in Masonry "to drcumscribe our desires and keep
our passions within due bounds towards all mankind." Our ritual
instructs us that Masonry is a progressive moral science; that it has for
its foundation the practice of the social and moral virtues. Masons
are .charged, as individuals, to practice the domestic and public virtues.
In the First Degree the novitiate is charged to let Temperance
chasten, Fortitude support, Prudence direct, and to let Justice be the
guide of all his actions. Thus Masonry is a great fountain from which
ever :flows the stream of truth to· all who take its vows. From its organ·
ization it has been what it is to-day, an ally and an apostle of the elemental forces that elevate, dignify and ennoble mankind. "In the companionships of the Lodge. men learn to love that whieh is high and noble
and to hate that which is base and degrading. They are lifted out of
the littleness of common life and their minds are tuned to a higher and
a nobler key."
For how long a time Masonry has exerted its beneficent in:fluence we
do not with certainty know. We teach in our Lodges that Masonry
originated at the building of King Solomon's Temple. Masonic scholars trace our Institution to a time in the Middle Ages when there was
no Masonic history or literature. At that time the origin, the traditions,

Masonry. In the First Degree the candidate is instructed that "as
created by one .Almighty Parent, and inhabitants of the same planet we
'
are to aid, support, and protect each other."
In another part of our Work it is taught "that we are descended
from the same stock, partake of the same nature, and share the same
hope."
From this belief comes those moral duties and obligations that bind
~~ 1'.<>gether -in civil society. The degree of happiness and well-being of
individuals and communities is determined by the extent to which these
obligations and duties are performed.
Masonry has ever been foremost in the practical application of
brot~erly l.ove to the affairs of life. Its influence is felt in every community where there are Masons as a ministering angel to soothe the
unhappy, to relieve the distressed, to compassionate the miserable, and
give succor to the sick and the poor. It is this idea of brotherhood that
cam:~ primitive man ~o form the family. All the idea developed it led
families to form the tnbe and tribes to form communities. And in the
fullness of time it led communities to form states and nations. ·It i1
through this principle that we hope for the Golden .Age when the sword
will be returned to the scabbard and men will learn war no more.
The belief in the Fatherhood of God is one of the grounds for the
belief in man's immortality. For if we are the children of the GodFather we must partake of His immortal nature. Thie belief in immortality i9 one of the most powerful factors influencing human actio~. It
strengthens and sustains men to bear the burdens and endure the· sacrifices of this life in the hope that there will be recompense in the life that
.
is beyond death.
But before these great truths can operate in controlling human cond~ct it is necessary that their full import and meaning should be per-

ceived and understood. For thus only can man realize his personal responsibility to society and to his fellow-men. .A mere intellectual assent
to these truths is not sufficient. Often · these great truths are mere
academic statements, and do not influence oi: control human action, because the ideas tlie words' contain are not apparent to the mind. When
a great truth has been fully established and accepted by men it is apt
to become a comJJlonplace or a truism.
This is illustrated by the great inventions and discoveries that have
blessed mankind. .At first they cause all the world to marvel. Then
they take their place with the accepted commonplaces of life. We were
amazed at the marvels of the telephone, the phonograph, the "X" ray,
and other wonders of electricity. But the generation growing up around

1904.J

GRAN.D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

1095

us accept them as matters of course. So it is with the great truths of
man's being and his relation to his Creator ..
Even in this enlightened age the real meaning of universal brotherhood is but feebly grasped and only partly understood. Prejudices,
hatreds, jealousies, covetousnei;s and greed still lead men and nations to
violate every obligation of brotherhood.
It was through long ages that man came to grasp the great truths of
his being as they are understood to-day. Each succeeding generation
gained more light until at last man came to his present knowledge of
his relation to God and his fellow-creatures. Though we have the heritage of the past, though we have the accumulated experience of ages, yet
each succeeding generation must confront and overcome the same diffi·
culties in acquiring knowledge. Each individual is a new being. All he
appea.rs upon the theater of action, and proceeds along the pathway from
infancy to manhood, he must learn these great truths for himself. He
cannot inherit a knowledge of them from hie ancestors. He must learn
them as every individual has who preceded him.
It is claimed by scientists as an establislied fact that the life of the
individual of tO-day is an epitome of the history of the race. It is said
that the development of the child before birth repeats every stage of evolution through the lowest forms of animal life up to man's present physical form. So, also, it is claimed that from birth to manhood man
repeats and is an epitome of the moral, spiritual and intellectual development of the race from the. primitive condition. It is claimed that
every man must go through the savage state and learn to subdue his
passions and appetites. But this development, which in our ancestors
took many thousaJid years, and only by gradual steps, must take place
in the modern man in the· brief time from birth to manhood. Hence, we
can understand why men find great difficulty in grasping the great truths
of their being, and how often the statement of them is to the mind a
mere sound of words.
From these observations we perceive the necessity and value of an
4ii.stitution that brings home to the consciousness l\nd the understanding
of men a perception. and an appreciation of these great truths of man's
being. and their significance in human affairs. .And this is one of the
missions and achievemeJ?,tB of Masonry, and constitutes one of its greatest contributions to the forces of progress. It acts directly upon the
mind of the individual who takes its vows. By its history and its ritual
it directs and focuses the attention upon the building of the first Temple
to God by human hands. It teaches that God is the Father of all. It
lifts man's contemplation to the worlds that keep their appointed paths
through the infinity of 'space. By enabling liim to perceive the qi.vine

1096

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 13,

order and harmony of the universe he learns that all things are governed by law, and that he himself is a moral being. He is made to see
that he is related to his fellow-men, and is bound by reciprocal duties to
them and to society. By dramatic representations in tile Lodge room,
by the meeting and communion of heart with heart, Masonry brings the
novitiate out of darkness into the light by which he sees and understands
the moral truths of his being.
It is generally admitted that Masonry has made inestimable contributions to human progress by its services in the cause of human freedom. I shall refer only to its work in the American Revolution.

1904.]

'

It is said that Washington was the sword, Patrick Henry was the
tongu~, and ,Jefferson was the pen of the American Revolution. With

equal justice it may be said that Masonry was the citadel of the Revolution. It is claimed with apparent truth that without the help that
Masonic Lodges contributed to the cause of .American liberty that Independence would not have been established on this continent.
Masonry was transplanted to our soil ~long with civil and religious
liberty. They grew and expanded together. Here Masonry found a congenial atmosphere and a favorable environment. Its teachings of equality and brotherhood, and its appeal to high and noble ideals, naturally
attracted to its altars those colonists who were imbued with the spirit
a,nd idea of personal liberty. Long before the Revolution began MasoniC
Lodges had been established throughout the colonies. 'l'o the sons of
{reedom they became a safe and inviting meeting place. The teachings.
of Masonry were in harmony with those impulses and aspirations that
had led the colonists to leave behind the graves of their fathers, sever
the traditions of the past, and seek an asylum in a new and unsettled
continent. In the security of the Lodge rooni the ideas of liberty and
equality had a natural and unobstructed development.
The Lodge was a deliberative body where the humblest member had
a right to be heard. Every Lodge was a School of Independence and
J,iberty. In every community they became the centers of Revolutionary
thought. .At the altars of Masonry the patriot fathers made their vows
to Freedom. In its temples, dedicated to the God of Nations, they gained
the faith and hope that sustained them through the darkness and gloom
that so often settled over the patriot cause. Under the benignant light
of the .All-Seeing Eye, looking down upon them from the East, they found
the devotion and fortitude that nerved them to endure the years of suffering and sacrifice, the defeat and agony,
"Till Danger's troubled height was past,
.And the star of peace returned."

,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

1097

Among the great names of the Revolution there are but few indeed
which were ·not recorded on the Masonic 1 oll. Our starry flag that now
"floats on every land, and over every sea, and under the whole heavens,"
as the symbol of liberty and equality, was suggested by \rasonic symbolism. Many ideas were borrowed from Masonry in the formation of
the new government.
The American Revolution and the establishment of the government
that followed was one of the most momentous epochs in human affairs.
Who can fully estimate the influence of America in spreading the idea
of constitutional government throughout the world? To-day every nation
of Europe lives under constitutional forms but Russia, and she is now
promised a constitution and a larger liberty.
Bartholdi's statue of Liberty Enlightening the World; holding aloft
the blazing torch, at the gateway of New York's harbor, is a fitting symbol of American genius and the American spirit.
.At the dawn of the twentieth century we saw Freedom· leap across
the Pacific,. and, under the protection of our flag, liberty and law and
order and protection to the rights of property were established in the
isles of the Orient. · May we not hope that progress will continue west'vard untiJ .Asia, the ~other of the race, is everywhere free T May we
not hope that the West may give back to the East "the peace and goodwill among men" that commenced its course two thousand years ago in
Western .Asia, when the Star of Bethlehem shone in the heavens! This
we can say to-day, that in all the achievements of the century that wait
on Freedom's triumphs Masonry can jus~ly claim to have contributed a
·
noble part.
One of the missions of free institutions under our government has
been to unite those who are born under the banner of Freed.om and the
millions who have come from the Old World to enjoy the blessings
of civil and religious liberty. The latter brought with them to our
shores their peculiar religious idetLS, their national prejudices and
hatreds, and often that spirit of suspicion and distrust engendered by
monarchical and despotic governments: These diverse elements have had
to be united, compacted and welded into a common type of patriotic
American character. The accomplishment of this taak is one of the
gnitifying achievements of the age. It has been accomplished, in a large
measure, through the idea of brotherhood disseminated by secret societies.
The growth of secret societies in the United States is one of the remarkable features of our Nation.al life. Their name is legion. There
are few men in every community who do not belong to some brotherhood.
Thus men are .b rought together who .would otherwise "have remained a.t

1098

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 18,

a perpetual distance." Thus prejudice has been removed, mutual regard
has been developed, and men have learned "that all hearts are good when
we explore their depths." These secret societies have been valuable fac·
tors in solvii:t a most serious national problem.
Here, a.gain, we have a . contribution from Masonry, for it is the
mother of secret societies. Its example and influence led to their organization, and it is entitled to a share of the credit for the beneficent pur·
pose they subserve.
Masonry has contributed to the advance of human t:hought as an '
apostle of religious liberty. In building the Temple of Solomon an outer
court was provided where all men _of every land might worship as they
chose. While Masonry .requires a belief in the Supreme Being, it recog·
nizes no dogmas, no creeds, no intolerance on account of reliW.ous ideas.
In religious toleration it has been in advance of every age. Its influ·
ence in mol.ding American thought is manifest in the fact that the wost
original contribution that America has made to Europe is the idea and
practice of religious toleration. Religious liberty is one of the necessary
conditions of man's advance. Without freedom of conscience the mind
must remain in the fetters of superstition and bigotry.
· Freedom of discussion and freedom of individual religious worship
are .necessary to the growth of knowledge and the attainment of the
highest truth. Doubtless religious bigotry is at times found within our
Lodges. But it is contrary to the spirit of Masonry, and has no place
within our portals.
·
Masonry has contributed to human progress by inculcating the prac·
tice of temperance, which it declares to be the first cardinal virtue of a
Mason. In our ritual we are taught to avoid excess and to practice
"that due restraint upon the affections and passions that renders the
body tame and governable and frees the mind from the allurements of
. vice." This virtue is a necessary attribute of every highly developed
character. It is an essential characteristic of the people in every well·
ordered state. Temperance is the subjection of the appetites to the con·
trol of the will.
In a rude and formative state of society this virtue was necessarily
practiced 'by reason of man's situation and condition. In the struggle
for existence, and in overcoming the hardships that accompany the first
establishment of society, men have neither the means nor the opportunity to indulge in excess.
Their environment causes them to develope stern and rugged virtues.
It was the necessities of their situation that developed the stern virtues
of the Puritans of New England, who have left su,ch an indelible impress
upon our National life. With the advance of a nation or an individual

1904.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

1099

in prosperity and wealth, with the consequent relaxation in the struggle
for existence, come the opportunity and the temptation to indulge in
intemperance and excess. It is then that temperance and self-control
must be self-imposed, if a people, or an individu.al, would maintain and
preserve the virtues by which prosperity and advance have been
achieved. Goldsmith has well said that "obscurity and indigence are the
p;..rents of vigilance and. economy; vigilance and economy of riches and
honor; riches and honor of pride and luxury; pride and luxury of im·
purity and idleness; and impurity and idleness again produce indigence
and obscurity."
We are the richest nation of the world. If we are to continue in our
career of National glory and renown, our people must impose upon
themselves that restraint, that temperance and that self-control which
distinguished the characters of the founders of the Republic. In teaching
the necessity and importance of the virtue of temperance Masonry is
doing a signal service to our country and mankind.
My brethren; there is one form of intemperance of which I wisli par·
ticularly to speak. It is the excessive indulgence in s~rong drink, the
intemperance that makes drunkards. The liquor traffic is the greatest
evil in the world to-day. Gladstone said that it destroys more human
bein:gs than famine, war and pestilence combined. It is filling our jails,
our asylums and our penitentiaries with our fellow-men. I~ fills the
world with sorrow and woe and lamentation. This giant evil is com·
bated by the purest women and the noblest men of tlie world. Yet, it is
arrogant and insolent in its attitude, and often defiant of the law. It is
intrenched in politics; it finds respectability and support in our social
customs, and, like a pestilence, it stalks through the land at mid-day.
In the march of progress we have left behind human slavery, polyg·
amy, imprisonment for debt, and many other ·e vils thl!-t degrade mankind. But this terrible evil flourishes and fattens at our very doors.
Are we as citizens and as Masons doing our whole duty in combating
intemperance ?
Lincoln said that our free institutions were framed for the elevation
of man, and that he was opposed to anything that tended tjl degrade
him.
Masonic institutions were framed for the elevation of men. Masonry,
with all its power, is arrayed against this evil. It requires us to declare, before we can enter as · candidates, that we "are influenced by a
sincere desire to be serviceable to our fellow-creatures." It teaches us
that ''we must do to our neighbor as in similar cases we would that he
should do to us." As Master Masons we are charged "to guard our les1
informed brethren against every allur~ment to vicious practices." Ma-

sonry teaches us that temperance is the :first cardinal virtue. And in
the Holy Bible, the great Light in Masonry, "which forever sheds its
benignant rays upon every lawful assemblage of Free and Accepted
Masons," and which is the rule and guide of our faith, we are taught the.
virtue of temperance.
In the second chapter of Habakakuk, in the sacred volume, which
Daniel Webster declared the most powerful language ever written, we
:find this admonition: "Woe unto him who giveth liis neighbor drink;
who putteth the bottle to him and maketh him drunken also."
I am reminded of another passage of Scripture used by the immortal
Lincoln in his Second Inaugural: "Woe unto the world becatise of
offenses, for it must needs be that offenses come, but woe unto him by
whom the offense comes."
While Masonry. thus. makes temperance a sublime virtue, and opposes
intemperance with all its great influence, is not the attitude of Masons
generally such that this is a subject that must be faintly mentioned and
but seldom heard at Masonic gatherings and in Masonic Lodges? Is it
not almost a forbidden subject among the Fraternity? Is it not generally true that a zealous Brother who pleads for this virtue or refers to
this subject brings upon himself derision or dislike? Cannot the profane too often charge that we are faithless to the Masonic teaching that
temperance is a cardinal virtue.
I·ask you, my brethren, to bear with me in all charity and "set down
naught in malice," but when we ask a Brother to the bar to drink, may
we not be helping him to the formation of an appetite that will drag
him down to ruin and blot out the Light of God from his face? Forgive
me when I ask, when we spend money at the bar and help support the
saloon, are we not to that extent responsible for the evil and degradation
these institutions bring to our fellow-men?
While the good and true men, the pure and noble women of the world
are praying, struggling, fighting this awful curse, while the contest is
raging around us, do not we Masons, who of all the world, by our teach·
ings and our vows, are pledged to the cause of temperance, shrink back,
trembling and afraid, when the subject is but mentioned? I am reminded of the words that fell from the lips of the immortal Baker, at
the American Theater, in this city, in October, 1860, in the struggle between freedom and slavery. He said:
''Even where despotism is rife, ideas of personal liberty are thriving.
Even under the shadow of the throne of Russia; on the banks of th"e
Seine, where the ashes of the First Napoleon repose; where the British
Queen in majestic dignity presides over' a nation of freemen--everywhere
abroad, the great ideas of personal liberty spread, increase, fructify.

1101

Here-<>urs is the exception. In this home of the exile, in this land of
constitutional liberty, it is left for us to teach the world that slavery
marches in solemn procession; that under the American stars sl:i.very
is protected, and the name of freedom must be faintly breathed, the
11ongs of freedom fa:i.Iltly sung! Garibaldi, Victor Emmanuel, hosts of
good men are praying, fighting, dying on scaffolds, in dungeons, oftener
yet on battle-fields, for freedom; and yet, while this triumphal proc011·
sion marches unil.er the arches of liberty, we alone shrink back trembling
and afraid when freedom is but faintly mentioned."
To-day there are more men enslaved by the appetite for strong drink
than were ever at one time subject to the master's lash. The struggle
.must go on until the demon of intemperance is driven from the world.
May the day come soon when Masons everywhere and at all times may
proclaim without a blush, without hesitation or misgiving, that temper·
ance is indeed a cardinal virtue practiced by Masons; when Masonry is
a bulwark and a force in the struggle against this mighty evil; when
Masonry is a very present help with those who are struggling to subdue
the appetite for strong drink. May the time come soon when all men
everywhere may have so conquered their pa_ssions as to gain the liberty
that makes men free.
Past Grand Master Henderson, in his address, one year ago, urged
that no drunkards be allowed within our portals. Those were courageous
words. But r pity the poor victim of his appetites. His slavery is a
sufficient punishment. It is the man whose avarice leads him to engage
in a business that makes drunkards against whom I speak. As to such
men, I would shut the door of Masonry, and bolt and double-lock it.
There are many other contributions that Masonry has made to progress, but I must forbear. I mention one, and that is the Masonic teach·
ing of the dignity of labor. God is a la.borer, and every hour of .the day
he is working in his universe, controlling the forces of nature and roll·
ing the planets and the stars in their courses through the boundless
realms of space. Only the man who labors, we are taught as Masons,
can be serviceable to his fellow-creatures.
I have endeavored to show that Masonry is tlie incarnation and the
embodiment of the forces that by divine interposition have operated
· through the ages, and are now operating, for the advancement of mankind towards the final perfect state on earth.
The past is secure. Our institutions have been a potent influence,
and our Lodges have ever been rallying places in the cause of liberty and
moral progress. This we believe they will continue to be. We believe
that in the after ages virtue, truth and justice will adorn the characters
and govern the relations of all men. And when that time comes, may

presented the following reports:To the M . ·• W. •• Grand Lodge oj California:On October 7th, 1903, at Honolulu, Hawaiian Islands, MORRIS MABCH ·
EsTEE, Past Grand Master of this Grand Lodge, passed from earth to the
Great Beyond. On that date he closed hie busy life and joined the Graod
Lodge above. With a consciousness· of duty well discharged and crowned
with honors that come to but few in this life, he fell asleep and entered the
promised rest of the faithful. True and constant to the las~, his blessed
example is worthy of all imitation. Honore never came to him by chance,
for he honestly earned every tribute that was paid to him in the way of pre.
ferment. He died at his poet of duty whither he had gone by appointment
from the President of the Nation to serve as District Judge of the Island
Territory. Hie absence from us to-day fills with sorrow the hearis of the great
Masonic Brotherhood of California.
Bro. ESTEE was born November !lad, 1834, in the township of Freelrol~,
Warren County, Pa. When a child his parents moved to Concord, Erie
County, Pa., where he was raised on a ~arm. He attended the public school,

and afterwards went to the Waterford Academy, in the County and State in
which he lived. He came to California in 1853, and began life as a miner in
Cold Springe, in Ei Dorado County. Later he entered the office of Judge F.
M. PAULING, and b0j!'an the study of law. In· 1859 he was admitted to practice in the Supreme Court1 and opened an office in Sacramento. He was niarried to Miss FRANCES DIVINE on February 2d, 1863, and was elected that
year to the Legislature, and at the close of hie term, was elected District
Attorney of Sacramento County. In 1866 he removed to this city. He was
again elected to the Assembly in 1875, and became Speaker of that body. He
was a member of the New Constitutional Convention. He was twice honored
by his Mrty with the nomination for Governor. He was a Presidential
Elector in 1876 ; and was a delegate to and Permanent Chairman of the
National Republican Convention in 1888. He was a member of the Pan~
American Congress. During his busy life he took time to prepare for publication, three law volumes-" Pleadings, Practice and Forms "-which stand
as monuments to his memory. Bro. ESTEE was made a Mason in 1864 at Sacramento. He afterwarda affiliated with " California" Lodge, No. l, became
its Master, and died a member of that Lodge. He was made a Royal Ar9h
Mason in 1870, in "California" Chapter, No. 5, and created Knight Templar
in 1885. Bro. EsTEE was elected Senior Grand Warden in 1886; was Deputy
Grand Master.in 1887, and Grand Master in 1888 and 1889.
Bro. ESTEE was endowed by nature with more than an ordinary mind1 and
he labored assiduously to multiply the talents with which God had blessed
him. He was ever in the front rank by hie unqoestioned ability, hie inherent tenacity, his indomitable energy, aud acknowledged integrity. He was
always a central figure, for hie upright course commanded respect everywhere.
He was ambitious, perhaps to a fault, but he never had an ambition that was
not a. laudable one. Whatever faults or weaknesses Bro. ESTEE may have
had were completely engulfed by hie grander life and nobler achievements.
His life was an open book ; and he veritably fought the battle of life in t he
open, without helmet or shield. Go on the streets of Napa, where our beloved
brother lived so long, and ask of the men, women and children that you may
meet there, what manner of man Bro. ES'l'EE was, and you will meet with the
unanimous verdict that he was a good and kindly man; imboed with the
spirit of benevolence, with charity for all mankind. That he was a man
unfettered by base and selfish motives. That he was true to all the obligations of life. That, so far as was possible, he made the Golden Rule the guide
of his !l.ctions. That he was patient, tender and gentle ; a 'kind and indulgent
husband and father, and a representative citizen. Such was the Chairman of
your committee's estimate of Bro. EsTEE'S character. It was in the Grand
Lodge that I first learned to know him ; where he was, and had been for
years, active in Masonry, laboring in harmony with STEVENSON and CUR'l'lS,
BBLCHER and PRATT, ABELL and BROWNE, and others who have passed over
the river and are resting under the shade of the t;eee. Here he wrought in
unselfish devotion to the cause which was ever dear to hie heart.

In my boyhood there hwig upon the wall of our sitting-room at home a.
group picture of the church of which my parents were zealous and consistent
mem hers. Often, as we sat around the fireside, I have heard my father dwell
upon their individual characteristics until my boyish admiration was roused
into veneration for those saintly men ·He spoke of one as havi11g wonderful
~ratorical powers ; of another as possessed of unusual executive ability ; of a
third'; remarkable piety; a.nd so on till each received that meed of praise to
which my father deemed him justly entitled. As time went on, one by one
they passed away and others, just as remarkable, perhaps, were chosen in
their stead ; but never could I be brought to feel that the places of those
whom I firHt learned to love and venerate could ever be filled. And so it is
with Bro. ESTEE. I do not wish to disparage those who have succeeded him ;
they have all had their spheres of usefulness, and doubtless occupy affectionate fraternal relations with the later members of the Grand Lodge by
comparison.
During the time that you honored the writer with the distinction of presiding over the Craft of this Grand Jurisdiction, Bro. ESTEE was the Deputy
Grand Master. His courtesy and kindness can never be forgotten. His
readiness to aid at all times, by counsel and advice, serve to strengt~en the
bonds of fraternal love and affection. The memory of his kindly face, his
p:enerous acts and his unselfish motives quicken anew the sorrow occasioned
by his deplorable loss. That Bro. EsTEl!:'S life was a blessing to the community in which he lived, there is no question. His daily example was wholesome, and will live on anrl on. He was an hono'r to the great Fraternity of
Free Masons. He was an honor to his adopted State; he was an honor to
the Nation of which it forms a part. Farewell, dear brother; mem:>ry of thy
pure life and noble deeds will ever be cherished by the Grand Lodge of California.

Bro. HENRY M. OWENS, from the Committee on p:rieve.nces, presented the following reports :-

•

To the M. ·. W.:. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom was referred the petition for.restoration to all
the rights and privileges of Masonry of M. J. SULLIVAN, late a member of
"Crockett" Lodge, No. 139, and expelled by" Oakland" Lodge, No. 188, on
April 1, 1893, have had the same under consideration, and beg leave to report
as follows :It appears that this petition has been in the hands of the Committee on
Grievances for several years without action, principally for the reason that the
Lodge that expelled him had not acted.
Prior to the last Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, "Oakland"
Lodge appointed a committee to thoroughly investigate and report, at the
request of the Committee on Grievances.
The committee so appointed by "Oakland" Lodge, reported to that Lodge
on October 1, 1904, that they were opposed to granting the request, one of
the members of the committee dissenting.

1112

· PROCEEDINGS OF THE

. [Oct. 14,

1904.]

Upon the report of the committee to "Oakland" Lodge, the said Lodge, at
a Stated Meeting held on October I, 1904, voted to sustain the decision of the
committee and :leny the request.

1113

Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. WILLIAM H.
CosB from the action of "Fidelity" Lodge, No. 120, in acquitting Bro. DAN·
JEL WEST WESBENBERG on the charges of unmasonic conduct, have carefully
examined the evidence in the case and report : We find the transcript carefully prepared, and that the Lodge had complete
jurisdiction to try the charges preferred. We are not willing to concur in the
judgment of the Commission. The accused was appealed to as a Ma~on by
the widow of a Master Mason to assist her in selling a house and lot which she
owned in San Francisco. He consented to dt> so. She says she had known
him from boyhood and that he said he would not charge her for his services,
but she would have to pay $2.50 for a power of attorney.
It appears that her husband had deeded her the property in 1883; that she
had placed a homestead upon the property one minute later than the deed of
· gift from her husband, thus necessitating a legal proceeding to determine the
homestead before a sale could be effected. The widow executed a general
power of attorney to the accused and delivered the same to him. Legal proceedings were taken through the accused to terminate the homestead. The
property was sold, as she was informed by the accused, for $3,500 on July 15,

We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption : -

Resolved, That the petit~on of the said M. J. 8ULLIVAN for restoration to
all the rights and privileges of Masonry be and the same is hereby denied.
Your committee, to whom was referred the trial of FRANK RIDGWAY Tonn,
expell~d by "Hartley" Lodge, No. 199, on a charge of having been convicted
of a felony, to-wit, embezzlement, have carefully examined the transcript in
said case and find nothing to sustain the action of the Trial Commissioners
but a letter of a Master Mason purporting to contain a copy of .an entry in a
book kept by a Justice of the Peace, passing sentence of fine on one F. R.
Tonn for mi.demeanor embezzlement. The entry was not certified to be a
copy of a record by its proper custodian, and the entire evidence can have
no .greater weight than is accorded to hearsay.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its ,doption ! Resolved, That the action of " Hartley" Lodge, No. 199, expelling FRANK
RIDGWAY Tonn, be set aside, and that a new trial of the accused be had in
said Lodge in accordance with our laws prescribing the admission of evidence.
Your committee have had produced before them a writing to 11he effect that
at a Stated Meeting of "Downey" ·Lodge, No. 220, held on the 24th day of
September, 1904, due notice having been given to all the members to be present
at that meeting, the following resolution was adopted by a two-third vote:Resolved, That" Downey" Lodge, No. 220, F. & A. M., respectfully petitions
the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of F. &. A. M. of California to restore to
all the rights a~d privileges of Masonry, Mr. HENBY ADISON SooTT, who
was expelled by said "Downey" Lodge l!'ebruary 22, 1902.
Thia writing is signed by the Secretary of the Lodge, with the seal of the
Lodge affixed.
We are not advised by this paper what motives operated upon the Lodge
in its action, and feel it our duty to impress ·Upon Lodges that it is the law
"that a Lodiie within whose jurisdiction an applicant for restoration to the
rights and privileges of Masonry resides, should give its opinion on a petition
for that purpose. The Committee on .Grievances in the Grand Lodge cannot
be cognizant of facts outside of the record, nor of t}le standing of applicants
in the community where they reside."
As the Lodge has requested the restoration, we submit the following resolution and recommend its adoption : Resolved, That the petition of "Downey" Lodge, No. 220, to restore Mr.
HENBY AmaoN SooTT to all the rights and privileges of Masonry be and the
same is hereby approved.

r9oa.

•

From the accused it was learned that he received $3,1150 for the property.
The accused claimed that all over $3,500 so received for the property wa.s to
go to the real estate dealers, presumably those that assisted in the sale. The
clerk ~f the. accused was selected by him for the wido'I\', to make a contract
for the sole of the•property-this clerk being an employee in a drug store.
A sale finally being made upon which $3,500 was reported realized, althoui;ch
$ 3 550 was received. the accused returned to the widow $2,880, with accounts
'
'
aggregating
$620, among
which was included an abstract, $50 ; lawyers ' fees
in connection with terminating homestead, $150; recording, power of attor·
ney, notary fees and legal advice from W. J. DEMARTINI, $35; drawinl( up
new deed, revoking power of attorney, $35; commissions o_n sale, $100; services of accused, $250,
These charges, in view of the understanding had between the widow and
accnsed, appear to us grossly exorbitant, not to express it in a more severe
term. Not satisfied with the actions of the accused, the power of attorney
was revoked, a new attorney employed and a suit against the accused com.
menced upon which the widow obtained a judgment for $358. An attempt to
collect this judgment on execution was avoided by accused, first, by giving as
security stock that was worthless and representing himself as a Mason to the
person having the collection in charge, who was also a Mason, obtaini'!g from
that person time in which to pay the judgment ; and in the meantime, accused
removed, or caused to have removed, everything from the store. Six hundred
and twenty dollars was claimed as expended by the accused in the sale. If
no harsher terms are appropriate, the charges of expense show improvidence
and lack of business tact ; but the discoveries in the testimony as to one item
of expense throw, at least, suspicion on the other parts of the trandactiona.

1114

[Oc~.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

14,

Among the expenses was the making of an abstract of title for which it was
claimed $50 was paid. This abstract was procured by accused from a company represented by one THEOBALD, for which it was claimed $50 was paid,
but in fact only $30 was paid, and the remaining $20 was divided into three
parts between THEOBALD, one KIP, the attorney whom accused had employed
"
for the widow, and one part to accused himself.
While the accused was entitled to reasonable compensation for his services,
we doubt the propriety of making the claim after he had volunte~red to act
without charge, when he had charged $250 for his own services, had paid
what were shown to be exorbitant legal charges and increased liability of
commissions on sale to his clerk, who was not a real estate dealer, but a clerk
in accuser's drug store. The commission was paid to this clerk by accused to
the amount of $140, he receiving a one-third part of $20 on the cost of the
abstract, which had cost $30 and reported by accused as having co_st $50.
Your committee is convinced that the accused was not acting as a - Mason
should act who had accepted the trust from a Mason's widow, and who had
applied to him for assistance.
We therefore dissent from the finding of the Trial Commissioners, and
·
recommend the adoption of the following resolution:

Resolved, That the action of "Fidelity" Lodge, No. 120, acquitting Bro.
DANIEL W . WESSENBERG, be set aside, and that he be expelled from all of
the rights, privileges' and benefits of Masonry.

The following report has been received from Suisun Lodge, No. 55 : To THE MosT 'WORBHJPl'UL GRAND MASTER, OFFICERS AND MEMBERS OF THE
GRAND LoDGE OF FREE AND ACCS:PTS:D MASONS OF CALIJl'ORNIA:GREETING-Suisun Lodg-', No. 55, Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California, begs herewith to offer its report to this Grand Body in
regard to the payment of the debt to Mr. James McCudden and a~y other
debt the said Lodge may have, and then proceed to disincorporate, as requested so to do by this Grand Lodge.
We are pleased to be able at this time to bring before this Grand Lodge
the following report, which we trnst will be in accordance with the wishes of
the said Grand Lodge, and be acceptably received by them.
With and by the valuable assistance rendered us by the committee ap·
pointed by the Grand Lodge in our behalf, " and we would especially mention
the name of Bro. W. Frank Pierce as one o( that committee who came to us
in the spirit of friendship and good will, and he also went to the representatives of Mr. James McCudden, and, by his able arguments to both, " a settlement was made which is satisfactory to both parties.

1903.J

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

63

By the said settlement we have turned over to the heirs our splendid and
magnificent hall and what money we had on hand at the time of making the
eettlement.
And also all other debts have been satisfactorily paid and discharged,
which leaves the corporation entirely free from debt and in a condition to be
di,eincorporated. .
·
Accordingly all lawful steps have been ta.ken as to court proceedings, and
on the 15th day of June, 1903, the said corporation, known as Suisun Lodge,
No. 55, F. & A. M., through its attorney, Bro. Elmore M. Billings, of Benicia,
did present to the Superior Court of the County of Solano, State of California,
a petition asking for permission to dissolve ea.id corporation, in accordance
with the wish of the said Grand Lodge.
A notice was given all the members of the said Suisun Lodge, No. 55,
that at the next stated meeting a resolution would be introduced to disineorporate the said corporation, and requesting their presence at said meeting
to vote upon the question ; the result wa.s a .vote of about thirte1:n-fourteenths
of the membership in favor and not one vote against the proposition.
Therefore, in conformity to said resolution, and from the fact that due
potice of the time set for the hearing of the same and no opposition having
been filed, the Court did, on the said 15th day of June, make and enter its
decree, dissolving the said corporation, known as Suisun Lodge. No. 55,
F. and A. M., which, as we now think and wish, places the said Suisun
Lodge, No. 55, Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California, in
favor of the said Grand Lodge of the State of California, so far as we are
able so to do.
All of the foregoing is respectfully submitted to your kind consideration
and approval by the said Suisun Lodge, No. 55, F ree and Accepted Masons
of the State of California.
JAS. H. PRATHER,
Worshipful Master.
The above report was adopted by the Lodge at the stated meeting of
August 8th, 1903, in its entirety, and ordered to be forwarded to the Grand
Lodge of the State of California.
In witneBB whereof, I hereunto set my hand and the seal ·of the Lodge,
this 8th day of Au~s.t, 1903.
